title: China is a predator; The China challenge Détente with beijing should be out oh the question
body:
It should be obvious by now that the world order that has sustained prosperity in the northern hemisphere in a 
mostly uninterrupted epoch of peace over the past 80 years is dramatically unravelling. It just might take a while yet 
before we can definitively pinpoint the moment or the event that caused everything to finally fall apart.
Russia's capture of Ukraine's Donbas and its annexation of Crimea in 2014, and the Kremlin's savage full-on war of 
conquest beginning in 2022, will be surely understood as major milestones in the paralysis of the elites in what we 
used to call the free world. U.S. President Donald Trump's capitulation to Moscow by way of his envoy Steve 
Witkoff's terms of Ukrainian surrender to Vladimir Putin in just the past few days will be surely understood, in 
hindsight, as a pivotal moment.
If the admission of the People's Republic of China into the World Trade Organization in December 2001 marked the 
old global order's point of Ono return, several events over the past few weeks stand out as harbingers of the 
emerging new world order of Xi Jinping's "community of the common destiny of humankind," as it expands ever 
outward from its military-industrial epicentre in Beijing.
Beijing's most brazen incursions into the world's shrinking democratic spaces are occurring in small ways and in 
leaps and bounds. They're occurring in such rapid succession that half the time they're barely noticed.
In Kazakhstan, 16 members of the Atajurt Kazakh Human Rights organization along with several first-hand 
observers of Beijing's concentration camps in Xinjiang were picked up off the street the other day in Almaty. At 
Shanghai Airport, an Indian national was detained and abused for 18 hours by Chinese immigration officials who 
deemed her passport invalid because her birthplace was shown as the Indian state of Arunachal Pradesh, which 
Beijing now insists is Chinese territory.
On Nov. 18, Britain's MI5 security agency warned the speakers of the House of Commons and the House of Lords 
that spies from China's Ministry of State Security, posing as corporate recruiters, were targeting parliamentarians to 
"conduct outreach at scale" in a co-ordinated influence-peddling operation. Canadians should be intimately 
familiar with clandestine foreign-influence operations of this kind, which Ottawa solemnly pledged to address with a 
foreign-agents registry that is either inexplicably dead or is mysteriously stalled.
In the latest of a rapidly growing number of alarms about Beijing's ability to disrupt, commandeer and otherwise 
weaponize infrastructure in the NATO countries, Danish transportation authorities have discovered that their fleets 
Page 2 of 4
China is a predator; The China challenge Détente with beijing should be out oh the question
of buses, manufactured in Zhengzhou, have been fitted with software that allows the fleet to be shut down remotely 
from China. Norway has discovered similar "kill switches" in its Chinese-made buses, and the United Kingdom is 
now investigating vulnerabilities in the Chinese buses on British streets.
While the G7 countries have spent several years warning the "developing world" to be wary of Beijing's Belt and 
Road debt traps, last week the AidData research lab discovered a Chinese "shadow portfolio" operating in the 
NATO countries that holds the debt on critical infrastructure projects from airports to electricity transmission lines. 
Beijing is now the world's largest official creditor.
Over the past two weeks, a succession of Chinese diplomats and senior Communist Party officials have declared 
that the "witch" Sanae Takaichi, Japan's prime minister, should be beheaded, or have her throat slit, depending on 
the translation. In a surprise attack on Japan's tourism industry, several Chinese airlines cancelled flights to Japan 
and offered travellers free cancellations for flights booked to the country. Departure data suggests about 500,000 
Chinese passenger reservations on flights to Japan were cancelled over a two-day period.
Beijing's pretext was Prime Minister Takaichi's notice to Japanese lawmakers that China's long-threatened 
invasion and annexation of Taiwan would have to be understood as an "existential threat" that would place Japan's 
military on high alert.
In recent testimony to the U.S. Congress, Admiral Samuel Paparo, commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, said 
China's tripling of military sorties around Taiwan over the past four years should be understood as "not just 
exercises - they are dress rehearsals" in line with President Xi's intention to have the People's Liberation Army fully 
capable of seizing Taiwan by 2027. Last week, Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te announced a special $US40-
billion budget for new weapons and a "Taiwan dome" air defence system with advanced detection and interception 
capabilities, on top of a pledge to boost Taiwan's military budget to five per cent of GDP.
"China's threats to Taiwan and the Indo-Pacific region are escalating," President Lai said, referring to the rise in 
Beijing's sophisticated greyzone sabotage and disinformation operations targeting several countries around the 
South China Sea, including Vietnam and the Philippines. According to U.S. intelligence assessments, the Chinese 
military's rapid expansion in troop strength, sea power, space-based weaponry, cyber-war technology, nuclear 
capability and precision-attack ballistic and cruise missiles have put the entire Western Pacific within striking 
distance of the People's Liberation Army. Last week, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's "Icebreaker" 
report noted that "unprecedented" numbers of Chinese military and research vessels have been observed in the 
Arctic. The report echoed the remarks from a few days earlier by Dan Rodgers, the new head of the Canadian 
Security Intelligence Service. Chinese and Russian activity in the polar seas is on the upswing. "It is not a surprise 
that CSIS has observed both cyber and non-cyber intelligence collection efforts targeting both governments and the 
private sector in the region," Rodgers said.
This brings us to Canada's exceptionally disorienting predicament in the matter of the Chinese Communist Party's 
intentions by stealth and by design to form the nucleus of a new global order - a long game that shifted into 
hyperdrive with Xi Jinping's ascendancy to the pinnacle of the party's ruling politburo in 2013. For 39 of the past 60 
years, Canada has been governed by a Liberal party that has tended to champion China's cause on "the world 
stage" while sheltering under the umbrella of Norad and Canada-U.S. trading partnerships.
We wanted to have it both ways, and after an interregnum forced on Ottawa by Beijing's kidnapping of Michael 
Kovrig and Michael Spavor in 2021, and by a series of shocking revelations exposing the Liberal party's determined 
inattention to Beijing's efforts in monkeywrenching the 2019 and 2021 federal elections to the Liberals' advantage, 
it's as though Canada is back in the old groove again.
In light of the belligerence and acts of continental-trade vandalism commit- ted by U.S. President Donald Trump, it's 
still a fool's errand to imagine that there are trade opportunities in China foreclosed by the lost opportunities for free 
trade with the United States. The best of both worlds may be off the table, but it isn't even clear whether Trump 
places a higher value on Beijing's purchases of American soybeans than Taiwanese sovereignty, or Ukrainian 
sovereignty, or whatever entanglements Canada might entertain in China.
Page 3 of 4
China is a predator; The China challenge Détente with beijing should be out oh the question
While he was vice-chairman of Brookfield Asset Management, Prime Minister Mark Carney developed intimate ties 
at the most senior levels of the Chinese Communist Party, and his government's approach is not simply to turn the 
page but to close the chapter on the reasons behind Canada's post-2021 diplomatic estrangement from China 
altogether. The new Beijing-Ottawa "strategic partnership" appears to consist mostly of an agreement by the 
Canadian side to avoid entirely such "irritants" as Beijing's brutal capture of Hong Kong, its vicious repressions in 
Xinjiang and Tibet, its vast strong-armed networks in Canada, its warmongering designs on Taiwan, its piracy in the 
South China Sea, and So on.
For a properly-informed perspective on these disorienting times, Canadians have the advantage of two new books 
that provide both a broad view and a more close up view of the ongoing events that are shaping the confounding 
political and economic terrain where we've all suddenly found ourselves.
Charles Burton's The Beaver and The Dragon (Optimum Publishing International) offers the wealth of Burton's 
lifetime of experience, from his days as a student at Fudan University and his study of Chinese language texts on 
Confucianism to his days as a diplomat in Beijing and a mainstream essayist, observer and trusty guide through 
Beijing's vast influence operations in Canada. The book's subtitle, How China Out-Manoeuvered Canada's 
Diplomacy, Security and Sovereignty, should give you something of an idea about the book's overall point.
Similarly, Dennis Molinaro's Under Assault: Interference and Espionage in China's Secret War Against Canada 
(Random House Canada) tells you what you need to know about the book's focus in the title. Molinaro, an 
academic, is necessarily rather opaque about his recent line of work, having served as an analyst for a federal 
agency in the national security sphere. He's currently teaching Canadian foreign policy and the history of 
intelligence-gathering at Ontario Tech University.
Burton's book is mostly an anthology of sorts, compiling various opinion pieces and analyses he's written over the 
years, and there's value in a book like this be- cause it reads almost like a diary, a chronicle of Beijing's deceptions 
and Canada's subversion by the Chinese Communist Party. Molinaro pays closer attention to the trajectory of 
Beijing's subterfuge through the Justin Trudeau years, going back to the doors thrown open to Beijing by his father, 
Pierre Elliott Trudeau.
If there's a big message Molinaro hopes Canadians will take away from his book it's that there is a deep disconnect 
between Canada's foreign-policy establishment and ordinary Canadians, and the differences are about values. 
"We have to get on the same page," Molinaro told me. "You can trade with China, but we have to recognize China 
for what it is, and not what we hope or want it to be."
What China is: a predator and an enemy of democracy. Canadians should take a furiously dim view of Beijing's 
friends and influencers in Canada, Molinaro says.
It's been 18 months since Parliament passed the Foreign Influence Transparency and Accountability Act, which 
was actively opposed by Beijing's Mandarin-bloc United Front Work Department networks in Canada. There is still 
Ono publicly accessible registry of agents acting on behalf of foreign states. There is still Ono independent foreign 
influence transparency commissioner. All Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree has said on the subject is 
that a "process" is still underway to get the initiative off the ground.
As for Burton's message, it's pretty straightforward. The history of Canada-China relations is a story of Canadian 
governments being led down garden paths, lured by false "win-win" promises that even if they were fulfilled would 
only benefit a small minority of Canadian corporations. After all our efforts over the years, only about eight per cent 
of our exports end up in Chinese markets.
Staying within Beijing's "red lines" is a mug's game, too. "Putting a sock in our own mouths is not going to do us any 
particular good. It hasn't in the past. We will not be rewarded for it. It will just make us look weak.
"The idea that China will be in control of all under heaven, and that Canada will be a subsidiary that feeds the 
Chinese dragon with natural resources and in return we'll get Chinese high tech, like self-driving taxis or whatever - 
it's silly" The prospects aren't all necessarily dreary, however. Beijing's accelerated surveillance-state exertions 
Page 4 of 4
China is a predator; The China challenge Détente with beijing should be out oh the question
reflect the regime's fear of the Chinese people. "I think better days are ahead," Burton said. There's a growing 
cohort of young people in China that finds nothing inspiring in President Xi, his despotism or his ideas about China 
ascending to the apex of global power and wealth.
"I don't think Xi Jinping's regime will last forever," Burton said. "A lot of people disagree with me on this point, but I 
see a lot of potential for China one day becoming a responsible nation in global affairs."

it's as though Canada is back in the old groove again.
In light of the belligerence and acts of continental-trade vandalism commit- ted by U.S. President Donald Trump, it's 
still a fool's errand to imagine that there are trade opportunities in China foreclosed by the lost opportunities for free 
trade with the United States. The best of both worlds may be off the table, but it isn't even clear whether Trump 
places a higher value on Beijing's purchases of American soybeans than Taiwanese sovereignty, or Ukrainian 
sovereignty, or whatever entanglements Canada might entertain in China.

While he was vice-chairman of Brookfield Asset Management, Prime Minister Mark Carney developed intimate ties 
at the most senior levels of the Chinese Communist Party, and his government's approach is not simply to turn the 
page but to close the chapter on the reasons behind Canada's post-2021 diplomatic estrangement from China 
altogether. The new Beijing-Ottawa "strategic partnership" appears to consist mostly of an agreement by the 
Canadian side to avoid entirely such "irritants" as Beijing's brutal capture of Hong Kong, its vicious repressions in 
Xinjiang and Tibet, its vast strong-armed networks in Canada, its warmongering designs on Taiwan, its piracy in the 
South China Sea, and So on.
For a properly-informed perspective on these disorienting times, Canadians have the advantage of two new books 
that provide both a broad view and a more close up view of the ongoing events that are shaping the confounding 
political and economic terrain where we've all suddenly found ourselves.
Charles Burton's The Beaver and The Dragon (Optimum Publishing International) offers the wealth of Burton's 
lifetime of experience, from his days as a student at Fudan University and his study of Chinese language texts on 
Confucianism to his days as a diplomat in Beijing and a mainstream essayist, observer and trusty guide through 
Beijing's vast influence operations in Canada. The book's subtitle, How China Out-Manoeuvered Canada's 
Diplomacy, Security and Sovereignty, should give you something of an idea about the book's overall point.
Similarly, Dennis Molinaro's Under Assault: Interference and Espionage in China's Secret War Against Canada 
(Random House Canada) tells you what you need to know about the book's focus in the title. Molinaro, an 
academic, is necessarily rather opaque about his recent line of work, having served as an analyst for a federal 
agency in the national security sphere. He's currently teaching Canadian foreign policy and the history of 
intelligence-gathering at Ontario Tech University.
Burton's book is mostly an anthology of sorts, compiling various opinion pieces and analyses he's written over the 
years, and there's value in a book like this be- cause it reads almost like a diary, a chronicle of Beijing's deceptions 
and Canada's subversion by the Chinese Communist Party. Molinaro pays closer attention to the trajectory of 
Beijing's subterfuge through the Justin Trudeau years, going back to the doors thrown open to Beijing by his father, 
Pierre Elliott Trudeau.
If there's a big message Molinaro hopes Canadians will take away from his book it's that there is a deep disconnect 
between Canada's foreign-policy establishment and ordinary Canadians, and the differences are about values. 
"We have to get on the same page," Molinaro told me. "You can trade with China, but we have to recognize China 
for what it is, and not what we hope or want it to be."
What China is: a predator and an enemy of democracy. Canadians should take a furiously dim view of Beijing's 
friends and influencers in Canada, Molinaro says.
It's been 18 months since Parliament passed the Foreign Influence Transparency and Accountability Act, which 
was actively opposed by Beijing's Mandarin-bloc United Front Work Department networks in Canada. There is still 
Ono publicly accessible registry of agents acting on behalf of foreign states. There is still Ono independent foreign 
influence transparency commissioner. All Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree has said on the subject is 
that a "process" is still underway to get the initiative off the ground.
As for Burton's message, it's pretty straightforward. The history of Canada-China relations is a story of Canadian 
governments being led down garden paths, lured by false "win-win" promises that even if they were fulfilled would 
only benefit a small minority of Canadian corporations. After all our efforts over the years, only about eight per cent 
of our exports end up in Chinese markets.
Staying within Beijing's "red lines" is a mug's game, too. "Putting a sock in our own mouths is not going to do us any 
particular good. It hasn't in the past. We will not be rewarded for it. It will just make us look weak.
"The idea that China will be in control of all under heaven, and that Canada will be a subsidiary that feeds the 
Chinese dragon with natural resources and in return we'll get Chinese high tech, like self-driving taxis or whatever - 
it's silly" The prospects aren't all necessarily dreary, however. Beijing's accelerated surveillance-state exertions

reflect the regime's fear of the Chinese people. "I think better days are ahead," Burton said. There's a growing

title: Christopher Skeete won't seek CAQ leadership, other candidates testing the waters
body:
QUEBEC - Christopher Skeete will not be in the race to replace François Legault( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/west-island-gazette/from-milkman-to-quebec-premier-francois-
legaults-rise-to-power ) as the leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec.
After leaving the door open last week to a possible run, Skeete, who is minister of international relations in the 
government, said on social media it was not going to happen.
"I want to clarify my intentions regarding the leadership race," Skeete wrote. "After careful consideration, I have 
decided to not be a candidate for the leadership of the Coalition Avenir Québec.
"I will continue to work actively on the promotion of Quebec's interests on the international scene, for those of 
Quebec's and that of Laval in an uncertain world context which will have more and more impacts on our daily lives.
"Quebec, like all of the Western world, is going through a pivotal time. The decisions we take today will have a 
durable impact on our quality of life and that of our children."
Skeete's name was on the long list of potential candidates to replace Premier François Legault, who announced 
Wednesday he is stepping down( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/premier-legault-steps-down-
with-no-obvious-successor-in-the-wings ) for the good of the party and of Quebec.
Skeete was first elected as the MNA for the Laval riding of Sainte-Rose in 2018. Besides international relations, 
Skeete is minister responsible for relations with English-speaking Quebecers( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/caq-quebec-anglophones-grievances-christopher-skeete ), the 
fight against racism and the region of Laval.
It did not take some of Legault's ministers long to start testing the waters( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/list-of-potential-legault-replacements-grows-to-10-party-starts-
leadership-process ) on a possible run after Legault's announcement. Making the move first was Economic and 
Energy Minister Christine Fréchette, who told reporters she was in reflection on a run for the job.
Not wanting to be out of country for the launch of the leadership race, Fréchette on Friday cancelled her presence 
next week at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland. Skeete will be replacing her on that trip, officials 
said Saturday.
Page 2 of 4
Christopher Skeete won't seek CAQ leadership, other candidates testing the waters
There have also been reports Fréchette will soon step down from her ministerial duties because it seems pretty 
clear the leadership race rules will not allow a minister to campaign at the same time.
Last week, Quebec's ethics commissioner, Ariane Mignolet, filed an advisory that said there is a risk of a conflict 
of interest if a minister is also candidate for the leadership.
Legault might be tempted to replace her with Finance Minister Eric Girard,( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/im-not-a-lobbyist-for-quebec-anglophones-eric-girard-says ) who now 
appears to be learning toward not running for the leadership because he would not be able to stay minister and 
present the government's eighth budget this spring.
Fréchette has already picked up the support of two other ministers, Gilles Bélanger, minister for cybersecurity and 
digital technology, and Mathieu Lacombe, minister of culture and communications.
But Justice Minister Simon Jolin-Barrette's name is also on the list of potential candidates and getting busy. On 
Thursday, two MNAs, Mario Asselin and Shirley Dorismond, endorsed him.
On Saturday, Transport Minister Jonatan Julien also went public, throwing his support to Jolin-Barrette. "If he 
decides to run, he will have my support," Julien wrote on Facebook.
Jolin-Barrette has been discreet, but did issue a message Friday on social media thanking people who see him as 
the next leader and saying the CAQ can be proud of its achievements.
"The departure of Mr. Legault, a great man of state, leaves a void in the caquiste family," Jolin-Barrette said, noting 
what the government has done for the economy and on identity issues.
"We should be proud of our accomplishments and redouble our efforts in the face of criticism. Ten months remain in 
our mandate and Quebecers want a government which works without stop to improve things in all the regions of 
Quebec. I am convinced we have all the talent and willingness to get there."
Many in the party are waiting to see what other potential candidates decide. That includes Education Minister 
Sonia LeBel, Municipal Affairs Minister Geneviève Guilbault and Environment Minister Bernard Drainville.
It's unclear Guilbault will be able to run. The Gallant commission into the SAAQclic fisaco( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/explainer-public-inquiry-begins-in-saaqclic-scandal ), where she testified, last 
week issued her a pre-advisory note of poor conduct,( 
https://www.ledevoir.com/politique/quebec/948522/genevieve-guilbault-membres-cabinet-vises-avis-mauvaise-
conduite?utm_source=recirculation&;utm_medium=hyperlien&;utm_campaign=corps_texte ) meaning she could 
shoulder some of the blame for the cost overruns.
On Friday, one of the few outsiders to have examined the idea of running, businessman Olivier Primeau( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/a-poutine-influencer-as-premier-olivier-primeau-rules-out-a-
run-to-succeed-legault ), said he would not seek the leadership.
On Saturday, Public Security Minister Ian Lafrenière repeated to reporters in Montreal that he's still interested but 
thinking it over.
Whoever wins will have to find a way to improve the government's image, plus reconcile the clans( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/change-is-in-the-political-air-in-quebec-as-election-looms ) 
within the party made up of people who see the party as more of an economic party and others who think 
aggressive nationalism is the ticket to woo voters.
The CAQ's political bread and butter has been the so-called "third way," which means being neither federalist or 
sovereignist. On Friday, Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon( 
Page 3 of 4

https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/parti-quebecois-pspp-legault-resignation-reaction ) said that 
option has been a "total failure."
Fréchette and Jolin-Barrette are very different people. Fréchette took over as the government's "super minister," 
after the resignation of Pierre Fitzgibbon. She is the former president of the Chambre de commerce de l'Est de 
Montréal.
Unlike Jolin-Barrette, who steered most of the government's language and identity projects, Fréchette, quit her job 
as associate chief of staff to former PQ leader Jean-François Lisée in 2014 when the PQ cooked up its charter of 
values plan.
Jolin-Barrette, a lawyer and son of a police officer, is seen as the keeper of the CAQ's third way vision and is known 
for being a very efficient minister, often handed the tough jobs by Legault. He was first elected in 2014.
He is better known by the party rank and file than Fréchette who did not join the CAQ until 2022. She is, however, 
more of a people person than Jolin-Barrette and might appeal to voters.
Jolin-Barrette is saddled with the government's very unpopular constitution project which has been met with 
widespread criticism( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/authoritarian-or-essential-quebec-
constitution-hearings-start-today ). The father of two young children, he has to consider his family's needs as well in 
his decision-making process.
The CAQ is to decide on the rules of the leadership race sometime next week. It is taking place at the same as the 
Quebec Liberals are looking for a new leader.
On Saturday, candidate Charles Milliard launched his campaign surrounded by supporters in Yamachiche.

Title: Christopher Skeete won't seek CAQ leadership, other candidates testing the waters

Body: QUEBEC - Christopher Skeete will not be in the race to replace François Legault( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/west-island-gazette/from-milkman-to-quebec-premier-francois-
legaults-rise-to-power ) as the leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec.
After leaving the door open last week to a possible run, Skeete, who is minister of international relations in the 
government, said on social media it was not going to happen.
"I want to clarify my intentions regarding the leadership race," Skeete wrote. "After careful consideration, I have 
decided to not be a candidate for the leadership of the Coalition Avenir Québec.
"I will continue to work actively on the promotion of Quebec's interests on the international scene, for those of 
Quebec's and that of Laval in an uncertain world context which will have more and more impacts on our daily lives.
"Quebec, like all of the Western world, is going through a pivotal time. The decisions we take today will have a 
durable impact on our quality of life and that of our children."
Skeete's name was on the long list of potential candidates to replace Premier François Legault, who announced 
Wednesday he is stepping down( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/premier-legault-steps-down-
with-no-obvious-successor-in-the-wings ) for the good of the party and of Quebec.
Skeete was first elected as the MNA for the Laval riding of Sainte-Rose in 2018. Besides international relations, 
Skeete is minister responsible for relations with English-speaking Quebecers( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/caq-quebec-anglophones-grievances-christopher-skeete ), the 
fight against racism and the region of Laval.
It did not take some of Legault's ministers long to start testing the waters( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/list-of-potential-legault-replacements-grows-to-10-party-starts-
leadership-process ) on a possible run after Legault's announcement. Making the move first was Economic and 
Energy Minister Christine Fréchette, who told reporters she was in reflection on a run for the job.
Not wanting to be out of country for the launch of the leadership race, Fréchette on Friday cancelled her presence 
next week at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland. Skeete will be replacing her on that trip, officials 
said Saturday.
Page 2 of 4
Christopher Skeete won't seek CAQ leadership, other candidates testing the waters
There have also been reports Fréchette will soon step down from her ministerial duties because it seems pretty 
clear the leadership race rules will not allow a minister to campaign at the same time.
Last week, Quebec's ethics commissioner, Ariane Mignolet, filed an advisory that said there is a risk of a conflict 
of interest if a minister is also candidate for the leadership.
Legault might be tempted to replace her with Finance Minister Eric Girard,( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/im-not-a-lobbyist-for-quebec-anglophones-eric-girard-says ) who now 
appears to be learning toward not running for the leadership because he would not be able to stay minister and 
present the government's eighth budget this spring.
Fréchette has already picked up the support of two other ministers, Gilles Bélanger, minister for cybersecurity and 
digital technology, and Mathieu Lacombe, minister of culture and communications.
But Justice Minister Simon Jolin-Barrette's name is also on the list of potential candidates. On Thursday, two 
MNAs, Mario Asselin and Shirley Dorismond, said they favour Jolin-Barrette.
On Saturday, Transport Minister Jonatan Julien also went public, throwing his support to Jolin-Barrette. "If he 
decides to run, he will have my support," Julien wrote on Facebook.
Jolin-Barrette has been discreet, but did issue a message Friday on social media thanking people who see him as 
the next leader and saying the CAQ can be proud of its achievements.
"The departure of Mr. Legault, a great man of state, leaves a void in the caquiste family," Jolin-Barrette said, noting 
what the government has done for the economy and on identity issues.
"We should be proud of our accomplishments and redouble our efforts in the face of criticism. Ten months remain in 
our mandate and Quebecers want a government which works without stop to improve things in all the regions of 
Quebec. I am convinced we have all the talent and willingness to get there."
Many in the party are waiting to see what other potential candidates decide. That includes Education Minister 
Sonia LeBel, Municipal Affairs Minister Geneviève Guilbault and Environment Minister Bernard Drainville.
It's unclear Guilbault will be able to run. The Gallant commission into the SAAQclic fisaco( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/explainer-public-inquiry-begins-in-saaqclic-scandal ), where she testified, last 
week issued her a pre-advisory note of poor conduct,( 
https://www.ledevoir.com/politique/quebec/948522/genevieve-guilbault-membres-cabinet-vises-avis-mauvaise-
conduite?utm_source=recirculation&;utm_medium=hyperlien&;utm_campaign=corps_texte ) meaning she could 
shoulder some of the blame for the cost overruns.
On Friday, one of the few outsiders to have examined the idea of running, businessman Olivier Primeau( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/a-poutine-influencer-as-premier-olivier-primeau-rules-out-a-
run-to-succeed-legault ), said he would not seek the leadership.
Whoever wins will have to find a way to improve the government's image, plus reconcile the clans( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/change-is-in-the-political-air-in-quebec-as-election-looms ) 
within the party made up of federalists and nationalists, some more to the right and some more to the left, members 
keen on identity issues and those more interested in economic questions.
The CAQ's political bread and butter has been the so-called "third way," which means being neither federalist or 
sovereignist. On Friday, Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/parti-quebecois-pspp-legault-resignation-reaction ) said that 
option has been a "total failure."
Page 3 of 4
Christopher Skeete won't seek CAQ leadership, other candidates testing the waters
The CAQ is to decide on the rules of the leadership race sometime next week. It is taking place at the same as the 
Quebec Liberals are looking for a new leader.
On Saturday, candidate Charles Milliard launched his campaign surrounded by supporters in Yamachiche.

title: Chrétien passing up chance to talk about himself raises eyebrows
body:
There are certain phrases that properly arouse immediate suspicion. "The dog did it," for example. "Trump 
apologizes." Or, "Jean Chrétien declines to talk about himself." The latter is in play because the former Liberal 
prime minister has declined to appear before a parliamentary committee to discuss certain rather unsavoury 
directives he might have given his immigration minister in 1995 with an eye to winning the Quebec independence 
referendum.
Teflon Jean loves to talk about himself and his genius the way most of us love breathing, which is to say it's 
essentially an involu -n tary function. He doesn't even need to think about it. And in the past that has certainly 
included matters pertaining to very nearly losing that referendum campaign, and subsequent efforts - known 
collectively as the Liberal Sponsorship Scandal - ostensibly designed to prevent it from happening again.
But Chrétien doesn't seem to want to engage with a remarkably casual recent admission by Sergio Marchi, who 
was immigration minister in the lead-up to the referendum. In an interview with the Journal de Montréal, Marchi 
admitted that Chrétien had pressured him into mass-naturalizing as many new citizens in Quebec as quickly as 
possible, on the reasonable assumption the majority of them would vote No.
"I remember Jean telling me, 'Listen, I know we have a backlog of citizenship applications, but do your best to move 
them along because the referendum is coming up and people want to vote'," Marchi told the Journal.
"Working nights and weekends" in the month of October 1995, the paper reported, Ottawa bureau- crats naturalized 
25 per cent of the people they did the entire year - roughly 11,500 new Canadians. And as soon as the referendum 
was over, wouldn't you know it, the overtime hours mysteriously dried up.
"Did it make a difference? Yes. Was it in Canada's favour? Yes," Marchi said. "To what extent? I have no idea. I 
don't think anyone can really know."
Marchi has also refused Parliament's invitation to appear before committee, despite his candour to the Journal's 
reporter, despite ha -v ing a new book to flog, and despite facing no peril: committee meetings are privileged; he's 
almost 70; his pension could sink a ship; he's not from Quebec; and, without wishing to seem unkind, nobody really 
knows who he is. In 1996, while still in government, Marchi argued that federal Liberal communications director 
Aurèle Gervais should wear illegal campaign-spending charges against him, with respect to the referendum, "like a 
badge of honour." Thirty years later, he has nothing to say publicly about all this - presumably in its defence?
Page 2 of 3
Chrétien passing up chance to talk about himself raises eyebrows
For the record, the No side's margin of victory was 54,388 votes (out of 4.8 million cast). So this mass-minting of 
new citizens certainly didn't turn things on its own. Combined with roughly $539,000 in illegal No-campaign 
spending uncovered by retired judge Bernard Grenier in a 2007 report, however, it's not unreasonable to imagine 
that federalist skulduggery could have changed the outcome. (We'll leave broadly similar allegations of separatist 
skulduggery aside for now.)
The difference it made isn't really the point, though. The punishment for electoral fraud doesn't hinge on whether it 
was successful, except in countries where the winners of elections (if any) control the police and prosecutors. Until 
relatively recently, many Canadians rightly viewed our immigration system as something to be proud of.
Accelerating citizenship ceremonies isn't the end of the world; comprehensively screwing up Canadian immigration 
fell to Justin Trudeau and his hapless immigration ministers, two of whom amazingly enough continue to haunt 
Mark Carney's cabinet room. And Canadian immigration policy has always been set with the ballot box at least in 
the back of mind.
"All's fair in love and war," I imagine Chrétien saying, were he buttonholed on this.
But what were he and Marchi so afraid of? It's a question that too rarely gets asked, and into which they might 
provide valuable insight.
The referendum question was ludicrous. It's difficult to believe a 50 per cent-plus-one Yes vote on that question 
would have roused the international community to recognize an independent Quebec. France had suggested it 
might, but if push had ever come to shove I really have to wonder if then French president Jacques Chirac would 
have emboldened his own country's separatist movements to placate a bunch of people who live in the French 
imagination paddling canoes and wearing beaver pelts.
It's certainly forgivable if Chrétien and Marchi were panicked about the referendum. A lot of people were panicked. I 
was one of them. Canadians might be inclined to forgive their transgressions, so long as they admitted they were in 
fact transgressions.
So what are they so afraid of now? Or would they just rather not bother testifying, a Commons committee often 
being a poor venue for self-aggrandizement?

title: Citing family reasons, CAQ 's Geneviève Guilbault will leave office at the end of her term
body:
QUEBEC - Geneviève Guilbault is leaving political life at the end of her term and will not attempt to succeed 
Premier François Legault.
Just days after Legault announced he is stepping down( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/premier-legault-steps-down-with-no-obvious-successor-in-the-
wings ) once the Coalition Avenir Québec finds a replacement for him as leader, CAQ minister Guilbault 
announced Sunday she, too, is dropping out of politics.
"It's a beautiful day for me today - a day I have been waiting for a long time," said Guilbault, confirming her decision 
at a news conference in her home riding of Louis-Hébert in the Quebec City region.
The minister of municipal affairs, Guilbault, 43, invoked family reasons. She was accompanied by her two children, 
Capucine, 8, and Christophe, 6, both born while she was in office. They arrived in their snowsuits holding their 
mom's hand.
"For eight years, I gave it all for politics," Guilbault said. "I worked seven days out of seven. It's a personal decision, 
a family decision that is the best for us because the most important thing (in life) is to be happy."
She said committing herself to run again would possibly mean another four years when she would not be fully 
available to watch her children grow.
"I have often said that I am not scared of much in life, but I do fear regret," Guilbault said in an emotional moment. 
"And for me it's clear that if I continued in politics for four more years, I would probably regret missing the childhood 
of my children because I was busy elsewhere for all these precious years."
Guilbault insisted her decision had nothing to do with Legault's resignation or the CAQ's low standing in the polls( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/caq-legault-support-low-january-2026-poll ). She said her 
decision to leave was made long ago.
"I am not closing the door to politics forever," she said. "As people say, the future is long, but today I need for my 
children and parents to come first."
Page 2 of 4
Citing family reasons, CAQ 's Geneviève Guilbault will leave office at the end of her term
She said she went into politics not only to change Quebec for the better, but also to advance the cause of women 
in politics. She said in her time in office, many women have told her they saw her as a trailblazer, even if the job 
was no bed of roses.
"Doing politics is living with falsehoods, insults and abundant and numerous critics," she said. "But if the relentless 
media is the price to pay for moving big issues forward, to put oneself at risk to advance Quebec, I would do it all 
again tomorrow morning."
Quebec Municipal Affairs Minister Geneviève Guilbault holds her son Christophe and walks with daughter 
Capucine after she announced she will not run in the coming election at a news conference in St-Augustin-de-
Desmaures on Sunday, January 18, 2026.
Guilbault's announcement took the political class by surprise.
Among the first to react was Legault, who praised Guilbault for her devotion to Quebec.
"Thank you Geneviève Guilbault for your commitment, energy, work on the ground and confidence," Legault wrote 
on social media. "Bravo for all the changes you made, including improving the safety of women and life in our 
beautiful national capital.
"I understand the need to spend more time with your children."
Justice Minister Simon Jolin-Barrette, himself touted as a possible candidate to replace Legault, posted a message 
saying he learned with regret that Guilbault was leaving.
He noted he and Guilbault have worked together in recent years in the fight against sexual and domestic violence.
"I want to salute her commitment to public service, to women and more widely to Quebecers," Jolin-Barrette said.
Conservative Party of Quebec Leader Éric Duhaime had a different take, saying Guilbault's decision came as a 
"thunderclap" on the political scene.
"Nobody incarnates the rise and fall of the CAQ better than Mme Guilbault," he wrote on X.
Considered one of the CAQ's stars in earlier days, Guilbault's name was mentioned on lists of potential candidates( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec/christopher-skeete-wont-seek-caq-leadership-other-candidates-testing-
the-waters ) to replace Legault.
But in her previous post as transport minister, Guilbault's name also came up in connection with cost overruns in 
the SAAQclic fiasco( https://montrealgazette.com/news/explainer-public-inquiry-begins-in-saaqclic-scandal ). Even 
though she became transport minister after the Société de l'assurance automobile du Québec's digital 
modernization project was conceived, she had to manage the chaos that followed the launch.
Last week, Guilbault and members of her former Transport Ministry team received advance notice that they would 
be blamed for "poor conduct" by the Gallant Commission, which is looking into SAAQclic.
At the commission, Guilbault had to answer questions about documents( https://montrealgazette.com/news/after-
legaults-deputy-premier-more-senior-caq-ministers-called-to-testify-in-saaqclic-scandal ) she received indicating 
she had been informed of the SAAQclic cost overruns back in 2023, though she previously insisted she had no 
knowledge of the problem.
In 2006, Guilbault started down the path of politics by becoming a press aide to then-public security minister 
Jacques Dupuis, a member of the Quebec Liberal Party. She then worked as a spokesperson for the Quebec 
coroner's office from 2009 to 2017.
Page 3 of 4
Citing family reasons, CAQ 's Geneviève Guilbault will leave office at the end of her term
After Legault approached her to run for the CAQ, she pulled off an upset byelection win in Louis-Hébert in 2017. 
Her victory in what had been a Liberal fortress riding set in motion other CAQ triumphs, including a big win in the 
2018 general election, when the party won 74 seats and formed a majority government.
At the time, Legault described Guilbault as a "new political star." He named her deputy premier and handed her the 
prestigious job of minister responsible for the provincial capital region. She was easily re-elected in 2018 and 2022.
She was given tough jobs in office, including having to explain to Quebec City voters in 2023 why the CAQ was 
breaking its election promise to build a third car link between Quebec City and Lévis. During the COVID-19 
pandemic, she was often sent to explain unpopular health restrictions.
In 2023, Guilbault was forced to apologize after it was discovered she was not wearing a seatbelt( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec/quebecs-transport-minister-was-caught-driving-without-a-seatbelt-she-
apologized ) when driving her car. She also tangled with Quebec municipalities over financing for public transit( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/quebec-taxpayers-shouldnt-completely-bail-out-montreal-area-transit-
companies-guilbault ).
Her announcement on Sunday marks the latest in a string of departures from the CAQ, a pattern that started with 
the departure of economy minister Pierre Fitzgibbon( https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/quebec-
economy-minister-pierre-fitzgibbon-is-stepping-down ) in 2024. Just before Christmas, health minister Christian 
Dubé - a close friend of Legault - quit the CAQ to sit as an independent( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/christian-dube-resignation-caq-health-minister ). He also will 
not run in the next Quebec election, scheduled for October.
A total of six CAQ MNAs left the ship in 2025 for various reasons. The list includes Dubé, Lionel Carmant( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-social-services-minister-lionel-carmant-quits-caq ), 
Isabelle Poulet( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/caq-mna-poulet-future-legault-bill-2-doctors ), 
Maïté Blanchette Vézina( https://montrealgazette.com/news/maite-blanchette-vezina-quits-caq-caucus-says-she-
has-no-confidence-in-legault ), Pierre Dufour( https://montrealgazette.com/news/legault-boots-pierre-dufour-out-of-
caq-caucus-after-mnas-threats ) and Andrée Laforest( https://montrealgazette.com/news/two-ministers-step-aside-
as-legault-prepares-for-long-awaited-cabinet-shuffle ).

title: Citizen report infuriated military officers; Newly released records say articles about sex assault of civilian in
body:
Canadian Forces officers were furious the Ottawa Citizen reported on the sexual assault of a civilian worker in 
Latvia, calling one of the articles "rubbish" and "diseased," according to newly released military records.
This publication had done a series of articles on Kristen Adams, who was working for the Canadian Forces Morale 
and Welfare Services (CFMWS) when she was sexually assaulted by a NATO soldier in 2022, according to 
Canadian military police records. The assault happened during her shift at a canteen operated by Canada for 
troops in Latvia.
Details of the assault and how poorly Adams, a Canadian, was treated by CFMWS management were first reported 
in the Citizen in October 2023, prompting staff at the agency to angrily raise concerns about the organization's 
failure to help a fellow worker. Adams had also personally appealed for help from then Chief of the Defence Staff 
Gen. Wayne Eyre, but received no response from the top soldier.
But one specific article in the series sparked a furious response from senior Canadian Forces public affairs officers. 
The Citizen reported comments from Adams in which she directly criticized Lt.-Gen. Lise Bourgon, head of military 
personnel and a "Defence Co-champion for Women," for labelling the sex assault as "alleged" despite numerous 
military police statements to the contrary. Bour- gon also described Adams as an "alleged victim."
After the article appeared, Bourgon's public affairs officer, Lt.-Col. Nicole Meszaros, wrote to the lieutenant-general 
to assure her that her team "is supporting and with you."
"I spoke with the CDS PAO and he was clear that the office new (sic) the article was rubbish and pathological (as in 
diseased)," Meszaros added in her email on Nov. 1, 2023.
She was referring to comments by Lt. Col. Yves Desbiens, who was Eyre's public affairs officer.
Neither Meszaros nor Desbiens responded to requests for comment.
Adams said she was disgusted, but not surprised, when she read the Meszaros email and saw the comments 
attributed to Desbiens.
Page 2 of 3
Citizen report infuriated military officers; Newly released records say articles about sex assault of civilian in 
Latvia 'rubbish'
She said the focus of the Canadian Forces wasn't to help those who had been sexually assaulted; it was to make 
sure such incidents weren't reported on in the news media.
"They're pissed because they want (the Ottawa Citizen) to go away and stop reporting on this (sex assault)," 
Adams said. "They also want me to go away. Well, I'm not going anywhere."
The records, released under the Access to Information Act, show Bourgon at first questioned why the Citizen 
wanted a comment. But then the general appeared to acknowledge her earlier characterization of the assault had 
"annoyed" Adams.
Meszaros recommended Bour- gon not talk to the newspaper. But the public affairs officer added: "I completely 
appreciate the point of view of Ms. Adams, and feel her despair and frustration. She must have felt that the only 
way to get responses was by taking this to the media."
Bourgon retired from the military in October 2025.
In 2022, some Canadian Forces personnel told former Supreme Court Justice Louise Arbour that the military saw 
sexual misconduct as a public-relations problem that needed to be managed to avoid negative media coverage 
rather than a serious issue to actually be dealt with. Arbour received those comments as part of her review on 
military sexual misconduct.
The CFMWS provides various programs and services for the military.
In a letter dated May 10, 2023, the CFMWS told Adams she should have realized she could have faced such an 
incident or other risks when she signed on for the job, according to documents obtained earlier by the Citizen.
CFMWS chief executive officer Ian Poulter did issue an apology to all his staff for the way the incident was handled, 
although he excluded Adams.
Department of National Defence records revealed why Poulter never sent Adams an apology, even though one was 
written up. Those documents noted DND and CFMWS didn't want the mea culpa reported in the Citizen.
"Because the story was unfolding in the pages of the Ottawa Citizen, we did not want to correspond with Ms. 
Adams in writing because we didn't want to perpetuate that cycle," DND officials wrote in one of the records. 
Poulter, a retired Canadian Forces major-general, has declined to be interviewed by the Citizen.
The DND records indicate that, rather than helping Adams, military and department officials were more concerned 
about whether other news media outlets would follow the Citizen coverage and report on the sexual assault.
Eyre's then chief of staff, Brig. Gen. Brendan Cook, warned Poulter in an Oct. 25, 2023, email that "Ms. Adams is 
likely to be coming back with more media coverage."
Cook also raised concerns that the office of Anita Anand, then the defence minister, could take an interest in the 
matter.
"Of note, we recently got some pressure from MNDO (Minister National Defence Office) about the recent internal 
message to CFWMS staff that was cited in the press for not apologizing to Ms. Adams," Cook wrote to Poulter in an 
email.
The documents also showed that some CFMWS managers belittled Adams and claimed the attack never 
happened, despite police records to the contrary.
The federal government has now reached a settlement with Adams, but the details remain secret. Under the 
agreement, Adams cannot discuss the CFMWS.
Page 3 of 3
Citizen report infuriated military officers; Newly released records say articles about sex assault of civilian in 
Latvia 'rubbish'
But in an article published before the agreement was put in place, Adams alleged the CFMWS failed to properly 
respond to the attack or to provide her with help. She stated at that time she believed the Canadian military was 
trying to sweep the assault under the rug because they didn't want to cause any embarrassment for the Canadian 
Armed Forces' high-profile mission in Latvia. !@COPYRIGHT=© 2026 Postmedia Network Inc. All rights reserved.

title: Committee MPs amend border bill to restrict health, other benefits to deportees
body:
OTTAWA - MPs on the House of Commons national security committee have amended the government's border 
security bill, C-12, to restrict the benefits people subject to removal orders can access.
MPs debated more than 50 amendments during a clause-by-clause analysis of the bill that began Tuesday 
afternoon and stretched into early Wednesday morning. 
Conservative immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner added an amendment that prevents anyone subject to a 
removal order from accessing federal social services beyond emergency medical care. Rempel Garner said part of 
the rationale for this change is to discourage deportees from using procedural methods to prolong their time in 
Canada, especially when there is a family doctor shortage. 
Another amendment proposed by Rempel Garner passed, requiring annual reporting on the types of benefits 
provided to asylum seekers and the cost of those benefits. 
This was part of a suite of amendments the Calgary MP said she planned to introduce ahead of the meeting. 
Quebec Liberal MP Jacques Ramsay introduced another revision that would give those individuals access to 
maternal health services and community health care for STDs, but it was voted down.
Liberal committee members, Qubec's Sameer Zuberi and Ontario's Peter Fragiskatos, also refined the legislation's 
wording on when the government can modify or cancel immigration documents in the "public interest."
The definition says these sweeping powers can be used in cases of fraud, threats to public health, safety or 
national security, or to correct an administrative error.
In prior committee hearings, Immigration Minister Lena Diab and department officials had said the term "public 
interest" was kept intentionally vague to give the government more flexibility.
Rempel Garner successfully moved an amendment that if the government uses these "public interest" powers the 
immigration minister will have to make a presentation in Parliament explaining why in a high level of detail. 

Page 2 of 3
Committee MPs amend border bill to restrict health, other benefits to deportees
Under the original legislation, the time period and who is being affected by "public interest" powers would be 
published in the Canada Gazette, along with rationale. 
Not all of Rempel Garner's more than 30 amendments were adopted; several were deemed inadmissible because 
they dealt with legislative changes outside the scope of C-12.
One Conservative amendment that was rejected by the committee was a measure to prevent people coming from 
the European Union or G7 nations from making asylum claims in Canada. This would have been applicable to 
residents or people transiting through these countries. 
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2025.

title: Compared to his competition, Legault believes he and the CAQ are a good bet for voters
body:
QUEBEC - Despite a dismal standing in the polls and an election 11 months away, Premier François Legault says 
he believes there is a future for his Coalition Avenir Québec( https://montrealgazette.com/news/masked-
demonstrators-encampments-and-sweetie-sentences-among-policy-subjects-at-caq-convention ) once Quebecers 
size up his adversaries and what they have to offer.
At a news conference wrapping up the winter sitting of the legislature, Legault was asked to speculate on the future 
of the movement he founded in 2011 as an alternative to the Liberals and Parti Québécois, and whether his four-
month campaign to jump start his government was having any effect.
The CAQ is currently mired in third place in public opinion polls. It has been in office since 2018.
Legault said he believes the party's fortunes will improve the closer Quebec moves to the election and people take 
a hard look at what the PQ and Liberals are offering.
He said voters will ask themselves if they want the Parti Québécois option, which includes an independence 
referendum, or if they want the Liberals he says are soft on identity issues.
Under the microscope, "maybe they'll think Legault's not too bad," he said, suggesting he hopes the election 
becomes a real three- way race( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec_elections/legault-
urges-quebecers-to-size-up-his-opponents-carefully-before-voting-in-2026 ).
"The closer we get to October, the more they will compare the options," Legault said. "I think the CAQ is in the right 
spot - a party that is economic and nationalist. I think that is what Quebecers want."
He speculated on his personal future as well, effectively telling anyone interested in taking his job as CAQ leader 
will need to be patient.
"Will there be an heir apparent? I think there are plenty of replacements," he said. "It's too soon to talk about this. 
I'm staying."
On the other hand, Legault didn't discourage a successor, either.
"Eventually, yes, there will be a place," he said. "I am not eternal."
Page 2 of 5
Compared to his competition, Legault believes he and the CAQ are a good bet for voters
Legault then revealed he never really seriously considered not running again and his remarks this week about 
"taking a walk in the snow"( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-legault-stays-election-
2026 ) and deciding to run again were more of a joke than anything.
"I didn't walk much in the snow," he said. "I walked as far as my car."
The phrase "walk in the snow" refers to the Pierre Trudeau's resignation as prime minister in 1984( 
https://ottawacitizen.com/news/national/trudeaus-third-walk-in-the-snow ) after taking a solitary walk in an Ottawa 
blizzard.
Speculation about Legault's future has been swirling for months. Last week, an Angus Reid survey on the popularity 
of Canada's premiers( https://montrealgazette.com/news/canadas-least-popular-premier-francois-legault-ends-
2025-in-the-basement ) placed Legault dead last, garnering praise from only 25 per cent of Quebecers.
At 68 years old, Legault has said repeatedly he would like to win a third mandate in office.
But as the session wrapped, Legault seemed proud his efforts to jump start his sagging government are underway. 
A quick look at the promises he made in his Sept. 29 inaugural address( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/unions-red-tape-and-radical-islamists-legault-lays-out-his-
battles-in-inaugural-address ) that followed a cabinet shuffle, shows he's made a start.
His secularism minster, Jean-François Roberge, tabled legislation to bar prayers in the street and extend the ban 
on religious symbols to public daycares (Bill 9( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-plans-
to-ban-street-prayers-as-it-moves-to-beef-up-secularism-law )). Labour Minister Jean Boulet presented Bill 3( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/unions-fume-as-legault-government-tables-bill-aimed-at-how-
dues-are-spent ) forcing Quebec's unions to be more transparent in how dues are spent and another (Bill 8), which 
would force them to offer essential services.
Finance Minister Eric Girard presented Bill 5( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/caq-
government-tables-bill-to-speed-approval-for-major-projects ) speeding up authorization for large-scale projects.
Acting on Legault's pledge to develop a law-and-order agenda, Public Security Minister Ian Lafrenière tabled Bill 
13( https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec-crime-bill-sex-offenders-gangs-protests ), which will ban gang 
colours, restrict protests and created a sex offender's registry.
And one of the largest bricks of legislation, tabled at the beginning of the session, was Bill 1 creating a Quebec 
constitution( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/caq-unveils-quebecs-first-constitution-amid-
controversy ), another promise of the inaugural address.
As the house recessed, none of the bills had been voted into law, but debate on them will resume when the house 
resumes sitting in February.
One bill, however, was presented and adopted in the same day to appease rancour in the medical profession over 
the government's Bill 2 imposing a wage agreement. As part of a new round of negotiations with doctors, Quebec 
adopted Bill 16, which repeals parts of Bill 2 and delays application of others( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec-bill-2-doctors-deal-sanctions-deadlines-scrapped ) until Feb. 28, 2026.
Despite the CAQ government's troubles, Legault said if there is one thing he wants to focus on in 2026 it is the 
economy and continuing to counter the threat from south of the border.
He seemed take some consolation in the fact the three opposition parties were themselves, at different times, mired 
in their own woes.
Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez speaks during a news conference marking the end of the fall session at 
the legislature in Quebec City, Friday, Dec. 12, 2025.
Page 3 of 5
Compared to his competition, Legault believes he and the CAQ are a good bet for voters
Only elected to the job six months ago, Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez ended his year facing calls from within his 
own party to resign after bad news landed on the doorstep almost every day of November and December.
By far the toughest blow was news Quebec's anti-corruption unit (UPAC) had opened a criminal investigation( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-upac-investigation ) over allegations of illegal 
fundraising in the Rodriguez leadership campaign.
On Thursday, there was news a dozen former Liberal MNAs and cabinet ministers had signed a letter calling for 
Rodriguez's resignation( https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/a-dozen-former-liberal-mnas-and-ministers-

Title: Compared to his competition, Legault believes he and the CAQ are a good bet for voters

Body: QUEBEC - Despite a dismal standing in the polls and an election 11 months away, Premier François Legault says 
he believes there is a future for his Coalition Avenir Québec( https://montrealgazette.com/news/masked-
demonstrators-encampments-and-sweetie-sentences-among-policy-subjects-at-caq-convention ) once Quebecers 
size up his adversaries and what they have to offer.
At a news conference wrapping up the winter sitting of the legislature, Legault was asked to speculate on the future 
of the movement he founded in 2011 as an alternative to the Liberals and Parti Québécois, and whether his four-
month campaign to jump start his government was having any effect.
The CAQ is currently mired in third place in public opinion polls. It has been in office since 2018.
Legault said he believes the party's fortunes will improve the closer Quebec moves to the election and people take 
a hard look at what the PQ and Liberals are offering.
He said voters will ask themselves if they want the Parti Québécois option, which includes an independence 
referendum, or if they want the Liberals he says are soft on identity issues.
Under the microscope, "maybe they'll think Legault's not too bad," he said, suggesting he hopes the election 
becomes a real three- way race( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec_elections/legault-
urges-quebecers-to-size-up-his-opponents-carefully-before-voting-in-2026 ).
"The closer we get to October, the more they will compare the options," Legault said. "I think the CAQ is in the right 
spot - a party that is economic and nationalist. I think that is what Quebecers want."
He speculated on his personal future as well, effectively telling anyone interested in taking his job as CAQ leader 
will need to be patient.
"Will there be an heir apparent? I think there are plenty of replacements," he said. "It's too soon to talk about this. 
I'm staying."
On the other hand, Legault didn't discourage a successor, either.
"Eventually, yes, there will be a place," he said. "I am not eternal."

Legault then revealed he never really seriously considered not running again and his remarks this week about 
"taking a walk in the snow"( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-legault-stays-election-
2026 ) and deciding to run again were more of a joke than anything.
"I didn't walk much in the snow," he said. "I walked as far as my car."
The phrase "walk in the snow" refers to the Pierre Trudeau's resignation as prime minister in 1984( 
https://ottawacitizen.com/news/national/trudeaus-third-walk-in-the-snow ) after taking a solitary walk in an Ottawa 
blizzard.
Speculation about Legault's future has been swirling for months. Last week, an Angus Reid survey on the popularity 
of Canada's premiers( https://montrealgazette.com/news/canadas-least-popular-premier-francois-legault-ends-
2025-in-the-basement ) placed Legault dead last, garnering praise from only 25 per cent of Quebecers.
At 68 years old, Legault has said repeatedly he would like to win a third mandate in office.
But as the session wrapped, Legault seemed proud his efforts to jump start his sagging government are underway. 
A quick look at the promises he made in his Sept. 29 inaugural address( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/unions-red-tape-and-radical-islamists-legault-lays-out-his-
battles-in-inaugural-address ) that followed a cabinet shuffle, shows he's made a start.
His secularism minster, Jean-François Roberge, tabled legislation to bar prayers in the street and extend the ban 
on religious symbols to public daycares (Bill 9( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-plans-
to-ban-street-prayers-as-it-moves-to-beef-up-secularism-law )). Labour Minister Jean Boulet presented Bill 3(

dues-are-spent ) forcing Quebec's unions to be more transparent in how dues are spent and another (Bill 8), which 
would force them to offer essential services.
Finance Minister Eric Girard presented Bill 5( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/caq-
government-tables-bill-to-speed-approval-for-major-projects ) speeding up authorization for large-scale projects.

economy and continuing to counter the threat from south of the border.

in their own woes.

title: Comprehensive tax reform would discourage scofflaws; Comment Reporting rules too onerous for Canadians
body:
Irecently visited one of my favourite restaurants and the food and service, as usual, were out of this world, 
something a food delivery service cannot replicate. The restaurant has a strict "cash only" policy, so I always need 
to remind myself about that before I go and, obviously, as a tax guy, I wonder if the cash-only policy is a signal that 
the owner is participating in tax evasion.
Cash-only businesses have often been a target for the Canada Revenue Agency to review and determine if the 
proprietor is reporting income in full.
In some cases, it's obvious that tax evasion is the objective. For example, I've interviewed many renovators of my 
homes over the years and some of the prospective contractors will have a two-tiered pricing structure: a lower cash 
price and a higher traditional invoice structure. In other cases, it's obvious that things, such as avoiding high 
banking costs or credit card fees, might be at play.
For the small number of cases that involve tax evasion, I'm often curious why such people engage in that illegal 
behaviour and are prepared to risk serious criminal penalties, including possible jail time.
The answers are important because if you can understand the motivation, governments can design policy to 
eliminate that. Tax evasion is not a pervasive problem in Canada - reliable statistics are lacking, but it is likely that 
less than three per cent of taxpayers willingly participate in such criminal behaviour - it is, again, important to 
understand the motivations.
There are several motiva- tions, with the most obvious being excessively high personal tax rates. Eight of the 13 
provinces and territories have marginal tax rates that exceed 50 per cent at the high end. In 1966, the Royal 
Commission on Taxationthe only time that Canada had a comprehensive tax review leading to reform - released its 
voluminous report and said this about personal tax rates:
"We are persuaded that high marginal rates of tax have an adverse effect on the decision to work rather than enjoy 
leisure, on the decision to save rather than consume, and on the decision to hold assets that provide monetary 
returns rather than assets that provide benefits in kind. We think there would be great merit in adopting a top 
marginal rate no greater than 50 per cent. We think there is a psychological barrier to greater effort, saving and 
profitable investment when the state can take more than one half of the potential gain."
That almost 60-year-old comment is just as valid today as it was back then.
Page 2 of 3
Comprehensive tax reform would discourage scofflaws; Comment Reporting rules too onerous for Canadians
Other reasons include: ? The complex and one -r ous reporting requirements that exhaust the average taxpayer. 
Tax preparers are stretched and scramble to ensure such reportings are accurate and timely filed. An obvious 
example of this is the foreign reporting requirements and the new mandatory disclosure rules. Governments around 
the world are infatuated with onerous reporting requirements, with one of the stated objectives being to reduce tax 
evasion.
While I appreciate the sentiment, the so-called bad guys won't comply no matter what the reporting requirements 
are. Instead, such requirements are pushed onto the average tax-compliant taxpayer, which simply adds to the 
already burdensome compliance.
? The punitive treatment of certain activities, such as the ridiculous short-term rental rules that prohibit the 
deduction of all expenses for certain owners. This, without a doubt, encourages non-compliance.
? The poorly targeted a -n ti-avoidance rules like the horribly complex tax-onsplit-income rules that attempt to 
prevent income splitting amongst family members on certain types of corporate and other income. Such rules often 
catch legitimate family business arrangements. The rules are often beyond the comprehension of many tax 
preparers/advisers, which breeds non-compliance, under-reporting or the encouragement of other informal 
arrangements to avoid such rules.
? The lack of access to a simpler tax filing system. Some do not like the idea of the government implementing an 
automatic tax filing system, but I do, especially since the government has access to much of a taxpayer's data, such 
as employment earnings, pension earnings, etc. Instead, taxpayers are often forced to navigate a complex tax 
compliance system that can encourage the non-reporting of other earnings.
Canada isn't just taxing people too much; it's exhausting them. When otherwise good people feel that exhaustion, 
they will resort to easier options.
It's similar to the reasons why successful Canadians are leaving Canada. The actual number of people leaving is 
small, but the amount of jobs, wealth and opportunity costs that is departing are staggering. It needs to stop.
The solution to all this is a tax system that is much less punitive from both a financial and compliance perspective, 
that is much simpler and approachable to the average Canadian, that rewards success rather than punishes it and 
that is much less political.
The answer isn't more enforcement or another layer of disclosure. It's meaningful tax reform that lowers the overall 
burden, simplifies compliance and rebuilds trust. Not surgical fixes but "Big Bang" reform that encourages 
compliance. Canadians deserve a system that rewards effort and contribution, not one that drives them 
underground or out of the country entirely.
Prime Minister Mark Carney promised an "expert review of the corporate tax system" during last spring's election 
campaign. Not surprisingly, that vague copycat promise - the Conserv -a tives promised a fulsome tax reform task 
forcenever made it into the Nov. 4 budget. Canadians don't need more rhetoric. We need bold action. 
Comprehensive tax reform is long overdue, and it's the only way to bring people back to the table.
In the meantime, I'll keep enjoying my favourite cash-only restaurant, and keep wondering how many more 
Canadians are quietly deciding that our tax system just isn't worth the price on the menu.

other leadership positions in the Canadian tax community.

title: Council pay for next Tiny term gives insight to job demands
body:
If anyone has considered running for public office in the upcoming municipal elections, then watching the recent 
hour-long discussion about Tiny Township remuneration might be somewhat of an eye-opener.
The discussion began regarding framework on proposed remuneration for the next term of elected officials during 
the committee of the whole, as per a report completed by the ad hoc citizens committee on council remuneration, 
headed by chair and former Tiny Township mayor and councillor Ray Millar.
Remuneration is a two-part compensation for elected officials, where they receive a base stipend (an annual salary) 
as well as per diem (or daily rate pay) for attended duties and obligations beyond regular council attendance.
The ad hoc committee sought to develop a methodology for determining remuneration as a quantifiable equation 
rather than presenting a number based on peer comparison of other municipalities, and provided a thoroughly 
detailed reasoning as justification.
Currently, Mayor Dave Evans receives an approximate base salary of $43,700; Deputy Mayor Sean Miskimins of 
$32,800; and members of council for $28,400. Per diems for council members amounted to roughly $18,400 in 
2024.
The suggested calculation would quantify the base stipend as the Ontario Living Wage Network rate ($24.60 per 
hour for Tiny Township in 2025), multiplied by a task multiplier, a role multiplier (such as mayor or councillor) and 
time commitment per month. The per diem remuneration, applicable to every elected official, was suggested as 
$120 for a full day of up to eight hours, or $60 for a half day of up to four hours.
Millar pointed out in the report that elected officials are temporary for their four-year terms in council and not 
municipal employees. Although council are entitled to Ontario Municipal Employees Retirement System (OMERS) 
currently, they could receive payment-in-lieu instead of participating in OMERS.
If approved as per the recommendations, the 2026-2030 term of Tiny Township council would see approximate 
base stipends of $46,000 for mayor, $33,800 for deputy mayor, and $30,700 for councillors. Also, if the OMERS 
pension contributions were discontinued as per the report recommendation, a further raise to the per diem model 
would be ‘offset almost exactly’ with the OMERS elimination for “no net loss,” said Millar.

Page 2 of 3
Council pay for next Tiny term gives insight to job demands
The intent was clarity and transparency, according to Millar, but during the presentation to the committee of the 
whole, council members shared that it was difficult to look objectively at the report and not feel that they were

title: Councillor pushes back on integrity commissioner’s report
body:
In a tension-filled council meeting Monday morning, members of council spent over two hours discussing the 
integrity commissioner's recently released report on councillor Todd Snooks and his alleged behaviour towards 
female members of township staff. 
 The integrity commissioner's (IC) report claims that Snooks had, on three separate occasions, made some female 
staff uncomfortable with unwelcome touching, such as hugging staff, tracing a staffer's arm tattoo with his finger, 
and, on one occasion, using a pickleball paddle to touch women's posteriors. The report said: "We find that the 
councillor’s conduct constitutes harassment, shows a lack of respect for the Township staff (and) his alleged 
conduct amounted to harassment and disrespect."
At the start of the discussion, Snooks said he wanted to apologize and said he would do his best never to make 
anyone feel uncomfortable.
 "I was devastated (by the report)," Snooks said. "I have always shown the utmost respect."
 Snooks then moved that his lawyer, William McDaniel, who was present, be allowed to take part to "educate 
council on what the report entails."
 "I have been in this process in isolation," he said. "'IC told me not to discuss this with anyone. This has not been a 
fair process."
 Janet Atwood-Petkovski, a co-principal at Principles Integrity, which is the company hired by the Township to act 
as integrity commissioner, appearing via a video hookup, said Snooks had no right to legal counsel during the 
course of the presentation she was making to council. Snooks, saying the IC has had other cases where legal 
counsel was allowed during a presentation similar to this, emphasized that he was not asking for a re-investigation 
of the complaints. He said his lawyer would address the IC process that was used by Principles Integrity. When 
asked by councillor Willie Popp what benefit would be derived from allowing the lawyer to take part, Snooks said it 
was to ensure "no one else has to go through the process I went through."
 In a recorded vote, with Snooks not allowed to take part due to conflict of interest, council voted to reject 
Snooks' motion. Only councillor Gord Shreeve supported Snooks' motion.

Page 2 of 3
Councillor pushes back on integrity commissioner’s report
 After the vote, Snooks said: "It is clear that council has made a decision prior to coming into chambers." 
 Regional councillor Bruce Garrod said during the discussion that he would not want his daughter or wife working 
at the township offices.
 "We need to make sure staff has a safe environment," he said.
When Uxbridge CAO Kristi Honey said a survey done in September showed 98 per cent of staff felt safe, Garrod 
responded: "That was before the report came out." Honey explained the two per cent minority represented in the 
survey were bylaw officers, animal control personnel and library staff, all of whom must deal with potentially 
dangerous situations at times during their work.
 Garrod, noting there are two codes of conduct within the Township, one for council members and one for staff, 
asked Honey if an employee who faced the same complaint would be fired. Honey replied "yes."
 At one point, Garrod pointedly asked Snooks if he felt people had not “spoken the truth” when speaking to the IC. 
Snooks said people recalling past events might not be lying but remembering things differently. At another point, 
councillor Pam Beach broke down in tears as she offered that some of the female staffers who had complained 
about Snooks' behaviour might have had past traumatic issues triggered.
 During the discussion, Garrod suggested the IC investigation and report could cost the township around $20,000 
and wondered if Snooks could be requested to cover part of that cost.
 When the discussion ended, council agreed that Honey should work with the integrity commissioner to determine 
appropriate training for Snooks and allow council to determine if all members of council should participate in the 
training or alternate training. Council also ruled that any one-on-one meetings between Snooks and staff should be 
also be attended by the CAO or her delegate, and that any correspondence to staff from Snooks be in writing and 
directly copied to the CAO.
