title: Playboy King abdicates to wed divorcee; This week in history: 1936 Edward VIII set off a royal scandal with his
body:
There was a civic election in Vancouver on Dec. 9, 1936.
Alderman George Clark Miller beat alderman L.D. McDonald to become mayor, but frankly, nobody seemed to care 
- the world was watching whether King Edward VIII would quit the monarchy to marry American divorcee Wallis 
Simpson.
He did. "Edward Abdicates; Duke of York New King," said the banner headline in the Dec. 10, 1936 Vancouver 
Sun.
"After long and anxious consideration, I have determined to renounce the throne to which I succeeded on the death 
of my father and I am now communicating this, my final and irrevocable decision," Edward wrote in his Declaration 
of Abdication.
"I, Edward VIII, of Great Britain, Ireland and the British dominions beyond the seas, King, and Emperor of India, do 
hereby declare my irrevocable determination to renounce the throne for myself and for my descendants and my 
desire that effect should be given to this instrument of abdication immediately."
Edward had been fighting with Britain's Conservative prime minister Stanley Baldwin and Parliament over whether 
he could marry a two-time divorcee and remain king.
Baldwin told him the British people wouldn't accept it. There were other objections as well: The king was the head 
of the Church of England, which didn't allow divorced people to remarry if their former spouse was still alive. 
Edward VIII offered to have a "morganatic" marriage with Simpson, where she didn't get to be queen. Baldwin said 
no to that as well.
Bizarrely, the controversy had been kept from the British public for months - and British newspapers kept their open 
affair hushhush until early December. But finally it came out, when everybody probably already knew.
"The government are sensible of the fact that statements published in American and some Dominion newspapers 
are being widely discussed," said the London Daily Telegraph on Dec. 3, 1936.
Page 2 of 3
Playboy King abdicates to wed divorcee; This week in history: 1936 Edward VIII set off a royal scandal with his 
desire to marry Simpson
The Telegraph still didn't mention Wallis Simpson until Dec. 4. But other British papers had been champing at the 
bit to release the news.
The entire front page of the Dec. 3 Newscastle Evening Chronicle, for example, was about the controversy. It 
included a photo of Simpson and a sympathetic story headlined "Mrs. Simpson, The King's Friend."
"Slim, dark-eyed, beautifully dressed and with her long black hair gathered becomingly on the nape of her neck, 
Mrs. Wallis Simpson has in four or five years reached the foremost ranks of Society," said the story. "(She is) quick-
witted, gay and possessed of that quality, which for want of a better name, in vaguely called 'charm.'" She met King 
Edward when her second husband, a British American businessman, took her to society parties in London. Edward 
was then the Prince of Wales, and a well-known playboy. They were introduced by Lady Thelma Furness, a married 
woman he was having an affair with. Edward and Wallis quickly hit it off.
"Mrs. Simpson, often accompanied by her husband, was seen often with the King at nightclubs and restaurants 
where there was dancing," said the Newscastle Evening Chronicle. "The tango was undoubtedly one of their 
favourite dances together."
Edward's family had been trying to set him up with suitable bluebloods for years. A story in the Dec. 10 Sun said in 
1911 his mother Queen Mary had tried to get the 17-year-old Edward interested in the German kaiser's daughter, 
Princess Victoria Louise of Prussia.
He was linked with one of the Russian czar's daughters, the Grand Duchess Olga; Princess Yolanda of Italy and 
her sisters Mafalda and Giovanna; Princesses Astrid, Martha and Ingrid of Sweden; Princesses Beatrice and Maria 
Christina of Spain; Princess Eudoxia of Bulgaria; Princess Juliana of Holland, and Princess Marina of Greece.
But he resisted attempts to marry himself off.
Finally he became king in Jan. 20, 1936, following the death of his father, George V. He was 42.
On Dec. 1, 1936, he informed prime minister Baldwin that he wished to marry Simpson, whose second divorce 
had gone through Oct. 27. But Baldwin said no.
"Cabinet Ready to Resign, Baldwin Tells the King," read the headline in the Dec. 2 Vancouver Sun. "Gov't Opposes 
Mrs. Simpson."
After he abdicated, Edward became the Duke of Windsor. He married Simpson in France on June 3, 1937.

title: PM plays politics; Trump's response to speech predictable
body:
U.S. President Donald Trump's threat to impose crippling tariffs should Ottawa and Beijing sign a trade deal is 
unacceptably coercive and mimics China's behaviour. Yet, at the same time, Prime Minister Mark Carney could be 
navigating this situation better, and seems to be prioritizing political theatre over Canada's interests.
Throughout his second presidency, Trump's approach to foreign policy has been erratic and disruptive. While his 
interventions in Venezuela and the Middle East have been commendable, their benefits have been outweighed by 
his bullying of traditional American allies, as well as his threats to punish western economies should they fail to 
obsequiously follow his agenda.
His recent fixation on annexing Greenland - which rightfully belongs to Denmark, a long-standing NATO ally - 
epitomizes this. European powers that objected to this proposed land grab were told by Washington that they 
should shut up or face retaliatory tariffs because this is apparently what being an ally looks like in the MAGA-verse. 
Although these threats were dropped after a framework for a future Greenland deal was reached, their use remains 
concerning.
Trump's musings of eventual annexation of Canada might be dismissed as a joke, but it is now glaringly obvious 
that Trump has little respect for Canadian sovereignty and few scruples about using coercion to bend Ottawa into 
submission.
In this context, bolstering Canada's strategic independence is a sensible move - which is what Carney, at least 
rhetorically, has committed to doing. His recently announced "comprehensive strategic partnership" with China may 
be misguided, because it risks fostering overdependence on Beijing, but the underlying rationaletrade diversification 
- is not.
Similarly, Carney's speech at Davos last week, where he called upon middle powers to stand united against 
coercion from great powers, was a clear-eyed assessment of the challenges Canada now faces in a multipolar 
world. Although he did not name Trump directly, his implicit denunciation of the American president was ob- vious 
and widely well-received.
The speech was a political victory for Carney, garnering him a wave of positive media coverage both within and 
outside Canada. Yet, its unnecessarily abrasive tone, which went beyond simply standing up to Trump, provoked a 
predictably histrionic response from Washington, further straining relations.
Page 2 of 3
PM plays politics; Trump's response to speech predictable
While this in some sense vindicated Carney and other critics of the MAGA movement, it further jeopardized 
Canada's national interests and raised concerns that Carney had, ironically, prioritized pathos and mudslinging 
over effective diplomacy and self-restraint.
"Canada lives because of the United States ... remember that, Mark, next time you make your statements," 
complained Trump at Davos last week, adopting the mannerisms of a mafioso. He further claimed that Canada was 
not "grateful" for receiving "a lot of freebies" from Washington.
Trump then escalated the situation on Saturday with a social media post threatening to impose 100 per cent tariffs 
on Canadian imports should a Chinese-Canadian trade deal be signed. "China will eat Canada alive, completely 
devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life," he wrote, claiming that 
Beijing would turn Canada into a "drop-off port" for Chinese goods to be transhipped into the United States.
Someone should remind Trump that Canada is not, in fact, an American state and that, as a sovereign country, it 
reserves the right to sign trade deals with whomever it likes within the constraints of its prior commitments. While 
many Canadians, myself included, have concerns about Carney's overenthusiastic pivot to China, this is a 
domestic issue that must be sorted out internally and democratically.
Trump's defenders might argue that the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) grants Washington a 
de facto veto over any free trade negotiations Ottawa might have with "non-market countries" (e.g. China). 
However, it is clear that Carney's deal with Beijing, being limited to cutting tariffs on a handful of goods, currently 
falls far below the definition of "free trade." As such, there is ono legal basis for retaliation, unless the Trump 
administration wants to interpret the deal so creatively as to render its clauses moot.
Of course, one could point out that countries routinely leverage international trade to signal displeasure with one 
another - but this power is generally exercised with great restraint among allies. By threatening to cripple Canada's 
economy on such flimsy grounds, Trump has shown, once again, that he fundamentally sees Ottawa as a 
supplicant, not an ally.
Canada obviously needs to strengthen itself and seek out partners who can counterbalance the United States, but 
Carney's actions don't always match his rhetoric, and his open antagonism sometimes seems motivated more so by 
political concerns than Canadian interests.
Since being elected prime minister nine months ago, Carney has promised to significantly boost military spending 
and removed all federal interprovincial trade barriers, which is commendable. Yet, his efforts to strengthen Canada 
have remained lacklustre in many other respects.
Why does our oil and gas industry remain shackled? Why have ono new pipelines been approved? The text of the 
new China deal emphasizes "clean energy" in lieu of resource extraction, suggesting that environmental concerns 
are still being prioritized over economic renewal. And what about combating foreign interference and transnational 
oppression? Very little is being done in this domain, too, despite its vital importance to national security.
Carney should be leveraging every tool available to him to maximize our national strengths, and he should be 
manoeuvring with more subtlety and cunning, so that he can extricate the country from dependence on Washington 
without incurring unnecessary wounds.
Unfortunately, many of these tools have remained unused when they are not expedient to the Liberals' political 
interests. Relatedly, it sometimes feels as if Carney wants to simply annoy Trump without any further plan, even 
though the costs of angering him are painfully predictable.
Perhaps the prime minister is deliberately positioning himself as a global foil to the MAGA movement, regardless 
of whether that furthers Canadian interests. Fear of Trump saved the Liberals from electoral oblivion last year, so 
it's not a stretch to imagine that it is being politically misappropriated, again.

navigating this situation better, and seems to be prioritizing political theatre over Canada's interests.
Throughout his second presidency, Trump's approach to foreign policy has been erratic and disruptive. While his 
interventions in Venezuela and the Middle East have been commendable, their benefits have been outweighed by 
his bullying of traditional American allies, as well as his threats to punish western economies should they fail to 
obsequiously follow his agenda.
His recent fixation on annexing Greenland - which rightfully belongs to Denmark, a long-standing NATO ally - 
epitomizes this. European powers that objected to this proposed land grab were told by Washington that they 
should shut up or face retaliatory tariffs because this is apparently what being an ally looks like in the MAGA-verse. 
Although these threats were dropped after a framework for a future Greenland deal was reached, their use remains 
concerning.
Trump's musings of eventual annexation of Canada might be dismissed as a joke, but it is now glaringly obvious 
that Trump has little respect for Canadian sovereignty and few scruples about using coercion to bend Ottawa into 
submission.
In this context, bolstering Canada's strategic independence is a sensible move - which is what Carney, at least 
rhetorically, has committed to doing. His recently announced "comprehensive strategic partnership" with China may 
be misguided, because it risks fostering overdependence on Beijing, but the underlying rationaletrade diversification 
- is not.
Similarly, Carney's speech at Davos last week, where he called upon middle powers to stand united against 
coercion from great powers, was a clear-eyed assessment of the challenges Canada now faces in a multipolar 
world. Although he did not name Trump directly, his implicit denunciation of the American president was ob- vious 
and widely well-received.
The speech was a political victory for Carney, garnering him a wave of positive media coverage both within and 
outside Canada. Yet, its unnecessarily abrasive tone, which went beyond simply standing up to Trump, provoked a 
predictably histrionic response from Washington, further straining relations.
Page 2 of 3
PM plays politics; Trump's response to speech predictable
While this in some sense vindicated Carney and other critics of the MAGA movement, it further jeopardized 
Canada's national interests and raised concerns that Carney had, ironically, prioritized pathos and mudslinging 
over effective diplomacy and self-restraint.
"Canada lives because of the United States ... remember that, Mark, next time you make your statements," 
complained Trump at Davos last week, adopting the mannerisms of a mafioso. He further claimed that Canada was 
not "grateful" for receiving "a lot of freebies" from Washington.
Trump then escalated the situation on Saturday with a social media post threatening to impose 100 per cent tariffs 
on Canadian imports should a Chinese-Canadian trade deal be signed. "China will eat Canada alive, completely 
devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life," he wrote, claiming that 
Beijing would turn Canada into a "drop-off port" for Chinese goods to be transhipped into the United States.
Someone should remind Trump that Canada is not, in fact, an American state and that, as a sovereign country, it 
reserves the right to sign trade deals with whomever it likes within the constraints of its prior commitments. While 
many Canadians, myself included, have concerns about Carney's overenthusiastic pivot to China, this is a 
domestic issue that must be sorted out internally and democratically.
Trump's defenders might argue that the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) grants Washington a 
de facto veto over any free trade negotiations Ottawa might have with "non-market countries" (e.g. China). 
However, it is clear that Carney's deal with Beijing, being limited to cutting tariffs on a handful of goods, currently 
falls far below the definition of "free trade." As such, there is ono legal basis for retaliation, unless the Trump 
administration wants to interpret the deal so creatively as to render its clauses moot.
Of course, one could point out that countries routinely leverage international trade to signal displeasure with one 
another - but this power is generally exercised with great restraint among allies. By threatening to cripple Canada's 
economy on such flimsy grounds, Trump has shown, once again, that he fundamentally sees Ottawa as a 
supplicant, not an ally.
Canada obviously needs to strengthen itself and seek out partners who can counterbalance the United States, but 
Carney's actions don't always match his rhetoric, and his open antagonism sometimes seems motivated more so by 
political concerns than Canadian interests.
Since being elected prime minister nine months ago, Carney has promised to significantly boost military spending 
and removed all federal interprovincial trade barriers, which is commendable. Yet, his efforts to strengthen Canada 
have remained lacklustre in many other respects.
Why does our oil and gas industry remain shackled? Why have ono new pipelines been approved? The text of the 
new China deal emphasizes "clean energy" in lieu of resource extraction, suggesting that environmental concerns 
are still being prioritized over economic renewal. And what about combating foreign interference and transnational 
oppression? Very little is being done in this domain, too, despite its vital importance to national security.
Carney should be leveraging every tool available to him to maximize our national strengths, and he should be 
manoeuvring with more subtlety and cunning, so that he can extricate the country from dependence on Washington 
without incurring unnecessary wounds.
Unfortunately, many of these tools have remained unused when they are not expedient to the Liberals' political 
interests. Relatedly, it sometimes feels as if Carney wants to simply annoy Trump without any further plan, even 
though the costs of angering him are painfully predictable.
Perhaps the prime minister is deliberately positioning himself as a global foil to the MAGA movement, regardless 
of whether that furthers Canadian interests. Fear of Trump saved the Liberals from electoral oblivion last year, so 
it's not a stretch to imagine that it is being politically misappropriated, again.

title: PM urged not to cut foreign aid, global health funding UNAIDS chief warns inequality will 'continue to widen'
body:
The head of the United Nations' HIV/AIDS program is urging Prime Minister Mark Carney to reverse his 
government's planned cuts to foreign aid and global health funding.
"My message to Prime Minister Carney, to Canada, and to all the other donors is, stay the course," UNAIDS 
executive director Winnie Byanyima told The Canadian Press on the sidelines of last week's G20 leaders' summit 
in Johannesburg.
"Without global solidarity, the inequality between countries will continue to widen. We will live in a more dangerous 
world as these inequalities increase."
Last week, Carney announced Canada's first-ever cut to funding for the Global Fund, a major program for fighting 
infectious diseases in the world's poorest countries.
The new funding pledge is 17 per cent lower than Ottawa's last contribution to the fund in 2022. The fund helps 
combat the spread of diseases such as AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria through measures like providing mosquito 
nets and medication for HIV patients.
The move came just weeks after the federal budget called for $2.7 billion in cuts over four years to foreign aid - and 
months after Carney vowed during the spring election campaign that his government would "not cut foreign aid."
The Carney government argues the aid cut brings spending back in line with Canada's pre-pandemic allocations.
Ottawa increased its development and humanitarian spending during the pandemic, in part to restore stalled 
progress on fighting major illnesses such as AIDS and tuberculosis as governments turned their attention to 
COVID-19. The United States radically cut back its aid spending this year.
Byanyima was at the G20 leaders' summit to help present a report commissioned by the South African government 
on rising global inequality.
The report argues economic polarization within and among countries is generating resentment which is chipping 
away at political cohesion and risking instability.
Page 2 of 3
PM urged not to cut foreign aid, global health funding UNAIDS chief warns inequality will 'continue to widen'
The authors call on governments to deter the spread of violence and autocracy by pursuing more egalitarian 
domestic policies and reforming financial systems so that developing countries can escape the debt trap caused by 
high interest rates and natural disasters driven by climate change.
Byanyima said Canada can look to leaders such as Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who said his 
country has reaped more economic benefits from gender equality in the domestic workforce over the course of 
decades than from oil revenues. 
"When we reduce inequality between countries and within countries, we actually have stronger economies," 
Byanyima said.
She also said Canada should get behind global efforts to counter tax evasion.
When pressed about the cutbacks during his time in Johannesburg, Carney pointed out that Canada's share of the 
organization's total funding has gone up. That's because the fund's total envelope has diminished. "We've had to 
take pragmatic, responsible decisions across the board in government, which also included returning our aid budget 
to the level pre-COVID," Carney said. "Within that, though, we're focused on where it has a maximum impact, very 
much including on this continent."
The Canadian Press

title: PM's Davos speech boosts voter support; New poll
body:
O T T AWA . Canada's Liberals have received another boost in voter support after Prime Minister Mark Carney's 
recent tour to China and Davos, Switzerland, with nearly half of Canadians now saying they would likely vote 
Liberal if a federal election were held today.
The Pos tmedia-L eger poll was taken Jan. 23-26, after Prime Minister Mark Carney's trade negotiations with 
Beijing and his widely covered speech to the World Economic Forum warning against truckling to "hegemons." It 
found 47 per cent of respondents would vote for the Liberals, a significant four-point jump from an early December 
Postmedia-Leger poll.
It also shows that satisfaction in the Carney government jumped nine points to 58 per cent and Carney's own 
popularity increased by eight points to 59 per cent in the same period.
The poll shows the Liberals' lead over Pierre Poilievre's Conservatives, at 38 per cent, has increased to nine points, 
while Conservative support increased two points, to 38 per cent.
The new results come just as Poilievre's support within the party will be tested in a leadership review in Calgary this 
weekend. The online poll, which surveyed 1,611 Canadians, was conducted just days after Carney's widely noticed 
speech in Davos about middle powers having to stand up to big ones, and the response from an annoyed U.S. 
President Donald Trump.
"It was a strong speech," Leger executive vice-president Andrew Enns said in an interview. "It's not often that a 
speech can have this level of impact ... It gets that patriotic mojo going again in Canada."
But beyond Carne y 's words, Trump's reaction to the speech, in which he claimed that Canada only "lives" 
because of the U.S., -al so boosted the Liberals' fortunes, Enns added.
"People rallied" when hearing that, Enns said. "When someone's attacking your leader and suggesting he's not 
grateful, that he should be careful, I think you're going to see a positive response by a lot of Canadians, and 
certainly that older population."
Carney's gains appear to be entirely at the cost of the NDP and the Bloc Québécois, whom Enns say have 
effectively "disappeared" from public discourse for different reasons over the last few months.
Page 2 of 3
PM's Davos speech boosts voter support; New poll
The Bloc has much to be concerned about, Enns said, as the poll shows its support has dropped a whopping 12 
points in Quebec since December, going from 38 per cent to 26 per cent.
On the flip side, Liberal support in Quebec sits at 46 per cent, over three points higher than the party's 2025 
election result that saw it win 44 of the province's 78 ridings.
The pollster said it's been difficult for Bloc Leader Yves-François Blanchet to carve out space in Quebec media in 
recent months due to the Quebec Liberal party's "meltdown" over corruption allegations, followed by CAQ leader 
and Premier François Legault's sudden resignation earlier this month.
"Even in this last 10-day period, there hasn't been really much of a narrative for the Bloc to step up and talk about 
things," he noted.
The NDP's support dropped three points to five per cent since early December, likely related to the party's 
leadership race that is garnering low interest among the Canadian public, he added.
As Poilievre, the Conservative leader, heads to Calgary for his party's general meeting this weekend, the pollster 
said he's likely to focus on issues that poll strongly for him, particularly affordability, while being cautious of overly 
criticizing Carney.
The recent poll suggests that one in four Conservatives (24 per cent) say they are satisfied with Carney's 
government.
"Poilievre has to acknowledge that it's an uphill battle," Enns said.
This was an online poll, but for comparison purposes, a probability sample of this size would yield a margin of error 
no greater than plus or minus 2.44 per cent, 19 times out of 20.

title: PM's embrace of critics is good for all
body:
Progressive-leaning folks are having a hard time watching Mark Carney link arms with the same forces that spent 
the past decade demonizing the Liberals.
Whether it's making a deal with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith or playing to the "bro" culture with all the sports 
talk and walking back feminist foreign policy, it seems like the prime minister is determined to cosy up to the 
Liberals' old, harshest critics.
Making enemies into friends may make political sense, but it may also make democratic sense, too. The level of 
toxicity in this country needed to be dialed back, not simply to improve Liberal fortunes, but to build some bridges 
between government and some of Canada's most disaffected citizens.
Smith quipped last week that Justin Trudeau invented Alberta separatism, but the well of antagonism goes far 
beyond just one Liberal leader and stretches to the idea of Ottawa's legitimacy itself. Smith saw that last week at 
her own party's convention, where the mere suggestion of dealing with Ottawa got a cool reception from a large 
chunk of the crowd.
Meanwhile, the rising hostility to Liberals among men during the Trudeau years - young men in particular - was not 
in small part rooted in the conviction that government doesn't work for them, and may well indeed be against them.
None of this is healthy in a democracy.
More than three decades ago, another Liberal government came to power and inherited a very grumpy citizenry. 
Brian Mulroney had worn out his welcome with the voters - to put it mildly - and there was widespread, still 
simmering anger over the introduction of the hated goods and services tax. So great was the antipathy to the GST 
that people were not paying it.
New finance minister Paul Martin quickly realized one of the largest problems on his hands was the underground 
economy, which he took not just as a threat to the country's coffers, but to the long-standing, democratic deal 
between government and the governed.
"The underground economy isn't all smugglers. It's hundreds of thousands of otherwise honest people who have 
withdrawn their consent to be governed, who have lost faith in government," Martin said in 1993.
Note the distinction. He saw it not as simple tax revolt, but revolt against government.
Page 2 of 3
PM's embrace of critics is good for all
Fast forward to another Liberal government coming to power during yet another wave of waning faith in democracy. 
As he was rebuilding the Liberal party, Trudeau and his team drew heavily on what they were seeing in the Occupy 
and Idle No More movements, which were channelling powerful fallings-out with the idea of government itself and 
its ability to grapple with wealth inequality and Indigenous reconciliation.
Carney, it should be said, is going to have to deal with that dissent, too - it hasn't gone away. But the number-one 
job requirement for a prime minister is to keep alive the basic pact of democracy, in which people consent to be 
governed. For progressives, that pact extends one step farther, to sustain the idea that government can be a force 
for good.
The COVID-19 pandemic was an interesting look into how shaky that deal can be. In the early days, it was looking 
like the pandemic could breathe new life into all those notions of government as a force for good. Millions of 
Canadians relied on government giving financial relief and getting vaccines.
But as it wore on, exasperation with vaccine mandates and pandemic measures started to be seen as an affront to 
liberty in many quarters. The so-called "freedom convoy" protests of 2022 put all that frustration on display, and it 
was evident that much of it was coming from the West and angry men (not exclusively in either case, of course.)
No matter who was going to be elected prime minister when Canada held its election this year, the lingering 
toxicity was going to have to be addressed. Even if Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre had won, he would have 
soon found he was dealing with more than just unrest with Liberals, but with Ottawa itself.
Just look at Smith, who has done her best to give vent to Alberta separatism and opposition to Ottawa, only to be 
confronting calls for her to be recalled. Put simply, once this kind of existential unrest in democracy has been 
whipped up, it's hard to rein it back in.
Witness what's going on in Donald Trump's America, where there's a president who seems too happy to confirm 
citizens' belief that government is fundamentally corrupt.
Many progressives are coming to the view that Carney is going overboard to appease the Liberals' old critics, in a 
bid to steer the party back to the centre. Maybe, but it could also be true that Carney is trying to do a democratic 
detox, too - trying to shore up the consent to be governed where it has been wavering the most in recent years.

title: Police budgets off limits, province says Mayors warned powers to override council votes don't include ability to
body:
Premier Doug Ford's government gave the mayors of more than 200 Ontario cities expansive new "strong mayor" 
powers that would allow them to override council and veto decisions in order to push through important city 
business. 
Now, the Ford government is warning those mayors their special powers have an exception: police budgets. 
In a letter sent to mayors and police boards across the province last month, Solicitor General Michael Kerzner and 
Municipal Affairs Minister Rob Flack warned that strong mayor powers do not include the ability to limit police 
budget increases or veto estimates of individual line items.
It is not clear what prompted the letter, which was first reported by the Sarnia Journal in its coverage of that city's 
battle over police spending.
The Ministry of the Solicitor General did not respond to multiple requests for comment. 
Its distribution comes at a tense time for policing in Ontario. Last Thursday, a month after the letter was sent, York 
Regional Police announced that a major criminal corruption probe nicknamed Project South had resulted in 
dozens of charges against seven Toronto police officers and one retiree.
Two more police officers in Toronto and three in Peel region have been suspended in relation to the probe but not 
criminally charged, the Star reported. Earlier this week, the province's inspector general of policing announced a 
review of all 45 police forces in Ontario. 
Mayor Olivia Chow, whose 2026 budget includeda $94-million increase for the Toronto police, confirmed she had 
received the letter, but said it didn't factor into her decision-making. 
She has described the police budget bump as the unavoidable result of wage increases promised in a new 
collective agreement. Chow previously vowed not to use her veto powers, describing them as undemocratic. 
Sarnia Mayor Mike Bradley called the province's letter "arrogance" and a "huge intrusion" into local government.
"They're saying that every mayor and council in this province has no right to contain police spending," Bradley said.
Page 2 of 3
Police budgets off limits, province says Mayors warned powers to override council votes don't include ability to 
limit funding increases
The battle in Sarnia stems from the police force's request for $5 million to build a new headquarters. Bradley, who 
wants the police to renovate their existing headquarters, used the veto powers he was granted under strong mayor 
legislation to reject that capital cost request. He says this move was supported by taxpayers in his city, which 
recently became debt-free. 
Police budgets are often municipalities' most expensive service, eating up 30 to 40 per cent of the total budget, he 
added, calling cities' struggle to manage policing costs a "huge issue."
The letter "is a licence for every police board to go wild," Bradley said. 
In Peel, where police funding submissions go to the regional government, Mississauga Mayor Carolyn Parrish said 
she interprets strong mayor powers as applying only to city budgets, not to police budgets set by arm's-length 
boards.
The Ford government in 2022 granted so-called strong mayor powers to the leaders of Toronto and Ottawa, arguing 
they needed wide latitude - including the ability to veto council decisions, hire and fire top officials, and set the 
annual budget - in order to expedite the construction of housing and other provincial priorities. The province has 
since expanded access to those powers to 216 of Ontario's 444 municipalities, the smallest of which has fewer 
than 400 residents.

title: Police corruption scandal demands these three actions
body:
When news broke this month of the Toronto Police Service corruption that "facilitated shootings, extortions and a 
conspiracy to commit murder," it felt like an escalation of the long and sometimes fraught relationship between the 
city and its police force.
A difficult time two years ago came to mind. Then, as now, it was municipal budget season and the police were 
asking for another substantial increase. As public debate swirled with a new mayor in power, the police mounted a 
bully campaign that the Star's editorial board called "emotional blackmail." Chief Myron Demkiw insinuated calamity 
would ensue if they didn't get what they demanded.
More inflammatory was an ad campaign run by the Toronto Police Association (TPA) that used carjacking images 
with a man pointing a gun at a driver while pulling him out of his vehicle.
Demkiw, along with Chief Jim MacSween and Deputy Chief Ryan Hogan from York Region, held a news 
conference Feb. 5 to discuss the investigation into corruption allegations that include links to shootings across the 
city, tow truck violence and even a conspiracy to murder a corrections officer. During the event, each chief 
conspicuously wore an identical flak jacket, as if ready for battle. But with whom, you might ask?
News conferences are not out in public and usually only attended by media and police officers. Looking at other 
photos of Demkiw in similar situations or actually in public, he's often just in shirt sleeves or a jacket, making the 
choice to wear body armour at this particular moment of contrition baffling.
TPA ads feel hypocritical now, too, considering that the activity Toronto police are accused of is not so different 
from what was meant to frighten Torontonians into supporting the budget increase two years ago.
Just the perception of gun violence can create great fear (it's why the TPA used it) so these very real allegations 
escalate this scandal high above others. There are even charges of uniform trafficking, creating another fear that 
police we meet day to day aren't who they appear to be.
So here we are, with Toronto's biggest police scandal in decades - one that undermines whatever level of trust 
people have in the police. The social contract of policing rests on trust.
While numerous groups within Toronto have had serious issues trusting police historically, the current scandal will 
have a much wider blast radius.
Page 2 of 3
Police corruption scandal demands these three actions
Here are three things that need to happen - soon:
The investigation must be open, transparent and entirely public
So often, police matters are dealt with internally, with little public scrutiny. Not this time. Ontario's Inspector General 
said last week he's going to review all 45 police forces across the province in the wake of this scandal.
A good start, but already there's opposition. The TPA submitted a letter to the Inspector General "expressing 
serious concern" over what might be an "overly broad review." That is exactly the kind of review needed, and the 
TPA's combativeness can be taken as a sign of how rank and file officers might co-operate with investigations.
Some, including Premier Doug Ford, have used variations of the "just a few bad apples" bromide. To extend this 
tired metaphor, if the rest of the apples appear hostile to an investigation, what should the public think about the 
whole bushel? Rot spreads.
There should be zero tolerance of police intimidation of civilian oversight and budget deliberations
The campaign two years ago seems to have worked, as there's been little push back since. The scandal should 
have been an opportunity to debate this year's $94-million budget increase. As my colleague Matt Elliot wrote last 
week, police are doing less and asking for more money, but no real debate occurred.
Related to this, the police board and its chair need to be far stronger and demand reform. So often they appear 
passive. Police have intimidated council in the past, as in 2000 when the TPA ran "Operation True Blue," raising 
money to investigate politicians who weren't friendly to the police - and they've done the same with the police board. 
Susan Eng, the late, courageous and outspoken chair in the 1990s, was spied on by police for doing so.
The conspiracy to murder a corrections officer, along with this history of intimidation, is enough to make any public 
official, Toronto resident or member of the media pause and think about criticizing the police now.
Demkiw must resign
This happened under his watch and the public needs a sign that it's being taken seriously from top to bottom. 
Demkiw should have resigned after his comments in 2024 implying he'd have liked a different verdict for Umar 
Zameer, the man acquitted of wrongdoing in the tragic accident that saw a plainclothes police officer killed, a case 
that also involved allegations that officers colluded to incriminate Zameer (speaking of long-term systemic trust 
issues).
This is the worst kind of corruption undermining the foundations of policing. Repairing it will need a relentless, 
unflinching effort.

title: Premier calls for investigation into Nova Scotia Power over handling of cyberattack
body:
HALIFAX - The premier of Nova Scotia is calling for an investigation into how a major power utility has handled a 
cyberattack, saying residents should not be responsible for paying for Nova Scotia Power's failures.
Tim Houston wrote to the chair of the Nova Scotia Energy Board, saying he wants the regulator to look into the 
way the private utility has billed customers since a system breach in March.
"The cyberattack was the not the fault of Nova Scotians, yet they are bearing the financial consequences of NSP's 
(Nova Scotia Power) operational shortcomings," Houston said in the letter he shared on social media Wednesday.
Nova Scotia Power, a subsidiary of Halifax-based Emera Inc., has said the personal and financial data belonging 
to 280,000 ratepayers was accessed by an unauthorized party as early as March 19. Since then, the utility has said 
it can no longer rely on remote meter readings and has chosen to estimate electricity consumption for some 
customers' billing.
As a result, Houston said customers have been dealing with inflated bills, consecutive charges within short periods, 
and a lack of communication about billing adjustments. “It’s not lost on me or the board that knowingly overbilling 
would constitute regulatory fraud and misreporting revenue to the markets is a form of securities fraud,” Houston 
said in his letter.
Nova Scotia Power did not immediately return interview requests.
Wednesday morning, before Houston shared his letter, the official Opposition NDP held a press conference calling 
on Houston's government to take meaningful action to help Nova Scotians dealing with inaccurate and unaffordable 
power bills. 
Party leader Claudia Chender said that instead of helping Nova Scotians, the government has kicked 46,000 
people out of eligibility for a home-heating assistance program and reduced the one-time rebate amount of that 
program by $200. The Houston government, Chender added, has also refused the NDP's proposal to lower bills by 
10 per cent through a new rebate "and has repeatedly refused to have government members come to committee to 
explain how they are going to make power more affordable and more reliable."

Page 2 of 3
Premier calls for investigation into Nova Scotia Power over handling of cyberattack
Reached after Houston shared his letter, a spokesperson for the Nova Scotia NDP said his call for an investigation 
does not go far enough.
"Tim Houston needs to answer Nova Scotians' questions, take urgent action to deal with escalating bills and launch 
a full review of Nova Scotia Power to restore public trust and to help people be able to afford heat and lights," 
Chender said. 
Danielle Fraser, a member of Westville, N.S., town council, said she's glad the premier has asked for an 
investigation into Nova Scotia Power, but thinks Houston can do more. Fraser is behind a nearly 13,000-member 
Facebook group called "STOP THE NSPOWER INSANITY." 
She said she created the group in September 2024, prior to the cyberattack, after her power bill shot up three to 
four times what it had been a year prior. Fraser said the company told her their meters are correct and that she 
must have been using more energy than usual. She said she filed a complaint with the energy board, and then 
discovered "hundreds" of posts on Facebook from others who were confused by spikes in their power bills.
"I started the Facebook page for us to gather and compare stories and that. It grew steadily from there until the 
cyberattack, and then it skyrocketed," she said. 
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Dec. 3, 2025.

title: Premier François Legault's replacement to be chosen April 12
body:
QUEBEC - The new leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec and next Quebec premier will be chosen April 12 but 
any ministers who choose to run for the job will have to quit cabinet for the campaign to avoid any potential 
conflicts of interest.
On Thursday, the party released the date and the rules for the race to replace Premier François Legault, who 
announced last week he is stepping down( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/premier-legault-
steps-down-with-no-obvious-successor-in-the-wings ).
Modelled off the leadership races of the other political parties, the rules require someone who wants to be a 
candidate to collect the signatures of 1,000 party members across 75 ridings of Quebec plus endorsements from at 
least 100 members of the party's youth wing.
To run, candidates also have to provide a deposit of $30,000 - half when they present their candidacy papers (by 
Feb. 21) and the other half before the first of two debates. The spending limit for each candidate will be $150,000.
The leader will be elected by all members using a preferential vote system, which means CAQ members will cast 
votes by order of preference. To win, a candidate has to obtain a majority of votes.
The voting will be by phone. The CAQ has about 15,000 members and believes the race will move that number 
higher when lapsed members renew their cards.
Where the party differs from other parties that have held leadership races is that candidates are required to obtain 
the support of 15 CAQ MNAs to be eligible.
At a news conference to present the rules, party director general Brigitte Legault (no relation to the premier) 
explained the guardrail is normal under the circumstances because the candidate running not only takes over the 
CAQ but he or she becomes premier responsible for a caucus of 78 MNAs.
"It's a significant moral guarantee to have," Legault told reporters. "For us it's not a brake for someone from the 
outside (who might want to run) because someone serious from the outside will have to appeal to members of the 
caucus regardless."
On its first go organizing such a race - François Legault is the only leader the CAQ has ever had( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec/quebec-premier-francois-legault-resigns ) - the party also had to deal 
Page 2 of 3
Premier François Legault's replacement to be chosen April 12
with the ethics of allowing sitting cabinet ministers run. So far most of the candidates interested in the race are 
ministers.
Acting on the advice of Quebec's ethics commissioner, Ariane Mignolet, who warned of a real or potential conflict 
of interest of ministers running, the CAQ rulebook requires any minister running to step down and their 
ministerial responsibilities be transferred to someone else.
The minister-candidate would be allowed to keep their taxpayer-paid driver/security agent for reasons of safety. A 
defeated candidate could re-enter cabinet if the new leader decided to keep the person, Brigitte Legault explained.
The party argued the campaign time frame is reasonable. It could not be too short to allow candidates to do the 
work, Brigitte Legault said.
The party also wants to incite Quebecers to buy a party membership card. A person has until March 13 to buy or 
renew a membership card in order to vote in the race.
"We didn't chose this race," CAQ party president Sarah Beaumier said at the news conference. "This is something 
we have to. But it is an opportunity. We want to invite people to come to the party and re-write parts of it because 
ultimately we want to represent the Quebec of today and the people's interests.
"We are are this coalition and we are inviting people to come in with their ideas. with their points of view, with their 
perspectives. We don't just want members to be able to get to a number. We want members because we want to 
represent Quebec's ideas."
The rules arrive as the field of potential candidates continues to narrow( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/list-of-potential-legault-replacements-grows-to-10-party-starts-
leadership-process ) and the race is on to obtain the support of non-aligned CAQ MNAs.
From a possible 10 people last week, the list has dropped to a few including Economy Minister Christine Fréchette, 
Justice Minister Simon Jolin-Barrette and Environment Minister Bernard Drainville.
To date, Fréchette leads the pack in caucus support with endorsements from five ministers and four MNAs. 
Drainville has the approval of two MNAs plus a group of CAQ youth members. Jolin-Barrette has the support of one 
minister and five MNAs.
Among those who have dropped out of the race are Finance Minister Eric Girard, Public Security Minister Ian 
Lafrenière, and International Relations Minister Christopher Skeete.
Two ministers on the initial list, Municipal Affairs Minister Geneviève Guilbault and Education Minister Sonia 
LeBel, announced in the last few days that they are not running and plan to leave politics.

work, Brigitte Legault said.

renew a membership card in order to vote in the race.

we have to. But it is an opportunity. We want to invite people to come to the party and re-write parts of it because 
ultimately we want to represent the Quebec of today and the people's interests.
"We are are this coalition and we are inviting people to come in with their ideas. with their points of view, with their 
perspectives. We don't just want members to be able to get to a number. We want members because we want to 
represent Quebec's ideas."

https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/list-of-potential-legault-replacements-grows-to-10-party-starts-
leadership-process ) and the race is on to obtain the support of non-aligned CAQ MNAs.

Justice Minister Simon Jolin-Barrette and Environment Minister Bernard Drainville.

Drainville has the approval of two MNAs plus a group of CAQ youth members. Jolin-Barrette has the support of one 
minister and five MNAs.
Among those who have dropped out of the race are Finance Minister Eric Girard, Public Security Minister Ian 
Lafrenière, and International Relations Minister Christopher Skeete.

LeBel, announced in the last few days that they are not running and plan to leave politics.

title: Premier supports rank-and-file officers Ford dismisses concerns around probe
body:
Premier Doug Ford has weighed in on the corrupt police officer scandal that was detailed by York Region Police 
in an investigation named Project South last week and the upcoming probe by Ontario's inspector general of 
policing. 
Ontario's Inspector General Ryan Teschner announced on Monday that he's going to be looking at all 45 police 
forces across Ontario in the wake of the Toronto Police Service announcement that seven police officers and one 
retiree are facing various charges, including allegedly passing along information to organized crime and drug 
trafficking. 
Ford described the upcoming investigation as a "review," and despite the allegations, voiced his support for rank-
and-file officers. 
"I just want to make sure that the people of this province understand that our police are there to support us, just to 
keep our community safe, and I believe 99 per cent of them do. Yes, are there are a couple bad actors in any 
organization? Yes, they're going to be held accountable," said Ford on Tuesday at a press conference outside of 
his office at Queen's Park. 
"Talking to front-line police officers that I do, they are frustrated and angry, more than the people are, but this 
investigation or review, I should say, is going to make sure that we continue to have the greatest police in the entire 
world."
On Monday, Teschner spoke about his plans for the wide-reaching investigation. 
"Organized crime is insidious, and ... we have to ensure that our organizations are sufficiently strong to prevent and 
where necessary, detect and intervene," Teschner said at Queen's Park.
Teschner said that the inspection would examine the following issues: supervision; screening and vetting during 
recruitment and throughout an officer's career; access and clearances for police databases; management of 
evidence and property; and substance abuse and fitness for duty.
Some police associations and critics see Teschner's probe as too broad, as opposed to digging into the alleged 
corruption that seems to be centred on Toronto's 12 Division. 
Page 2 of 2
Premier supports rank-and-file officers Ford dismisses concerns around probe
Ford disagreed with those concerns.
 "I have confidence in Ryan Teschner, he's going to dig deep. He's not going to leave any stone unturned. And this 
is also supported by all our chiefs right across the province, the commissioner and everyone else. They're more 
frustrated than the people right now, and the police officers, front-line police officers, are frustrated as well. We have 
to have trust in our police services right across the board, and I'm confident they'll do a great job," said the premier.

title: Premier, city leaders slam RCMP remark that Surrey extortion shootings 'not a crisis'
body:
Premier David Eby, Surrey Mayor Brenda Locke and Surrey Coun. Mandeep Nagra expressed alarm Wednesday 
after B.C. RCMP Assistant Commissioner John Brewer labelled the city's recent extortion-related shootings "not a 
crisis," warning the comment undermines public confidence amid escalating gun violence.
"It's hard to think of a situation where you're unable to do business, you don't feel comfortable in your own home, 
you're facing gunshots, and where residents in their homes are shooting back at people who are shooting at their 
homes, as anything other than a crisis," Eby said.
He added that if Brewer does not feel the urgency, "perhaps he is not the right person to head up this task force."
"The reason we established this task force ... was to respond to a crisis," Eby emphasized at a news conference, 
stressing that Brewer's remarks could erode public confidence.
The controversy arose as Surrey faces a surge in extortion-related violence. Police reported 132 extortion attempts 
in 2025 - 49 involving shootings - and eight more so far this year.
Brewer, the head of the B.C. Extortion Task Force, made the controversial comment at a news conference on 
Tuesday after being asked whether police had lost control of public safety in Surrey.
"This is not a crisis. A crisis is what's happening out there with drug overdoses - that's a crisis, people are dying," he 
added. "This is a threat to public safety, absolutely, and I take it very seriously."
Brewer's comments came hours after Surrey police reported the city's 35th suspected extortion case of 2026, 
involving a shooting at a business earlier that morning. Brewer acknowledged Tuesday that there has been an 
"uptick" in extortion-related gun violence so far this year.
On Wednesday afternoon, Brewer walked back his remarks.
"I want to apologize for challenging the term 'crisis' yesterday, as it has become the focus and called into question 
the RCMP's commitment to addressing extortions in B.C. That was not my intention. The opportunity to provide an 
update and reassure the public has instead impacted public confidence.
Page 2 of 3
Premier, city leaders slam RCMP remark that Surrey extortion shootings 'not a crisis'
"The task force's commitment to addressing the ongoing threats and violence has not wavered. Our efforts have 
never been limited because of a term. Extortions remain one of our highest priorities."
A business in the 7200-block of King George Boulevard was targeted in an extortion shooting on Tuesday, Jan. 20, 
2026.
A provincial task force was formed in September, including the RCMP, municipal police agencies, transit police, and 
the Canada Border Services Agency. Task force investigators have handled 32 cases across the Lower Mainland, 
according to an RCMP news release.
Charges have been approved against seven people, some Canadian and some not, while 111 foreign nationals are 
under investigation for potential inadmissibility to Canada under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, 
RCMP said. To date, nine of those individuals have been removed from Canada.
In the Lower Mainland, extortion cases have mostly targeted South Asian communities, with victims threatened with 
violence if they do not meet demands for money.
Earlier in the week, Surrey police said people targeted in an extortion-related shooting on Saturday tried to shoot 
back. Brewer urged people not to take matters into their own hands, saying, "We are now actively hunting these 
extortionists. We will root them out from every dark corner they try to hide in, and we will either put them before the 
courts, or they will be deported."
Surrey's elected leaders weighed in with criticism.
Mayor Brenda Locke said that residents and business owners are living in constant fear, and communities "cannot 
wait any longer."
"Police are working hard, but we need a coordinated, nationwide approach that prevents these crimes and protects 
Canadians," Locke said in a statement.
Scenes from the Ustaad G 76 restaurant at 2160 King George Boulevard following an extortion related shooting in 
Surrey on Oct 6, 2025.
The mayor urged Ottawa to appoint a national extortion commissioner to address the root causes of extortion and 
implement immediate solutions.
"Canadian law enforcement tools are not enough to protect the public from the magnitude of extortion and violence 
we are experiencing. We need strong federal leadership to protect Canadian communities and restore public 
confidence."
Surrey Coun. Mandeep Nagra said Wednesday that Brewer's statement that extortion-related shootings were not a 
crisis was "tone-deaf, outrageous and insulting."
"There has been one extortion shooting per day since the start of the year," Nagra said. "Businesses shot up. 
Families terrorized. Victims arming themselves. And the RCMP Task Force says it's not a crisis?"
Nagra is demanding that the province instruct the RCMP to prioritize extortion in Surrey and boost funding and 
resources for the Surrey Police Service.
"Surrey is paying the price for a broken RCMP policing model and provincial neglect," Nagra said. "The RCMP has 
failed Surrey. The province has failed Surrey. And now we know why, because they don't even think this is a crisis."

title: Pressure mounts on Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez to resign amid crisis
body:
QUÉBEC - Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez is facing increasing pressure from prominent Liberals to step 
down amid an ongoing crisis within the party. 
But the former federal cabinet minister insists he will remain in office and that he can still win the next provincial 
election. 
"I was elected by the party members because they know I have the experience to beat the (governing Coalition 
Avenir Québec) and beat the Parti Québécois," the embattled leader told reporters Thursday morning on the 
sidelines of his party's caucus meeting in Quebec City. "I'm not going anywhere."
A day earlier, Quebec's anti-corruption police announced they were launching a criminal investigation of the 
Quebec Liberals, following allegations of vote-buying during the leadership race that Rodriguez won in June.
The news has prompted some Liberals to call openly for the leader's resignation, claiming the ongoing crisis has 
damaged the party with less than a year to go before the next election. 
Former Liberal minister Christine St-Pierre said the anti-corruption unit's investigation is the straw that broke the 
camel's back.
"It's undermining his leadership," she said in an interview with The Canadian Press on Thursday. "It's up to him to 
make the decision, but I urge him to seriously consider the best interests of the party."
Another former Liberal minister, Serge Simard, called for Rodriguez to step down. 
"The die is cast. The damage is done. So, from this point on, if we want to put this behind the party — a party that 
has done a lot for Quebec, it must be said — we have to stop this now and replace the leader. We have no choice, 
we've reached that point," he said. 
Simard supported one of Rodriguez's rivals, Charles Milliard, in the leadership campaign, and is now inviting 
Milliard to re-enter the race if the Liberal leader were to step aside. "I had confidence in Charles. I still have 
confidence in him," he said Thursday. 

Page 2 of 3
Pressure mounts on Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez to resign amid crisis
On Wednesday, Rodriguez's other main leadership rival, Karl Blackburn, told Radio-Canada that the situation is 
"extremely worrying."
"I think that Mr. Rodriguez, in this context, certainly has to ask himself some serious questions," he said. 
Blackburn did not rule out replacing Rodriguez if he were to resign. 
A third former Liberal minister, Jean D'Amour, is also calling on Rodriguez to step down for the good of the party.
"I think the time has come for him to prove his commitment to the party and, unfortunately, to leave. I'm not doing 
this lightly, but I talk to activists, I talk to association presidents, and these people are a little fed up, exasperated 
with the situation," he said in an interview with The Canadian Press on Wednesday.
The Liberal caucus was thrown into turmoil in November after former parliamentary leader Marwah Rizqy fired her 
chief of staff without consulting Rodriguez. He later expelled her from the caucus, saying she had not explained her 
reasons to him and that she lacked loyalty.
Shortly after Rizqy dismissed her chief of staff, Le Journal de Montréal published text messages suggesting some 
party members who voted for Rodriguez could have received cash rewards. It's unclear whether the two stories are 
connected.
Last week, Rodriguez announced he had expelled a second Liberal member of the legislature, Sona Lakhoyan 
Olivier, from his caucus because of an investigation by Quebec’s ethics commissioner. 
The office of the ethics commissioner said it would examine whether Lakhoyan Olivier used resources from her 
constituency office for partisan purposes during the leadership race. 
Montreal radio station 98.5 FM named Lakhoyan Olivier as one of the two people behind the text messages 
reported by Le Journal de Montréal, but she has denied that claim and has sent a legal letter to station owner 
Cogeco.
The Canadian Press has not verified whether the text messages were authentic.
Rodriguez has said he welcomes the investigations, and he has nothing to hide. He has separately asked a retired 
judge to investigate the claims. 
In Quebec City on Thursday, the mood among Liberal caucus members was downcast, though they have not 
publicly broken ranks with their leader. Liberal Enrico Ciccone said his constituents were beginning to talk to him 
about the controversy. 
"We are in a difficult situation today. We are terribly hurt. We work so hard for the people in our ridings. What we 
want to know is the whole truth," he said. 
Another Liberal member of the legislature, Monsef Derraji, reminded reporters that he was not involved in any 
candidate's leadership campaign. "These are extremely difficult times," he said. "Every day, we learn something 
new."
But others reiterated their support for Rodriguez. "I am prepared to go to war with him," said Liberal Linda Caron. 
"Nothing wrong was done during the campaign."
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Dec. 11, 2025.

title: Prime Minister Mark Carney deserves time to get results, says former Arctic College president
body:
Russia has been banned from the Olympics since 2017 due to a doping scandal and, as long as they’re making 
war on other countries, they should stay banned, says Mike Shouldice, of Rankin Inlet. 
Shouldice said the harsh part of the ban is that athletes only have so many years before they’re no longer of 
Olympic calibre. 
He said an athlete trains for four years, then misses an Olympics and has to wait an additional four years and, in 
many cases, their Olympic career is nearing its end. 
“Is it unfair?” ponders Shouldice. “That must be a brutal moment when your government gets you banned from 
competing, but the world has changed. 
“Look at all the international events — FIFA (International Association Football Federation) and many other 
international agencies are discussing what’s the U.S.A.’s next role? Is it still a safe place for athletes? They have 
their doubts. 
“There’s consequences for all these actions we’ve been witnessing.” 
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney put himself in the history books earlier this month due to his speech given 
at World Economic Forum, according to Shouldice. 
He said he views Carney’s speech as extremely positive, but now he worries somebody might seek revenge 
against him. 
“As far as our relationship with China, you know what the deal breaker is? There is none. 
“I mean, I think he’s (Carney) right. Somebody mentioned to me recently that our carbon footprint will be much 
greater. And I thought, is a carbon footprint a deal breaker for me if Canadian industry and Canadians in general 
stay strong and we don’t have massive layoffs and unemployment? No, it’s not a deal breaker for me.” 

Page 2 of 3
Prime Minister Mark Carney deserves time to get results, says former Arctic College president
Shouldice said, to him, the focus right now is the car industry in Ontario. He said that industry is concerned it’s 
going to lose something, because (U.S. President Donald) Trump has said, ‘If you boys don’t come back and build 
in the States, then all deals are off.’ 
“The auto industry is huge in this country and I want to see our workers continue to earn those nice, big pay 
cheques. They make big money. 
“So, if we cozy up to some different partners; if we send our lumber somewhere else, if our potash is being sold in 
Europe, if we do these large projects across Canada where, say, the Churchill Port develops in Manitoba and we 
ship out elsewhere and avoid a lot of foolishness by not going through the States — then we’re moving in the right 
direction to strengthen our own economy, I would say.” 
Carney hasn’t been prime minister for a year yet, Shouldice noted, recommending that Canadians give him a 
chance to see what develops under his leadership. 
“Trump was confusing Greenland with Iceland this past week, and I think we’re seeing the start of a slippery slope 
for this guy and his silliness. Let’s see where we go.”

for this guy and his silliness. Let’s see where we go.”

title: Property crime down during July to September
body:
Pearl Lorentzen Local Journalism Initiative Reporter, Lakeside Leader
Staff Sgt. Casey Bruyns is the detachment commander for the Slave Lake RCMP. Last week, he reported to the 
Town of Slave Lake and M.D. of Lesser Slave River on the July to September crime statistics. Crimes were done in 
both, he said.
Town
Bruyns attended the December 16 town council meeting. 
Property crimes have decreased, said Bruyns, over the last few years. The number of mental health calls are also 
down. He’s not sure why mental health calls are down, but a nurse from Athabasca has come up several times 
recently which might be part of it. This is through the Police and Crisis Team (PACT) program, which pairs a nurse 
and RCMP officer. 
The Slave Lake RCMP’s top priority is targeting offenders of property crimes. 
From July to September, said Bruyns, the detachment did 191 patrols in hot spots, 202 in industrial areas, and 84 in 
rural areas. 
The second priority is to enhance public confidence and engagement. 
An officer goes into school each month, said Bruyns, and the RCMP has engaged with the community in other 
ways. 
The written report mentions Riverboat Daze, Coffee with a Cop, a meeting with the hospital manager, a 
presentation at Northern Lakes College, Beach Fest, meeting with town council, Slave Lake air show, and a 
presentation to seniors at the Slave Lake Native Friendship Centre on fraud and telephone scams. 
The detachment also sends out media releases on specific cases and monthly overviews. 
Councillor Cindy Williams asked if the decrease in mental health calls was seasonal.

Page 2 of 4
Property crime down during July to September
Usually, until hunting season starts the calls are higher, says Bruyns, and go down when people are hunting and 
fishing. However, this year, it was down before then. The RCMP officers have been using an app in non-crisis 
situations to get a sense of what types of support a mental health call might need. 
Bruyns mentioned three investigations in town during July to September, which had gone through the court system. 
A person assaulted someone with a baseball bat and broke their arm, he said. The Crown prosecutor dealt with this 
through a peace bond, which means the perpetrator has to keep conditions, but does not get a criminal record. 
The second case was a break and enter with a fire. The person had other outstanding files. They dealt with four of 
them including this one, which had a total sentence of 110 days in jail and one year of probation. 
The third case was of a curfew check on someone who was on conditions, but who wasn’t home. A warrant was 
issued for their arrest. They were found, arrested, released, went to court, and pled guilty. They were fined $500. 
The Slave Lake RCMP detachment has 17 RCMP officers. Of these, 13 positions are paid for by the town, and four 
are paid for by the province, with support from the M.D. of Lesser Slave River. As of the end of September, the 
detachment had 11 out of 13 municipal officers.
Since then, said Bruyns, he’s hired a corporal who will move as soon as he can sell his house. 
The municipal officers are allowed to take training, but the province has frozen training for officers it is paying for.
All of the officers patrol the town and M.D. of Lesser Slave River. 
Councillor Kimberly Hughes asked for a greater RCMP presence in school zones in the morning and afternoon. 
She’s very concerned about illegal turns, etc. 
It is a priority, if nothing else comes up, said Bruyns, but the afternoons have been very busy with motor vehicle 
collisions. 
Councillor Craig Hudson asked if the RCMP patrolled Mitsue Roads during shift changes for the mills and if the 
RCMP contacted Alberta Transportation when roads need cleared from snow. The answer was yes.
M.D.
Flatbush area is patrolled by the Westlock RCMP and the rest of the M.D. of Lesser Slave River is patrolled by the 
Slave Lake RCMP. Westlock detachment commander Staff. Sgt. Jeff Sehn and Bruyns both presented to council on 
December 18.
The priorities were similar for the detachments: property crimes, community engagement, and prolific offenders.
From April to September, Westlock RCMP had a 20 per cent drop in property crimes, including a 52 per cent drop 
in break and enters. Crime was also down in the rest of the M.D.
Bruyns said property crime was down 25 per cent and persons crime 30 per cent. Crime in Slave Lake had been 
going down for seven quarters, but the M.D. often fluctuates.
One investigation into a Westlock prolific offender resulted in the seizure of suspected drugs and 15 criminal code 
and drug charges, said Sehn. For Westlock, three people with mental health issues are the source of many calls.
In the rest of the M.D., the mental health files are down, said Bruyns.
Bruyns mentioned three files in the M.D. In Canyon Creek, a man breached a no-contact condition. He was 
arrested and held in custody. He went for a mental health assessment and was deemed fit to stand trial. The trial 
will be in January 2026. In Smith, a prolific offender tried to steal a pickup. Police returned to the area several times, 
arrested him, and he was released on conditions. The case is before the courts. By Chisholm, the RCMP were 
Page 3 of 4
Property crime down during July to September
called to a roll-over. The pick-up was stolen and the police found suspected cocaine and methamphetamine. The 
driver was charged and the matter is before the courts.
M.D. Councillor Lester Vanhill lives in the Cross Lake area. He asked about an RCMP officer, who was working 
out of the Westlock detachment, who was charged with breach of trust.
The officer was part of the Alberta Traffic Services Unit, said Sehn, so had an office in the detachment, but wasn’t 
under his command. Sehn had updated the M.D. CAO about the case when the man was charged, and can provide 
another update.
Deputy Reeve Norm Seatter mentioned that council had toured the RCMP real-time operations centre in Edmonton, 
and he was impressed. He could see how the centre supports officers working in rural areas.
Council asked about the status of traffic patrols moving from the Westlock to Slave Lake detachment. The positions 
are empty, said Bruyns. They would just need to be transferred on paper, then hired, but nothing has happened so 
far.
“We’ll keep pushing from this end,” said Reeve Murray Kerik.
Councillor Brad Pearson asked if there were people sleeping rough in the community who were in danger from the 
cold.
“Yes,” said Bruyns. There is no homeless shelter, and “nothing on the horizon,” but a University of Alberta 
professor will be doing a study in Slave Lake in March, which may shed some light on the situation.

title: Province advances rejected condo project Plan has Oakville council at odds with Queen's Park
body:
The Ford government is moving ahead with controversial plans for a condo project that would see 11 skyscrapers 
built on an Oakville plot the size of the Rogers Centre - all against the local town council's wishes.
The government recently posted a proposal for minister's zoning orders to greenlight the project, which would bring 
more than 11,000 people to an area under five hectares near the Oakville GO station. The project would benefit a 
company partly owned by a developer Ford has described as a personal friend.
The orders, known as MZOs, allow the province to make changes to land zoning rules, overriding municipalities' 
visions for what best suits their communities. The Ford government has been criticized for being overzealous in its 
use of the fast-tracking tool to the benefit of certain developers.
Oakville council and the province have been at odds over their vision for the land near Oakville GO station for the 
past year. 
After the town council did not approve the original building applications filed by the developers, the Ontario 
government stepped in and proposed a similar complex be built through a provincial initiative known as transit-
oriented communities (TOC), which is not required to conform with local policies and is typically authorized through 
an MZO.
The Ministry of Infrastructure is now seeking public input on the request for MZOs for the Oakville TOC until Jan. 2.
Council members have repeatedly objected to the TOC plan. In November, the province slightly revised its plan for 
the high-density development. It lowers the tallest building height from 59 storey to 56 while trimming 20 residential 
units down to 6,881.
Oakville Coun. Janet Haslett-Theall called the changes "minuscule" and said her concerns remain about the "mega 
density" of the proposed development.
"What we need is responsible density. We need some common sense about how many people you put in such a 
small area," the councillor said.
Haslett-Theall said Oakville council continues to be blindsided with the province's plans over the development. 
Page 2 of 3
Province advances rejected condo project Plan has Oakville council at odds with Queen's Park
She said she only learned about the MZO proposal from a member of the community who stumbled upon it on the 
Environmental Registry of Ontario website.
Ash Milton, a spokesperson for the Office of the Minister of Infrastructure (MOI), said the TOC program will deliver 
homes of different sizes near GO transit and "community benefits that wouldn't exist without this program." Using 
MZOs "provides critical zoning certainty, enabling new homes and public amenities to be built quickly," he said.
A previous Star investigation found that Distrikt Developments and affiliated companies spent more than $120 
million buying the four plots of land from 2020 to 2024 that now make up the TOC. One of the landowning 
companies is co-directed by Christopher Bratty. Bratty is a developer who sat at Table 3 at Ford's daughter's 
September 2022 wedding, according to a copy of the reception's seating plan. Ford had told Ontario's integrity 
commissioner that the developer attendees were personal friends. Bratty and Emil Toma, president of Distrikt 
Developments, have been active donors to Ontario's Progressive Conservatives since Ford became the leader.
Distrikt also hired Amir Remtulla to lobby the Ontario government for intensification in Oakville's Midtown area. 
Remtulla worked as chief of staff to the late Rob Ford, the premier's brother, from 2011 to 2012.
Distrikt's Toma has previously defended the proposed development, saying it "will provide new housing, privately-
owned publicly accessible open spaces (POPS), office and retail spaces, as well as public amenities directly next to 
the busiest GO station, other than Union Station, in all of Ontario."
"Locating density on underutilized lands next to existing transit infrastructure to meet population growth targets 
makes sense and is widely supported by planning professionals and provincial policy direction," Toma told the Star 
earlier this year.
Critics in Oakville say the province's approach is an unsettling echo of the Greenbelt scandal, where Ford 
government decisions that disproportionately benefited certain developers were imposed over local objections.
"Once you get the zoning, then he's (landowners) got the money. It's all about the zoning," Allan Elgar, a town and 
regional councillor, said, noting the developer may sit on the land and wait for the best time to maximize returns.
The transit-oriented communities program is a provincial initiative designed to increase housing supply, create jobs, 
build complete communities and offset the cost of station construction. Upon approval, the Oakville TOC 
development is expected to be built in 25 years, according to the TOC website.
"How does this accelerate housing? It's the opposite," Elgar said.
Distrikt and the province did not answer questions about when the construction is expected to start.
It's unclear who first suggested Distrikt's lands could be developed as a transit-oriented community.
Oakville Mayor Rob Burton told a council meeting that "Distrikt was approached by the province." In an interview 
with the Star, Burton would not elaborate on his statement except to say it was accurate and he stood by it.
Burton, who says his opposition to the TOC plan remains unchanged, told the Star that he appreciates the 
province's voluntary posting of MZO proposals as "an additional opportunity for public consultation."
In early 2025, the town council voted unanimously not to endorse the province's TOC plan and passed its official 
plan amendment for its Midtown area, which includes the four parcels owned by Distrikt.
The Distrikt land sits roughly 300 metres away from the Oakville GO Station, and makes up just five per cent of 
what Oakville's planners have dubbed "Midtown," a 103-hectare belt of underutilized commercial and industrial land 
just south of the QEW.
Under Oakville's official plan amendment for Midtown - which is still awaiting approval by the province - the 
development of the Distrikt land would add less than half of the population the provincial TOC plan would bring, as 
Page 3 of 3
Province advances rejected condo project Plan has Oakville council at odds with Queen's Park
the amended plan set maximum residential density and tower height threshold much lower than what the province 
put forward when it designated the area a transit-oriented community.
The province can override Oakville's plan for the land through an MZO.
Last December, Ontario's auditor general released a report that found the province had used MZOs 114 times from 
2019 to 2023 under Premier Doug Ford's government, which is a 17-fold increase in usage from the previous 20 
years.
The report also found that infrastructure and site servicing issues were often not identified before the province 
issued an MZO. This has resulted in significant delays in roughly one-in-five projects.
An Oakville staff report said the traffic volumes from the TOC will exceed the capacity of the already-congested 
roads, and could block buses from getting in and out of the Oakville GO Station and affect GO transit operations.
Distrikt plans to build new roads within the TOC to address the increase of vehicle traffic, as well as widening 
existing roads, the minister's spokesperson Milton said, noting the proposal also includes pedestrian-friendly 
streetscapes, bike paths, green spaces, and community amenities.
