title: Province launches review of all 45 policing services Inspector general probe met with call for independent
body:
Ontario's inspector general of police is launching a review of all 45 police services across the province after 
Toronto officers were snared in an organized-crime corruption probe last week.
While seven Toronto police officers and one retiree are now facing charges, Ryan Teschner, a lawyer and former 
executive director of the Toronto Police Services Board, announced Monday that his office will inspect all police 
services to "ensure that our systems are as strong as possible to detect these instances."
The Toronto officers were swept up in a York Regional Police investigation into organized crime related to the 
towing industry and face various charges, ranging from mischief to conspiracy to obstruct justice to drug-trafficking. 
"Organized crime is insidious, and ... we have to ensure that our organizations are sufficiently strong to prevent and 
where necessary, detect and intervene," Teschner said.
However, the decision to scrutinize all police departments has led to criticism that Ontario's largest force may not 
get proper scrutiny.
Liberal MPP Karen McCrimmon (Kanata-Carleton) is calling for a "full, independent judicial inquiry" that can run at 
the same time as Teschner's inspection.
"This is not a matter that can be handled quietly or internally," said McCrimmon, the critic for the solicitor general 
and public safety.
An inquiry, she said in a statement, would "investigate the full scope of these actions, identify systemic failures, and 
recommend meaningful reforms.
"The public deserves transparency, truth, and justice. Trust in our institutions can only be restored through 
openness, accountability, and real consequences for wrongdoing - no matter who is involved."
Lawyer Ian Scott, who was previously director of the Ontario Special Investigations Unit that examines serious 
injury or death involving police officers in the province, said the inspectorate is limited to reviewing policies and 
procedures.
Page 2 of 3
Province launches review of all 45 policing services Inspector general probe met with call for independent 
judicial inquiry
"There's going to be massive deflection over to the inspector general, who I don't think will be able to deliver the 
kind of punch that ultimately people think he can deliver just statutorily," Scott told the Star.
He said it's important to understand who knew what at the divisions where these officers worked, because officers 
have a duty to report any misconduct to their superiors.
"Someone had to know what's going on. I just can't believe they didn't know."
Last week, Toronto police Chief Myron Demkiw and police services board chair Shelley Carroll wrote a letter to 
Teschner calling for an inspection - with a "sector-wide strategy."
"In making your decision, please consider the extent to which these issues are not unique to any one police 
service," Demkiw and Carroll wrote.
Teschner also followed their specific request that the inspection would examine the following issues: supervision; 
screening and vetting during recruitment and throughout an officer's career; access and clearances for police 
databases; management of evidence and property; and substance abuse and fitness for duty.
Teschner said his inspection will not extend beyond those issues.
"We're not looking at individual conduct. That is not our role. We're not looking at criminal conduct. That's obviously 
the role of this ongoing investigation," Teschner said, in reference to York's probe.
At a separate news conference at city hall on Monday, Carroll and Demkiw said they were grateful the inspector

title: Province publisher named B.C. 's lieutenant-governor; This week in history: 1920
body:
The last thing a newspaper wants to do is to be scooped on some major announcement. Particularly when it 
involves your own editor and publisher.
But that's what happened on Dec. 18, 1920, when the Toronto Evening Telegram reported "Walter C. Nichol, editor 
and publisher of the Vancouver Daily Province, has been offered the lieutenant-governorship of British Columbia."
B.C. needed a new LG because the previous one, E.G. Prior, had died on Dec. 12. But Nichol told a Province 
reporter "that the dispatch in the Toronto Telegram is news to him: that he had heard nothing about the matter."
It was pure bunk. He was appointed to the job on Dec. 24, 1920.
The Province got scooped a second time on Christmas Day, when The Vancouver Sun published the official 
confirmation. The Province didn't publish on Christmas or Boxing Day. It wouldn't deliver the news until Dec. 27.
Being named the lieutenant-governor capped a remarkable career for Nichol, who had initially moved from Ontario 
to B.C. in 1897 to make his fortune in mining in the Kootenays.
That didn't work out, so he went back to his first love, newspapers. Nichol had started working as a cub reporter at 
the Hamilton Spectator in 1881, when he was only 15. In 1886, he moved to the Toronto Evening News, which had 
a weekly newsmagazine, Saturday Night.
By 1889, he was back in Hamilton, where he rose to editor of the Hamilton Herald. In 1896, he moved to London, 
Ont., and founded the London News, but left for the Kootenays the next year.
In Kaslo, he became the editor of The Kootenaian newspaper, and friends with the area's MP, Hewitt Bostock. 
According to Bessie Lamb's 1942 history of early Vancouver newspapers, Bostock was "a wealthy young 
Englishman ... who, having political aspirations, regarded a newspaper ally as an important factor in advancing his 
ambitions."
Bostock had founded the Province in 1894 as a weekly in Victoria, and after meeting Nichol hired him as editor. 
Nichol then convinced Bostock to move the paper to Vancouver in 1898.
Page 2 of 3
Province publisher named B.C. 's lieutenant-governor; This week in history: 1920
The first daily Province was printed in Vancouver on March 26, 1898, and Nichol would buy the paper from Bostock 
in 1901. The Province became known as a quality paper, and politically independent.
Nichol could have a sharp tongue - according to his listing in the online Dictionary of Canadian Bi- ography, he was 
sued for libel in December 1897 by then premier John Herbert Turner and attorney general Charles Edward 
Pooley. Nichol was found not guilty.
Like many newspaper editors of his day, he didn't always see eye to eye with his competitors, trashing the Victoria 
Daily Colonist as the "chief mouthpiece" of the Turner government in 1897.
Vancouver's longest-serving mayor, L.D. Taylor, worked for the Province before purchasing the World in 1905.
Taylor and Nichol feuded for years afterward, culminating in a full-page story/ad in the World on March 22, 1913 
that was headlined "The Smallness of Walter C. Nichol."
Nichol probably laughed all the way to the bank. The World went bankrupt and Nichol made a fortune, living in one 
of Shaughnessy's landmark mansions on The Circle, across the street from Hycroft.
He sold the Province to the Southam chain in 1923. He died Dec. 19, 1928 in Victoria, and left an estate of $2.7 
million, which is worth about $47.8 million today.
There were no hints of any scandals in Nichol's obituaries, but there could have been. His playboy son, Jack, was 
implicated in one of Vancouver's most sensational murders, the Janet Smith case.
Smith's death on July 26, 1924 was initially ruled a suicide, but many suspected foul play. A Chinese houseboy was 
framed for her death, but cleared, and the case affected race relations in Vancouver for decades.
After Ed Starkins published the book Who Killed Janet Smith in 1984, he got a tip that on his death bed in 1941, 
Jack Nichol had confessed to his nurse that he was there when Smith died.
Nichol had been having an affair with Lucille McRae, daughter of Hycroft owner Gen. A.D. McRae. She caught 
Nichol with Smith, and became enraged.
"She started attacking them, and Janet slipped, hit her head on a spigot and died," Starkins wrote in an updated 
version of his book in 2011.
Nichol and McRae were married to other people, so they faked the suicide to prevent a scandal.

title: Province sues youth group for $3.29M Non-profit accused of failing to train hundreds of marginalized young
body:
A Toronto youth group is facing a $3.29-million lawsuit by the provincial government over alleged misuse of money 
from the controversial Skills Development Fund.
In a statement of claim dated Dec. 11, the Ontario government says Justice Fund Toronto and its director, Yonis 
Hassan, the not-for-profit's "sole director, alter ego and directing mind," was awarded nearly $4 million by the 
Ministry of Labour in March 2023 to give "life skills training" for roughly 800 marginalized young people but failed to 
do so.
Filed in Ontario Superior Court, the lawsuit claims Hassan and the Justice Fund benefited from "unjust enrichment" 
of taxpayer dollars. 
Its allegations have not been proven in court. The Star made numerous attempts to contact Hassan, but did not 
receive a response. 
Hassan has had a media presence in recent years, including events with Noah "40" Shebib, a music producer and 
friend of the rapper Drake. Shebib, who previously referred to himself as a Justice Fund co-founder, is quoted, 
along with Hassan, in an August 2023 CBC story, saying Drake planned to donate $1 from every ticket sold to his 
"It's All a Blur" tour to the group.
Hassan is the only director named on the federal corporate records for the Justice Fund. Neither Shebib nor Drake 
face any allegations and neither were named in the lawsuit.
In the 12-page statement of claim, the government alleges that Hassan and his organization "repeatedly avoided or 
neglected" visits from Labour Ministry staff investigating "non-compliance" of the funding agreement. Justice Fund 
did not file all of the required expenditure reports which, the lawsuit said, led to a government-led forensic audit that 
found "inappropriate use" of the SDF money.
Last summer, on July 3, the ministry demanded repayment of $3.29 million. Two weeks later, the Justice Fund filed 
articles of dissolution to shoot down operations which, the government claimed, was a "breach of trust and 
fiduciary duties." That action was later cancelled and the organization remains active.
Page 2 of 3
Province sues youth group for $3.29M Non-profit accused of failing to train hundreds of marginalized young 
people
This is the second lawsuit filed by the province in the past two months that seeks repayment of the labour ministry's 
SDF grants.
Both demand millions of dollars paid out by the fund that says it gives grants to programs meant to provide training 
for in-demand jobs - with a focus on supports for "underrepresented communities." 
In early January, Keel Digital Solutions and its subsidiary, Get A-Head, were hit with a government lawsuit 
demanding the return of $22.3 million in grants from the Ministry of Colleges and Universities and $3.2 million from 
the Skills Development Fund, with an additional $400,000 in punitive damages.
Keel has said it will fight the lawsuit, promising to take legal action against the government. Last December, the 
Ontario Provincial Police launched a criminal investigation into Keel. 
While the Keel Digital lawsuit was announced by Premier Doug Ford's office, the government did not respond to 
the Star's questions on the Justice Fund statement of claim. 
On its Instagram site, the Justice Fund said it is "dedicated to supporting communities in conflict with the law."
Many of its posts speak against inequality in Toronto, noting a city divided, with some living in relative affluence 
while others struggle in communities traumatized by gun violence, poverty and higher rates of incarceration. 
When the funding was approved in early 2023, the agreement said the money was to be used "only" for the Justice 
Fund's Creative Pathway's project, which included "training and wraparound supports" to help young people find 
employment in creative industries. 
As part of its SDF agreement, Justice Fund was to provide ongoing expenditure reports, audited financial 
statements to the ministry and scheduled visits to the ministry staff. 
But Hassan, the lawsuit alleges, tried to evade oversight and problems began six months after the grant was 
approved. 
Ministry staff reported failed attempts to schedule a site visit, the lawsuit alleges. Hassan responded a day late to 
an official letter citing breach of agreement, the lawsuit said. He promised to file the required reports and offered a 
site visit.
When the government bureaucrat met with Hassan and another man for the planned "site" visit, it was not held at 
the group's place of business.
The men showed her an "incomplete" website for the program; requested an extension of the funding agreement 
and "disclosed that they were no longer providing on-site training to their participants," according to the lawsuit.
By August 2024, a forensic audit was underway and the following summer, in July 2025, the government sent 
Hassan a "demand letter" noting the auditors found "inappropriate use" of the SDF money. It sought "immediate" 
repayment. But two weeks later, the lawsuit said, the federally incorporated Justice Fund, filed for the dissolution 
that was later reversed.
In the lawsuit, the government lawyer said, "The defendant's misconduct demonstrates a high-handed, wanton, 
callous and contumelious disregard for the rights and interests of Ontario, resulting in significant losses, both 
financial and reputational."
According to legal dictionaries, contumelious means "insolent, rude or to act with disdain."
None of the money has been repaid, the lawsuit said.
"To date, no response to the demand letter has been forthcoming."

title: Provincial government responds to Deloitte report found to contain false citations likely generated by A.I.
body:
The provincial government says Deloitte is standing by its “conclusions and findings” in the Health Human 
Resources Plan report which The Independent found to contain citations that don’t exist.
In an email Saturday afternoon, Department of Health and Community Services Director of Communications Brian 
Scott said the department has “directed Deloitte to confirm the accuracy of the citations and literature review,” and 
that the global consulting firm “has since acknowledged the four citations noted are incorrect.”
As previously reported by The Independent, Deloitte used the four fabricated citations to support claims related to 
recruitment strategies, virtual care, monetary recruitment and retention incentives, and impacts of the COVID-19 
pandemic on healthcare workers.
“Deloitte has committed to expeditiously conducting a full of review of all the citations and will be required to report 
back to government with its findings,” Scott said. “We look forward to them completing their review so we can 
assess how serious an issue this is and take the appropriate steps.”
NAPE President Jerry Earle took to social media Saturday to say the Deloitte report revelations serve “as a 
cautionary note on potential consequences” of using artificial intelligence.
“NAPE has significant concerns about the planned integration of artificial intelligence in our healthcare system,” he 
said, adding the union was “contacted by a [Department of Health and Community Services] official to ensure the 
latest occurrence does not impact the overall Human Resources Plan completed by Deloitte, while also stating a 
comprehensive review is being conducted.”
Earle said that “despite assurances, if public funds are being allocated to private companies, we should expect 
higher standards. If a human employee made this error, it would likely result in disciplinary action. This is 
unacceptable and warrants immediate attention.”
This is the second time in under three months that non-existent academic articles have been found in major 
government-commissioned reports. In September, CBC/Radio-Canada reported that the province’s Education 
Accord, led by a team of researchers from Memorial University, also contained citations which appeared to have 
been generated using artificial intelligence technology.

Page 2 of 3
Provincial government responds to Deloitte report found to contain false citations likely generated by A.I.
That report cost the province more than $755,000. The Deloitte report, which was developed to help guide the 
government toward stabilizing human resources in the health sector, came at a cost of $1.6 million.
Last month Deloitte’s firm in Australia was found to have used generative AI in the production of a report for the 
Australian government. The story made international headlines and the company agreed to reimburse the 
government a portion of the fee.
Deloitte did not respond to The Independent’s questions by the time of publication.
In October Premier-designate Tony Wakeham told the Newfoundland and Labrador Teachers’ Association it was 
“embarrassing to the Liberal government that the Education Accord contains errors,” and that “when a report that 
is supposed to guide the future of education includes mistakes, it creates doubt among readers and undermines its 
credibility.”
The Independent asked the premier and the Department of Health and Community Services if the government will 
be requesting a refund from Deloitte in light of the errors, and if it will consider developing a policy around the use 
of AI in reports it commissions from third parties. They did not answer the questions.
The premier has also not yet publicly addressed the scandal.

pandemic on healthcare workers.
“Deloitte has committed to expeditiously conducting a full of review of all the citations and will be required to report 
back to government with its findings,” Scott said. “We look forward to them completing their review so we can 
assess how serious an issue this is and take the appropriate steps.”
NAPE President Jerry Earle took to social media Saturday to say the Deloitte report revelations serve “as a 
cautionary note on potential consequences” of using artificial intelligence.

said, adding the union was “contacted by a [Department of Health and Community Services] official to ensure the 
latest occurrence does not impact the overall Human Resources Plan completed by Deloitte, while also stating a 
comprehensive review is being conducted.”
Earle said that “despite assurances, if public funds are being allocated to private companies, we should expect 
higher standards. If a human employee made this error, it would likely result in disciplinary action. This is 
unacceptable and warrants immediate attention.”
This is the second time in under three months that non-existent academic articles have been found in major 
government-commissioned reports. In September, CBC/Radio-Canada reported that the province’s Education 
Accord, led by a team of researchers from Memorial University, also contained citations which appeared to have 
been generated using artificial intelligence technology.

That report cost the province more than $755,000. The Deloitte report, which was developed to help guide the 
government toward stabilizing human resources in the health sector, came at a cost of $1.6 million.

government a portion of the fee.

credibility.”

be requesting a refund from Deloitte in light of the errors, and if it will consider developing a policy around the use 
of AI in reports it commissions from third parties. They did not answer the questions.

title: Public needs to 'push back' before another covered bridge is lost, says official
body:
For over 50 years, Bev Mitchell has lived near the quaint Poirier covered bridge, about a 25-minute drive north of 
Moncton.
He still passes it daily on his walks with his trusty shepherd by his side, even if the sound of machinery buzzing on it 
is distressing.
Reminiscing, he chuckles at the thought of the wedding party that had to send for a painter to cover up some lewd 
graffiti on the bridge before the photographs were taken of the bride and groom at the cherished pastoral scene.
Mitchell also fondly recalls the children who would play nearby and swim in the cool waters of the Cocagne River 
below.
But now, like two other historic covered bridges that met their demise in the province this year, the Poirier Office 
Road Covered Bridge is coming down, the victim of neglect and disrepair.
Despite covered bridges promoted on tourism brochures and as familiar to New Brunswickers as lighthouses, sugar 
maple taps and lobster traps, the Holt Liberal government has no special plan for saving them.
Mitchell thinks that’s a mistake.
“I come down here probably two or three times a day. And believe me, I’m going to miss it,” he said recently as 
workers from the Department of Transportation disassembled the wooden span built in 1942, soon to be replaced 
by a steel modular bridge. “The guys working on it said that was one of the better ones they had to dismantle.”
Preservationists are lamenting that New Brunswick lost three covered bridges this year, the greatest number that 
has perished in a single year since 1989, leaving the province with only 56. In their heyday in the 1940s, the 
province had 340 covered bridges, one of the greatest collections in Canada.
The William Mitton Covered Bridge in busy Riverview was demolished in late February, and the Shepody River No. 
3 Covered Bridge, also called the Germantown Lake bridge, in Albert County, visible from Route 114, a major 
tourism corridor, was taken down in April.

Page 2 of 4
Public needs to 'push back' before another covered bridge is lost, says official
Kelly Cain, the deputy minister of transportation and infrastructure, or DTI, told a committee of politicians on Oct. 3 
that covered bridges are triaged just like any other spans in the provincial network.
Overall, New Brunswick has more bridges, roads and culverts than it can pay for upkeep and repair. The province 
prioritizes infrastructure that has more traffic, often leaving covered bridges in less busy rural areas behind.
“The covered bridges fail, and you can’t use them for transportation, school buses can’t cross, garbage trucks can’t, 
nothing,” she said. “Everybody wants you to keep the covered bridge and fix the covered bridge for pedestrians and 
ATVs and snowmobiles, which isn’t really, quite frankly, necessarily the number one mandate of DTI. Those are 
‘nice to haves.’
“So, you can invest all your money, because you only have so much, or actually spend it on transportation 
connectivity.”
Cain, who used to be the deputy minister of tourism, said covered bridges were “beautiful” and “iconic,” but her 
department did not have enough money to give them special attention. Her department’s mandate, she reminded 
the politicians on the public accounts committee, is to get traffic to where it needs to go as efficiently as possible.
“We have another one in St. Martins, everyone knows that’s the kissing bridge,” Cain said. “But to preserve and 
protect these assets simply for pedestrian recreational leisure use isn’t necessarily the mandate of our department 
in the throes of all the other things that we have to deal with.”
Bill Caswell has heard that argument before. The long-serving president of the National Society for the Preservation 
of Covered Bridges in the United States says officials often forget that the historic spans are appealing to tourists 
who have money to spend.
A native of Rhode Island, Caswell had never seen a covered bridge until he graduated from college and moved in 
1984 to take up a job at the New Hampshire Department of Transportation.
A supervisor gave him a pamphlet and told him if he wanted to get to know the state, start with the covered bridges.
It wasn’t long before Caswell began driving his family to out-of-the-way spots, eager to see something beautiful and 
different.
“Sunday afternoon drives became weekend long trips, became weeklong vacations,” he said, recalling he’d often 
pack up the camper with his kids. “From New Hampshire, to Vermont, to Quebec, to New Brunswick.”
Those trips have special memories, such as his middle daughter out of five children celebrating her 19th birthday in 
New Brunswick on a covered bridge and lighthouse tour, enjoying her first legal alcoholic drink.
Caswell has seen all 56 remaining covered bridges in New Brunswick and some that have since been destroyed. 
Most recently, he came to see the Mitton covered bridge last year before it was gone.
“It gets you off the road, going to see covered bridges. It gets you to places you normally wouldn’t see just driving 
the highways. And it wasn’t just the bridges – it was being able to explore these other communities and areas you 
wouldn’t normally visit,” he said.
“There’s a benefit to promoting that. You draw the tourists in, you bring them in to see the bridges, and they spend 
money at the restaurants and the hotels and the shops. There’s an economic benefit to the community when you 
promote covered bridges.”
Caswell recommended New Brunswick politicians and policymakers look at Vermont’s dedication to preserving its 
covered bridges, which began in earnest more than two decades ago. He said some states, counties and local 
towns in the United States have had such success celebrating their covered bridges that they are now erecting new 
ones.
Page 3 of 4
Public needs to 'push back' before another covered bridge is lost, says official
The United States has about 850 covered bridges, most of them in the northeast of the country, but only 600 are 
considered historic. Only the state of Pennsylvania, with more than 200 covered bridges, and Quebec, with 88, 
have bigger collections than New Brunswick’s.
Patrick Toth, president of the Covered Bridges Conservation Association of New Brunswick, doesn’t want his 
province to lose any more of the iconic spans.
He’s seen several success stories when communities rallied to save their bridges. A resident of Moores Mills, in the 
southwestern corner of the province, he remembers in 2013 when Trout Creek No. 5 Covered Bridge about five 
kilometres from his house was hit by a car. The province planned to replace it with a steel bridge, creating a public 
outcry. Following a public meeting, Toth said, the local MLA Robert Tinker got involved, and the bridge was 
eventually repaired, strengthened, and re-opened.
A similar rally was held to save the Vaughan Creek covered bridge in St. Martins. Because of the high volume of 
traffic going to the Fundy Trail Parkway, the province ultimately decided to build a new wooden span in 2022, the 
first double-barreled covered bridge in Canada, itself a tourism draw.
“Politics got involved, that’s why it was saved,” Toth said. “It’s the same in Hartland. They have the longest covered 
bridge in the world, and it gets a lot of attention. A lot of the other bridges, they’re dear to the locals, ‘I learned to 
fish there with my grandfather, and I learned to swim there underneath,’ and there are all kinds of nostalgic stories, 
adding an intrinsic value to the bridge other than a transportation network across the stream. But they’re not seen in 
the same light by DTI.”
He was saddened to see the Poirier bridge dismantled. Last month, he walked across it, half way through the 
demolition.
“I’ve seen bridges in a lot worse condition that were saved.”
Having met with DTI officials in the past, Toth believes the only way to save New Brunswick’s covered bridges is 
for local communities to rally and fight for their preservation.
“Public awareness is vital. People say, ‘oh, I thought covered bridges were protected.’ Well, they’re not. 
Unfortunately, DTI runs hot and cold on this issue depending on who’s in office.
“It’s up to the public to push back and save our covered bridges.”
– with files from Sarah Seeley

title: Public service watchdog calls for more funding to protect whistleblowers
body:
The Public Sector Integrity Commissioner is sounding the alarm that her office has a backlog of complaints so bad 
that it's threatening the office's credibility with whistleblowers.
In a letter to Treasury Board President Shafqat Ali, public service watchdog Harriet Solloway asked for a one-time 
injection of $6.7 million in addition to ongoing funding of $14.3 million. Solloway's request comes at a time when 
many departments and agencies are cutting their operational budgets( https://ottawacitizen.com/public-
service/ministers-carney-spending-review ) by up to 15 per cent over three years.
As a watchdog, Solloway's office is not required to undergo the same cut.
Solloway said the funding requested was necessary to "shore up the whistleblower and accountability regime and 
avert collapse."
Solloway's office received 638 complaints in 2025 alone, up from 419 in 2024, 313 in 2023 and 245 in 2022.
The office of the public service watchdog, which investigates cases of alleged wrongdoing( 
https://ottawacitizen.com/public-service/public-service-integrity-watchdog-investigations ) in the public service, 
launched 37 investigations last year and completed 17 of them.
In 2024, the office launched 46 investigations and completed 22, and in 2023 it launched 24 investigations and 
completed 20.
In an interview with the Ottawa Citizen, Solloway said that the funding requested would be used to increase staffing 
and to provide more space to speak confidentially with whistleblowers. Her office currently only has one interview 
room.
"We need space for interview rooms, space for offices, and we need an adequate fit-up so that we minimize the 
risks of people being seen," she said.
If granted, the $6.7-million boost would go towards a "fit-up" of the current office space as well as the procurement 
of additional space for "planned growth." The ongoing $14.3 million per year would go towards hiring 58 new "full-
time equivalents" or FTEs, a term designating the work of one full-time worker.
When asked about an increase in funding with thousands of public servants across the federal government set to 
lose their jobs in coming cuts( https://ottawacitizen.com/public-service/public-service-job-cuts-budget-2025 ), 
Solloway pointed to the need and value for a strong integrity regime.
Page 2 of 3
Public service watchdog calls for more funding to protect whistleblowers
"If looked in the context of the government budget, and one looks at what is accountability worth in the context of 
the overall government budget, I really think public servants as well as Canadians would think that this is a 
bargain," she said.
Solloway also pointed to an open letter to the public service( https://ottawacitizen.com/public-service/michael-sabia-
era-public-service-letter ) written by Michael Sabia, the clerk of the Privy Council, in which he advocated for more 
accountability.
"I really doubt that Canadians would disagree with that, I think Canadians want to see accountability," she said.
Solloway added that it's not an "either-or situation."
The Public Sector Integrity Commissioner's office was set up in the wake of the sponsorship scandal that plagued 
the governments of then-prime ministers Jean Chrétien and Paul Martin.

title: Quebec 'brownie bill' would ban vote buying in party leadership races
body:
QUEBEC - The CAQ government moved Friday to plug a hole in the electoral code that, up until now, has made 
vote buying in party leadership races legal.
The bill comes in response to allegations( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-
rodriguez-vote-buying-allegations ) that certain Quebec Liberal Party members received "brownies" - or $100 bills - 
to support Pablo Rodriguez in his successful run for party leader this spring. The proposed legislation was tabled 
Friday.
The Liberals have since launched an independent investigation( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebecs-liberals-inquiry-vote-buying-allegations ) into the 
matter and Quebec's anti-corruption unit( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/upac-quebec-
liberals-vote-buying-allegations ) has interviewed witnesses.
"Before the events of these last weeks, I didn't think it was necessary to table a bill like this one," Democratic 
Institutions Minister Jean-François Roberge said Friday after tabling the bill.
Roberge said he had been surprised to learn cash-for-vote schemes were legal in leadership races under Quebec's 
electoral laws.
"It was a blind spot," Roberge said. "I saw this problem, I wanted to fix it."
The bill would apply both to party leadership races and riding nomination contests. It would make it illegal to either 
offer or accept "a gift, loan, office, employment or other benefit" in exchange for a vote. It would impose a maximum 
penalty of $20,000 for a first offence and $30,000 for any subsequent offence.
Trading cash for votes is already illegal during a general election.
Vote-buying allegations surfaced in late November, when the Journal de Montréal published text messages 
between two unnamed people that suggested some voters had been paid $100 each to support Rodriguez.
While the Journal didn't name the individuals, Cogeco political analyst Jonathan Trudeau said the exchange was 
between Liberal MNA Sona Lakhoyan Olivier and Coalition Avenir Québec MNA Alice Abou-Khalil, who had been 
rumoured to have been trying to join the Liberals ahead of the 2026 election.
Page 2 of 3
Quebec 'brownie bill' would ban vote buying in party leadership races
Both MNAs deny the allegations and have threatened legal action.
On Thursday, Quebec Liberals excluded Lakhoyan Olivier from caucus( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/ethics-commission-investigation-liberal-sona-lakhoyan-olivier-
excluded-from-caucus ) pending an investigation from the legislature's ethics commissioner.
Prior to November, Roberge said he had never heard of allegations of a cash-for-votes scheme in a leadership 
race.
All three opposition parties had indicated ahead of the bill's tabling that they would support the proposed legislation.
"It's a good thing and it should be adopted," Liberal MNA André Albert Morin said Thursday. In November, 
Rodriguez had promised the Liberals would support such a measure.
"We were all surprised that it was legal," Québec solidaire MNA Alejandra Zaga Mendez said Friday ahead of the 
bill's tabling. She said that while her party would want to look over the bill first, "on the principle, we will be in 
favour."
Parti Québécois legislators had also said they would support the legislation. "We're surprised that it was not already 
forbidden," MNA Joël Arseneau said Friday.
"We never thought that people would be so creative as to say: 'We'll pay you to vote for our leader,'" Arseneau said. 
"That never crossed our minds."
Roberge said the government plans to pass the bill through an accelerated procedure, ideally before the session 
ends Dec. 12. "I had some discussion with other parties and I think we are committed as a group to do so," he said.

title: Quebec 's 'brownie bill' passes, banning vote buying in leadership races
body:
QUEBEC - Legislators rushed through approval of a law Thursday to plug a hole in Quebec's electoral code that, 
until now, had made vote buying in party leadership races legal.
The vote passed unanimously using an accelerated procedure.
Nicknamed the "brownie bill," the legislation responds to allegations that certain Quebec Liberal Party members 
received "brownies" - $100 bills - to support Pablo Rodriguez in his successful run for party leader this past spring.
Those allegations have spiralled into a deepening crisis for Rodriguez, who faces calls to resign( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-rodriguez-leadership ) following confirmation 
Wednesday that Quebec's anti-corruption police have begun an investigation( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-upac-investigation ) into his party.
"Unfortunately, there was a gap in the electoral law" allowing for vote buying, Democratic Institutions Minister Jean-
François Roberge said Thursday after the vote.
"We didn't know about that gap," he said, "and there were allegations about how that gap was used in the Liberal 
party."
The bill applies both to party leadership races and riding nomination contests, and makes it illegal to either offer or 
accept "a gift, loan, office, employment or other benefit" in exchange for a vote.
Such an act was already illegal during a general election.
Members of all four parties in the National Assembly have said they were surprised to learn cash-for-vote schemes 
were legal under Quebec law.
Rodriguez said in November( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/rizqy-doubles-down-on-chief-of-
staffs-firing-as-quebec-liberals-set-to-meet-in-montreal ) that he and campaign staff had been under the impression 
that vote buying was illegal during the leadership race. He committed at the time to amending his own party's rules 
to ban the practice if such a measure didn't pass the National Assembly.
Liberals voted for the bill "because they had an ethics problem," Roberge suggested. "The Liberals wanted to put 
this behind them, and I understand."

He said he couldn't "predict everything" when it comes to other possible gaps in election rules.
"Again and again, (the Liberals) find a new way to cross lines," Roberge charged.

title: Quebec auto board lied about cost overruns for online platform, inquiry finds
body:
QUÉBEC - Quebec's automobile insurance board lied to the provincial government to conceal exploding costs in 
the creation of the agency's online platform, says a public inquiry into the cost-overrun scandal.
Overseen by Judge Denis Gallant, the inquiry's final report says officials at the auto insurance board — Société de 
l’assurance automobile du Québec — undertook a conscious effort to mislead the public about the total cost of the 
project. 
“The commission concludes, based on particularly significant evidence, that the deceptive information disseminated 
by the (auto board) was not the result of careless errors, but rather a conscious action aimed at hiding the total cost 
of the program from parliamentarians and the government — and therefore from the public,” reads an excerpt from 
Gallant's report published Monday.
In February 2025, Quebec's auditor general reported that the new platform was expected to cost taxpayers at least 
$1.1 billion by 2027 — $500 million more than originally planned. The auditor's report followed the botched rollout in 
February 2023 of the platform, which led to major delays and long lineups at insurance board branches, where 
Quebecers take road tests, register vehicles and access other services. 
In response to the auditor general, Quebec Premier François Legault launched the inquiry last year led by Gallant, 
a Montreal municipal court judge. The judge's role was not to determine guilt, but rather to draw conclusions and 
make recommendations. His report says the online platform project was "too vast, too ambitious, and had to be 
implemented too quickly."
Speaking to reporters Monday, Gallant said, "People deliberately lied throughout this whole affair. We can ask 
ourselves, 'What can we recommend in a case like this?' It's difficult to recommend transparency and honesty, 
since that should be the absolute standard for those working in the public administration."
Among those named repeatedly in the report was Karl Malenfant, the former vice-president of information 
technology at the auto board. Malenfant held a news conference last week suggesting he was being scapegoated 
for the problem-plagued platform. He said he had nothing to reproach himself for and that the project he led is not a 
fiasco.

Page 2 of 3
Quebec auto board lied about cost overruns for online platform, inquiry finds
Gallant said that despite the agency's actions, members of the government and certain public servants did, at 
various times, obtain reliable information about the problems at the auto board.
The judge noted that in June 2023, Éric Ducharme, then president and CEO of the board, met with Geneviève 
Guilbault, the transport minister at the time, to discuss the status of the contract with the consortium of three 
private firms that were building the platform. During that meeting Ducharme had also told her about the auto board's 
intention to increase the value of the contract for a second time, the report said.
However, Guilbault, who is now municipal affairs minister, has always maintained — including during testimony 
before the Gallant inquiry — that she only became aware of the cost overruns in February 2025. She stood by that 
testimony on Monday, noting in a statement that her focus in 2023 was getting services back to normal and that she 
didn't have any specific recollection of that meeting with Ducharme involving project costs.
Gallant's report adds that Dominique Savoie, the secretary-general of the government, was informed in March 2023 
that costs were increasing, as was Legault's director of communications. The report says one of Legault's political 
advisers was also told about rising costs as early as August 2023. 
"In short, several government representatives were informed in 2023 of the (auto board's) decision to increase the 
value of the contract," Gallant wrote, specifying that those amendments did not provide "a complete history of the 
cost evolution."
Legault told a Montreal news conference on Monday the results of the inquiry confirm that his government was 
never told the project had reached $1.1 billion until the auditor general's February 2025 report.
"I'm not saying the government was perfect, we could perhaps have been more suspicious, we could have asked 
more questions," Legault said, adding, "the truth is important — that the (auto board) management lied to our 
government for years about the revised cost of the … project."
Legault said he will look into potential legal recourse against auto board directors who lied, adding that the 
province's anti-corruption police unit, known as UPAC, is investigating the scandal.
Gallant's report includes 26 recommendations, including that the government create a centralized entity specialized 
in IT transformation projects. It said the government's Cybersecurity Department — which includes a unit designed 
to accelerate IT projects — lacks "structural influence on decisions." The new entity, he said, should have stable, 
predictable funding, and public bodies should be required to use it for any digital transformation projects. He also 
recommends tightening the governance rules for state-owned corporations and promoting transparency and access 
to reliable information. 
"Learning from failures can only be based on one categorical imperative: the honesty of all public actors," Gallant 
wrote. "Every government official must make a conscious choice to be frank."
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Feb. 16, 2026.
- with files from Sidhartha Banerjee in Montreal

title: Quebec Liberal leader calls for external investigation into report on cash for votes
body:
MONTREAL - Pablo Rodriguez is facing his biggest crisis since becoming leader of the Quebec Liberals in June, 
after a news report on Wednesday alleged some party members were paid to vote for him in the leadership 
campaign.
Visibly shaken and combative, Rodriguez repeatedly told reporters he has nothing to hide and that he asked the 
president of the Liberals to investigate the allegations. He also said anyone found to have committed wrongdoing 
would face "extremely serious" consequences.
"I was a minister for many years, MP for many years — never did anyone question my integrity," Rodriguez said at 
party headquarters in Montreal, referring to his time in federal politics before he left to run provincially.
Rodriguez made the comments in response to a report by Quebecor alleging two people who "actively worked" to 
elect Rodriguez as Liberal leader had exchanged text messages suggesting some members would receive cash 
rewards in exchange for their votes.
The news outlet did not identify the names of the people who had allegedly sent the text messages and The 
Canadian Press has not verified whether the messages are authentic.
On Wednesday morning, 98.5 FM reported that Liberal MNA Sona Lakhoyan Olivier and CAQ MNA Alice Abou-
Khalil were the people involved in the exchange of text messages, but the two members of the legislature quickly 
denied the allegations.
"We don't even know if these texts are real or fake," Rodriguez said. 
Party president Rafael Primeau-Ferraro said that the party learned about "very vague" allegations in April with zero 
documentation. He didn't go into details.
The party executive added that the investigation would be handled by a third party.

Page 2 of 3
Quebec Liberal leader calls for external investigation into report on cash for votes
The latest revelations are piling on to other bad news this week for the party and Rodriguez. On Tuesday, 
Rodriguez dismissed Marwah Rizqy from her position as parliamentary leader and suspended her from the caucus, 
citing a "breach of trust."
He said he took the decision after learning that Rizqy had fired her chief of staff, Geneviève Hinse, without 
consulting him first, adding that he had “no idea” Hinse was dismissed.
Rodriguez, who doesn't hold a seat in the legislature, had entrusted Rizqy to serve as the party's leader in the 
national assembly until the 2026 general election. She had endorsed Rodriguez in the leadership race.
It's unclear whether the allegations in the text messages published on Wednesday are related to the drama 
between Rizqy and Hinse.
Rodriguez said the timing of the allegations in the text messages was not lost on him, saying the reports are 
diverting attention from the work the party has been doing to rebuild support among voters, especially 
francophones.
He said since he was elected leader, about 250 people have come forward to run for the party in the 2026 election. 
"The money is coming in … old donors are coming back. For the polls — it's clearly a two-way race and we are not 
far from the (Parti Québécois)."
In recent months the Liberals have been slowly climbing in the polls, with a November Leger survey putting them 
five points behind the first place PQ.
The crisis within the Quebec Liberals reached Ottawa on Wednesday, where a few of Rodriguez's former 
colleagues expressed their support for him.
"Pablo was not only my colleague, he was also my friend. I think he's the right person to manage crises," Stéphane 
Lauzon, the Liberal MNA for Argenteuil—La Petite-Nation, told reporters.
“Obviously, Pablo is a great friend. I support him,” added Pontiac—Kitigan Zibi MP Sophie Chatel.
“He’s a longtime colleague I’ve known for a very long time. I trust Pablo,” added Steven MacKinnon, leader of the 
government in the House of Commons.
For his part, Quebec Centre MP Jean-Yves Duclos acknowledged that the matter raises several questions. “I think 
a lot of people are asking questions about the situation, and obviously, I’m one of them, but we’ll see what the 
details are."
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2025.
—With files from Thomas Laberge and Caroline Plante in Quebec City, and Émilie Bergeron and Frédéric Lacroix-
Couture in Ottawa

body:
Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez has decided to resign, The Gazette confirmed Wednesday.
Only six months after winning the leadership, the pressure on Rodriguez following a series of allegations of ethical 
problems during his leadership campaign was too great.
Rodriguez is to announce his decision to the caucus later Wednesday. He is expected to meet the media Thursday.
The first sign he would leave came with news that an early-morning meeting of the party's MNAs Wednesday was 
delayed until the afternoon, which fuelled speculation.
La Presse reported( https://www.lapresse.ca/actualites/politique/2025-12-17/crise-au-plq/pablo-rodriguez-remet-en-
question-son-avenir-politique.php ) Wednesday that Rodriguez had called people close to him "in tears" Tuesday, 
questioning his future as Liberal leader following a series of events that have rocked the party.
His decision became almost inevitable as soon as it became clear he had lost the support of some members of the 
18-MNA Liberal caucus, which had previously been staunchly behind him.
There had been reports at least two MNAs had planned to ask Rodriguez to resign, but sources said ultimately the 
choice to leave was his alone.
"It was his decision," the source said.
Rodriguez, 58, a former federal Liberal MP, will have been leader of the provincial party for only six months, a first 
since it was founded in 1867.
He won the leadership in June( https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec-liberals-choose-pablo-rodriguez-as-new-
leader ), defeating four other candidates: Charles Milliard, Karl Blackburn, Marc Bélanger and Mario Roy.
Just last Friday at a news conference wrapping up the session at the legislature, Rodriguez vowed to stay on.
"The wind is blowing strongly, but I have a thick skin," he said at the time. "I know why I am here. It's because I'm a 
fighter. A captain does not leave the ship in the middle of the storm."
One source indicated early Wednesday that Rodriguez's hold on the caucus was no longer a given, following the 
latest allegations about fundraising in the leadership campaign.
Page 2 of 4
Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez is resigning
"He should do what is best for all of Quebec, the Liberals and for him," the source said.
Last week, as he entered an emergency caucus meeting, Nelligan MNA Monsef Derraji, who was neutral in the 
leadership race,( https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/a-dozen-former-liberal-mnas-and-ministers-call-on-
pablo-rodriguez-to-resign ) refused to say whether he supported Rodriguez.
The latest allegations of ethical shortcomings affecting the party were published in Le Journal de Montréal on 
Tuesday. A series of such reports have now rocked the Liberals for a month.
Tuesday's report said a businessman had reimbursed participants $500 each at a fundraising event that Rodriguez 
attended, in exchange for contributing to Rodriguez's campaign.
Organizers who worked for Rodriguez's leadership campaign said later Tuesday that they had confronted the 
businessman, who allegedly admitted to reimbursing donors.
Both the organizers and a spokesperson for Rodriguez say Rodriguez did not have any knowledge of the alleged 
payments( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-rodriguez-cash-envelopes-
campaign-allegations ). The organizers have asked Quebec's anti-corruption unit, known as UPAC, to investigate 
the allegations.
Le Journal, La Presse and Radio-Canada have all reported that wine and port importer and producer Emanuel 
Cabral, president of Global International Networks Wines &; Spirits, is the businessman in question. His lawyer, 
Mario Proulx, would not confirm or deny Cabral was involved in the alleged transactions.
Le Journal reported Wednesday( https://www.journaldemontreal.com/2025/12/17/enveloppes-de-500-pour-la-
chefferie-de-pablo-rodriguez--genevieve-hinse-a-signe-comme-responsable-de-levenement ) that Geneviève Hinse, 
the fired chief of staff of ex-Liberal house leader Marwah Rizqy, had been tasked with overseeing financing at the 
fundraiser in question. According to the publication, Hinse's signature could be found on the Élections Québec 
finance report for the event.
There is "no evidence" Hinse was aware of the alleged reimbursements, Le Journal reported.
Jacques Martineau, who was spokesperson for Rodriguez's campaign, told Le Journal that Hinse's role in the event 
was "administrative" and said she hadn't necessarily organized the event. The Gazette has reached out to Hinse's 
lawyer for comment.

The Liberals entered crisis mode on Nov. 17, when then-Liberal parliamentary leader Rizqy fired Hinse( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/genevieve-hinse-pablo-rodriguez-quebec-liberals ), her chief 
of staff. Hinse is a longtime associate of Rodriguez, who followed the former federal MP into Quebec politics. 
Rodriguez responded by firing Rizqy from her role as parliamentary leader and suspending her from caucus.
Why Rizqy fired Hinse remains unclear - a point Rodriguez made several times throughout the snowballing crisis.
While Rizqy hasn't spoken about Hinse's removal, she said via a legal letter that Hinse had committed "significant 
ethical breaches." La Presse reported that Hinse was fired over the alleged use of parliamentary funds for political 
activities, which is not allowed.
Hinse, for her part, is suing Rizqy for $500,000 and accusing her former boss of firing her without a valid reason.

liberal-caucus-as-crisis-grows ), Rodriguez expelled Rizqy from caucus, citing her refusal to meet with him.
Piling onto the conflict with Rizqy is a series of ethics allegations surrounding Rodriguez's campaign for Liberal 
leadership.
Page 3 of 4
Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez is resigning
Among the most explosive was a Journal de Montréal report landing just two days after Hinse's removal, alleging 
that certain Quebec Liberal Party members had been paid $100 each to vote for Rodriguez in the leadership race. 
The report was based on screengrabs of an alleged text exchange between two unnamed people who referred to 
payments of "brownies," a slang term for brown-coloured $100 bills, that would be exchanged for votes.
Such payments were not illegal at the time of the leadership race, though Rodriguez said his campaign was 
operating under the assumption that such payments weren't permitted. He maintains he had no knowledge of the 
allegations ahead of the Journal report. The Liberals have since ordered an inquiry into the allegations.

cash-for-vote exchanges during leadership races( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebecs-
brownie-bill-passes-banning-vote-buying-in-leadership-races ).
Cogeco political analyst Jonathan Trudeau said the alleged text exchange about the "brownies" was between 
Coalition Avenir Québec MNA Alice Abou-Khalil and then-Liberal MNA Sona Lakhoyan Olivier, prompting denials 
and threats of lawsuits from both politicians. Abou-Khalil was rumoured to have been planning a jump to the 
Liberals, but remains in the CAQ caucus.
While the CAQ said it took Abou-Khalil at her word, the Liberals said they would wait for the results of their 
independent investigation.
Then, in December, Rodriguez suspended Lakhoyan Olivier from caucus pending the results of a separate 
investigation by the legislature's ethics commissioner, in line with parliamentary rules.
The unfolding crisis has also caught the interest of Quebec's anti-corruption unit, which is investigating the 
fundraising allegations.

title: Quebec Liberal Party crisis: A timeline of events so far
body:
A conversation at the inauguration( https://montrealgazette.com/news/rem-inauguration-day-montreal-deux-
montagnes-branch ) of the Réseau express métropolitain's Deux-Montagnes branch this month may have been the 
unexpected start of the recent crisis within the Quebec Liberal Party, La Presse reported( 
https://www.lapresse.ca/actualites/politique/2025-11-26/crise-au-plq/la-discussion-qui-aurait-tout-bouscule.php ) 
Wednesday.
Drama has been brewing within the official opposition party since early last week, when Marwah Rizqy, 
parliamentary leader and MNA for St-Laurent, fired chief of staff Geneviève Hinse( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/genevieve-hinse-pablo-rodriguez-quebec-liberals ).
In the time since, Rizqy was ousted from her role as parliamentary leader by party leader Pablo Rodriguez; Hinse 
fired back at Rizqy( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-rizqy-hinse-lawyer-letter ) 
with a legal letter, then sued her; and it was revealed that the firing may have been related to the alleged misuse of 
National Assembly funds for partisan activities.
The turmoil in the party comes ahead of the 2026 provincial election, when Rodriguez plans to run for a seat in the 
National Assembly.
Here's a timeline of events thus far:
June 14: Quebec Liberals elect Rodriguez( https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec-liberals-choose-pablo-
rodriguez-as-new-leader ), former federal Liberal MP from Montreal,( https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec-
liberals-choose-pablo-rodriguez-as-new-leader ) as the new leader of the party. He won with 52.3 per cent of the 
vote, narrowly overtaking contender Charles Milliard, who received 47.7 per cent of the vote.
June 19: Rodriguez selects Rizqy( https://montrealgazette.com/news/pablo-rodriguez-picks-marwah-rizqy-to-lead-
liberals-in-legislature ) - known for her ability to hold the Coalition Avenir Québec government's feet to the fire - to 
lead the party in the National Assembly since he's not an MNA.
Liberal MP Fayçal El-Khoury, highlighted left, and Liberal MNA Marwah Rizqy among a group of politicians posing 
for photos during an inauguration event for the the Deux-Montagnes branch of the REM in Deux-Montagnes on 
Nov. 14, 2025.
Page 2 of 5
Quebec Liberal Party crisis: A timeline of events so far
Nov. 14: Federal, provincial and local politicians attend a ceremony for the opening of the REM's long-awaited 
Deux-Montagnes branch. A discussion between Rizqy and Liberal MP Fayçal El-Khoury may have sparked the 
drama that unfolded days later, according to La Presse. El-Khoury denied having a discussion with Rizqy about 
Rodriguez's leadership race and insisted he had no connection to the campaign, but La Presse later discovered he 
had raised funds for Rodriguez.
Nov. 17: Rizqy fires her chief of staff in a short email to members of the Liberal caucus, taking the party by surprise.
"We would like to inform you that Mme. Geneviève Hinse ... is no longer employed as chief of staff of the leader of 
the official opposition as of now," the email read.
La Presse reported the dismissal was related to the alleged use of the party's National Assembly budget to pay for 
partisan activities like Rodriguez's recent tour of the regions, which isn't permitted.
Nov. 18: Rodriguez ousts Rizqy as parliamentary leader over the firing of Hinse, claiming he wasn't consulted or 
given an explanation. Hinse was Rodriguez's chief of staff when he was a federal politician and decided to follow 
him into Quebec politics.
Rodriguez's decision to oust Rizqy, "while difficult, was necessary to ensure the cohesion and the good functioning 
of the Liberal caucus at the National Assembly," the party said in a statement.
Rizqy was replaced as parliamentary leader by Pontiac MNA André Fortin. She remains a Liberal but is suspended 
from the caucus until further notice.
Geneviève Hinse in 2019.
Nov. 19: Hinse fires back with a legal letter giving Rizqy 24 hours to admit the "absence of justified motive" for the 
firing, warning that she may sue her if she refuses.
In the letter, Rizqy is accused of violating the customs of the party by firing Hinse because such decisions are 
supposed to be made by the party leader.
Before the letter came out, Hinse defended herself in a statement: "I am obviously hurt by this situation, especially 
since I know nothing justifies my firing."
The same day, the Journal de Montréal reported( https://www.journaldemontreal.com/2025/11/19/il-faut-encore-
payer-pour-que-le-monde-vote-pablo-des-textos-troublants-derriere-la-crise-au-plq ) Élections Québec was looking 
into text messages insinuating Liberal Party members were paid to vote Rodriguez in as leader.
One exchange reads:
"So, everyone's going to get paid (this) week?"
"Yes. And don't forget, we're only returning the membership cards on May 8 in case something goes wrong. All 
that's left is the voting process and they get a brownie for voting."
A $100 bill is sometimes referred to as a "brownie" in slang.
Cogeco political analyst Jonathan Trudeau claimed the exchanges were between Alice Abou-Khalil, CAQ MNA for 
Fabre, and Sona Lakhoyan Olivier, Liberal MNA for Chomedey, both of whom denied the accusations.
Rodriguez called in an external auditor to investigate the Journal report, saying he had no knowledge of the 
allegations.
"We have nothing to hide," he said at the time. "I have nothing to hide. Nobody has anything to hide."
Page 3 of 5
Quebec Liberal Party crisis: A timeline of events so far
According to the Directeur général des élections du Québec, there are no rules against someone being 
compensated for voting for a candidate in a leadership race (though, it's not allowed in general elections or 
byelections).
Premier François Legault and Rodriguez have both since said they'd be in favour of having the law changed if it's 
considered legal to buy votes.
Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez speaks to media while surrounded by the Liberal caucus in Montreal on 
Friday, Nov. 21, 2025. The caucus was held in the aftermath of vote-buying allegations and other turmoil in the 
party that continued throughout the week.
Nov. 21: Rodriguez says the party might take the Journal de Montréal to court unless it shares more information 
about the alleged vote-buying scheme, requesting the names and phone numbers from the text exchange.
"You cannot just put things like that in a paper and accuse people," he said.
Also on this day, Cogeco journalist Louis Lacroix read a letter on air from Rizqy's lawyers to those of Hinse, 
defending the firing. The lawyers declined to share a copy of the letter with The Gazette but confirmed one had 
been sent. According to Lacroix, the letter said the decision was made after reviews of many "concerning situations" 
related to the performance of Hinse's duties, conduct and obligations as chief of staff.
"Your client's dismissal was imposed due to significant ethical breaches, particularly with regard to compliance with 
the standards of the National Assembly of Quebec, the internal procedures and expectations related to her 
position," the letter said. "In addition, there were repeated acts of insubordination, including non-compliance with 
clear instructions issued by our client. Notably, your client refused to follow our client's directive to consult with the 
ethics commissioner."
Lacroix said the letter noted Rizqy couldn't say Hinse had been fired without motive "because that would be a false 
and erroneous declaration."
Later that day, Hinse claimed $500,000 in moral and punitive damages against Rizqy. She claims it was Rizqy who 
acted in bad faith and "completely resisted" attempts to go to the National Assembly's ethics commissioner to clear 
up operational issues, including what spending should be covered by public funds and what should be considered 
partisan activities paid for by the party.
The claim says Rizqy resisted because she didn't have confidence in the ethics commissioner to "open such a 
dialogue," based on her personal experience with the commissioner and that of her husband, Jacques-Cartier MNA 
Greg Kelley.
"A conflict of personalities developed between the two, fed by Mme. Rizqy's mood swings," the claim states.
When Hinse presented a document outlining an operational plan for such spending, Rizqy refused to touch it. It was 
shortly after that incident that she received the letter from Rizqy informing her she was fired.
The claim also notes that if Rizqy apologizes in writing and admits the "existence of a grave error" on her part in 
firing Hinse, she would drop the case.
Nov. 23: Rizqy breaks her silence, insisting that she acted within her right and pointing out that she's not allowed to 
discuss human resources matters publicly.
That night, Rodriguez appears on Radio-Canada talk show Tout le monde en parle, saying Rizqy had spoken to 
him about some kind of political "fling flang" (or funny business) linked to Ottawa.
Liberal MP Fayçal El-Khoury speaks to reporters before a meeting of the Liberal caucus on Parliament Hill in 
Ottawa in this October 2024 file photo.
Page 4 of 5
Quebec Liberal Party crisis: A timeline of events so far
Nov. 26: In the wake of the La Presse report tying the tension within the party back to the REM inauguration, 
Rodriguez acknowledges that El-Khoury raised funds for his leadership race. He noted El-Khoury's activities were 
legal because he had a campaign certificate permitting him to raise funds.
"He raised money like lots of people," Rodriguez said.
El-Khoury did not respond to The Gazette's request for comment Wednesday and refused to answer questions from 
reporters outside the federal Liberal caucus in Ottawa, but told La Presse his comments may have been 
"ambiguous" last week. He said he assumed he was being asked if he helped acquire membership cards for 
Rodriguez, which he said he didn't. That's why he said he was never involved in the campaign.
He added that his exchange with Rizqy at the REM inauguration was about her decision not to seek re-election next 
year and the fact that she had been an inspiration to his daughter, who is thinking of entering politics.
Later in the day, Quebec's Unité permanente anticorruption (UPAC) confirms it is verifying "allegations of 
reprehensible acts targeting the Liberal Party of Quebec" but has not yet launched a formal investigation. 
"Following the analysis of this information, we will be able to take a decision to know if we need to go further with 
the investigation or not."
Rodriguez says he will fully co-operate with UPAC. "If someone, somewhere, committed an illegal act or contrary to 
our ethics, the truth must come out and we will fully co-operate. If shortcomings are revealed, I will act. There is no 
place for this in the Liberal Party of Quebec. Tolerance zero. Period," he writes in a social media post.

The turmoil in the party comes ahead of the 2026 provincial election, when Rodriguez plans to run for a seat in the 
National Assembly.
Here's a timeline of events thus far:
June 14: Quebec Liberals elect Rodriguez( https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec-liberals-choose-pablo-
rodriguez-as-new-leader ), former federal Liberal MP from Montreal,( https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec-
liberals-choose-pablo-rodriguez-as-new-leader ) as the new leader of the party. He won with 52.3 per cent of the 
vote, narrowly overtaking contender Charles Milliard, who received 47.7 per cent of the vote.
June 19: Rodriguez selects Rizqy( https://montrealgazette.com/news/pablo-rodriguez-picks-marwah-rizqy-to-lead-
liberals-in-legislature ) - known for her ability to hold the Coalition Avenir Québec government's feet to the fire - to 
lead the party in the National Assembly since he's not an MNA.
Liberal MP Fayçal El-Khoury, highlighted left, and Liberal MNA Marwah Rizqy among a group of politicians posing 
for photos during an inauguration event for the the Deux-Montagnes branch of the REM in Deux-Montagnes on 
Nov. 14, 2025.
Page 2 of 5
Quebec Liberal Party crisis: A timeline of events so far
Nov. 14: Federal, provincial and local politicians attend a ceremony for the opening of the REM's long-awaited 
Deux-Montagnes branch. A discussion between Rizqy and Liberal MP Fayçal El-Khoury may have sparked the 
drama that unfolded days later, according to La Presse. El-Khoury denied having a discussion with Rizqy about 
Rodriguez's leadership race and insisted he had no connection to the campaign, but La Presse later discovered he 
had raised funds for Rodriguez.
Nov. 17: Rizqy fires her chief of staff in a short email to members of the Liberal caucus, taking the party by surprise.
"We would like to inform you that Mme. Geneviève Hinse ... is no longer employed as chief of staff of the leader of 
the official opposition as of now," the email read.
La Presse reported the dismissal was related to the alleged use of the party's National Assembly budget to pay for 
partisan activities like Rodriguez's recent tour of the regions, which isn't permitted.
Nov. 18: Rodriguez ousts Rizqy as parliamentary leader over the firing of Hinse, claiming he wasn't consulted or 
given an explanation. Hinse was Rodriguez's chief of staff when he was a federal politician and decided to follow 
him into Quebec politics.
Rodriguez's decision to oust Rizqy, "while difficult, was necessary to ensure the cohesion and the good functioning 
of the Liberal caucus at the National Assembly," the party said in a statement.
Rizqy was replaced as parliamentary leader by Pontiac MNA André Fortin. She remains a Liberal but is suspended 
from the caucus until further notice.
Geneviève Hinse in 2019.
Nov. 19: Hinse fires back with a legal letter giving Rizqy 24 hours to admit the "absence of justified motive" for the 
firing, warning that she may sue her if she refuses.
In the letter, Rizqy is accused of violating the customs of the party by firing Hinse because such decisions are 
supposed to be made by the party leader.
Before the letter came out, Hinse defended herself in a statement: "I am obviously hurt by this situation, especially 
since I know nothing justifies my firing."
The same day, the Journal de Montréal reported( https://www.journaldemontreal.com/2025/11/19/il-faut-encore-
payer-pour-que-le-monde-vote-pablo-des-textos-troublants-derriere-la-crise-au-plq ) Élections Québec was looking 
into text messages insinuating Liberal Party members were paid to vote Rodriguez in as leader.
One exchange reads:
"So, everyone's going to get paid (this) week?"
"Yes. And don't forget, we're only returning the membership cards on May 8 in case something goes wrong. All 
that's left is the voting process and they get a brownie for voting."
A $100 bill is sometimes referred to as a "brownie" in slang.
Cogeco political analyst Jonathan Trudeau claimed the exchanges were between Alice Abou-Khalil, CAQ MNA for 
Fabre, and Sona Lakhoyan Olivier, Liberal MNA for Chomedey, both of whom denied the accusations.
Rodriguez called in an external auditor to investigate the Journal report, saying he had no knowledge of the 
allegations.
"We have nothing to hide," he said at the time. "I have nothing to hide. Nobody has anything to hide."
Page 3 of 5
Quebec Liberal Party crisis: A timeline of events so far
According to the Directeur général des élections du Québec, there are no rules against someone being 
compensated for voting for a candidate in a leadership race (though, it's not allowed in general elections or 
byelections).
Premier François Legault and Rodriguez have both since said they'd be in favour of having the law changed if it's 
considered legal to buy votes.
Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez speaks to media while surrounded by the Liberal caucus in Montreal on 
Friday, Nov. 21, 2025. The caucus was held in the aftermath of vote-buying allegations and other turmoil in the 
party that continued throughout the week.
Nov. 21: Rodriguez says the party might take the Journal de Montréal to court unless it shares more information 
about the alleged vote-buying scheme, requesting the names and phone numbers from the text exchange.
"You cannot just put things like that in a paper and accuse people," he said.
Also on this day, Cogeco journalist Louis Lacroix read a letter on air from Rizqy's lawyers to those of Hinse, 
defending the firing. The lawyers declined to share a copy of the letter with The Gazette but confirmed one had 
been sent. According to Lacroix, the letter said the decision was made after reviews of many "concerning situations" 
related to the performance of Hinse's duties, conduct and obligations as chief of staff.
"Your client's dismissal was imposed due to significant ethical breaches, particularly with regard to compliance with 
the standards of the National Assembly of Quebec, the internal procedures and expectations related to her 
position," the letter said. "In addition, there were repeated acts of insubordination, including non-compliance with 
clear instructions issued by our client. Notably, your client refused to follow our client's directive to consult with the 
ethics commissioner."
Lacroix said the letter noted Rizqy couldn't say Hinse had been fired without motive "because that would be a false 
and erroneous declaration."
Later that day, Hinse claimed $500,000 in moral and punitive damages against Rizqy. She claims it was Rizqy who 
acted in bad faith and "completely resisted" attempts to go to the National Assembly's ethics commissioner to clear 
up operational issues, including what spending should be covered by public funds and what should be considered 
partisan activities paid for by the party.
The claim says Rizqy resisted because she didn't have confidence in the ethics commissioner to "open such a 
dialogue," based on her personal experience with the commissioner and that of her husband, Jacques-Cartier MNA 
Greg Kelley.
"A conflict of personalities developed between the two, fed by Mme. Rizqy's mood swings," the claim states.
When Hinse presented a document outlining an operational plan for such spending, Rizqy refused to touch it. It was 
shortly after that incident that she received the letter from Rizqy informing her she was fired.
The claim also notes that if Rizqy apologizes in writing and admits the "existence of a grave error" on her part in 
firing Hinse, she would drop the case.
Nov. 23: Rizqy breaks her silence, insisting that she acted within her right and pointing out that she's not allowed to 
discuss human resources matters publicly.
That night, Rodriguez appears on Radio-Canada talk show Tout le monde en parle, saying Rizqy had spoken to 
him about some kind of political "fling flang" (or funny business) linked to Ottawa.
Liberal MP Fayçal El-Khoury speaks to reporters before a meeting of the Liberal caucus on Parliament Hill in 
Ottawa in this October 2024 file photo.
Page 4 of 5
Quebec Liberal Party crisis: A timeline of events so far
Nov. 26: In the wake of the La Presse report tying the tension within the party back to the REM inauguration, 
Rodriguez acknowledges that El-Khoury raised funds for his leadership race. He noted El-Khoury's activities were 
legal because he had a campaign certificate permitting him to raise funds.
"He raised money like lots of people," Rodriguez said.
El-Khoury did not respond to The Gazette's request for comment Wednesday and refused to answer questions from 
reporters outside the federal Liberal caucus in Ottawa, but told La Presse his comments may have been 
"ambiguous" last week. He said he assumed he was being asked if he helped acquire membership cards for 
Rodriguez, which he said he didn't. That's why he said he was never involved in the campaign.
He added that his exchange with Rizqy at the REM inauguration was about her decision not to seek re-election next 
year and the fact that she had been an inspiration to his daughter, who is thinking of entering politics.
Later in the day, Quebec's Unité permanente anticorruption (UPAC) confirms it is verifying "allegations of 
reprehensible acts targeting the Liberal Party of Quebec" but has not yet launched a formal investigation. 
"Following the analysis of this information, we will be able to take a decision to know if we need to go further with 
the investigation or not."
Rodriguez says he will fully co-operate with UPAC. "If someone, somewhere, committed an illegal act or contrary to 
our ethics, the truth must come out and we will fully co-operate. If shortcomings are revealed, I will act. There is no 
place for this in the Liberal Party of Quebec. Tolerance zero. Period," he writes in a social media post.

title: Quebec Liberal Party crisis: Rodriguez accuses opponents of playing a 'political game'
body:
QUEBEC - The day after the province's anticorruption unit confirmed it was meeting witnesses in connection with 
allegations against the Quebec Liberal Party, leader Pablo Rodriguez said his opponents were playing a "political 
game."
Speaking to reporters Thursday morning, Québec solidaire MNA Alejandra Zaga Mendez was playing show and 
tell, holding up a copy of PLQ Inc., a 2019 book that investigated allegations into corruption in the Quebec Liberal 
Party under former premier Jean Charest.
"When we see UPAC and the Liberal Party of Quebec in the same newspaper headline, it reminds us of just one 
thing," she said. "Every day, we wake up and we learn of a new scandal in the Liberal Party of Quebec."
Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon accused the Liberal party of a "culture of corruption," which he 
said stemmed from a loyalty to the "Canadian regime."
Rodriguez rejected St-Pierre Plamondon's assertion, defining his party as the oldest in Quebec, "the party of the 
economy" and "the party of a just society."
Québec solidaire's reference to alleged corruption under Charest "is just their political game," Rodriguez said, 
"because they don't have anything else to say."
First reported in the Journal de Montréal, the Unité permanente anticorruption (UPAC) confirmed Wednesday that it 
was looking into fundraising allegations involving the Quebec Liberal Party, but stressed that it hadn't started a 
formal investigation.
The Journal reported Thursday that UPAC had met with Marwah Rizqy, who Pablo Rodriguez removed from her 
post as parliamentary leader after she fired Geneviève Hinse, her chief of staff. Rodriguez maintained Thursday 
that he still didn't know why Rizqy had removed Hinse.
If UPAC proceeds with an investigation, "we're going to collaborate," he promised. "We have nothing to hide."
A Pallas Data poll published by L'actualité on Wednesday showed only 13 per cent of Quebecers have a favourable 
impression of Rodriguez - placing him behind Plamondon, Québec solidaire's Ruba Ghazal and Quebec 
Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime - and tying him with Premier François Legault.
Page 2 of 2
Quebec Liberal Party crisis: Rodriguez accuses opponents of playing a 'political game'
Rodriguez is the only leader less popular than his party, the poll said, reporting that 25 per cent of Quebecers 
intend to vote for the Liberals.
This report will be updated.
