title: Quebec Liberal Party welcomes new leader Charles Milliard takes over after predecessor's resignation last
body:
About 600 people welcomed Charles Milliard as the new head of the Quebec Liberal Party in Trois-Rivières on 
Sunday, days after he was acclaimed in a leadership race that no one else joined.
Milliard, who entered the room at the Delta Hotel in the city about halfway between Montreal and Quebec City on 
the north shore of the St. Lawrence River, takes over a party recently shaken by the December resignation of 
former leader Pablo Rodriguez.
"We have gone through a difficult period, but today we look forward," Milliard said. "Under my leadership, integrity, 
transparency, and accountability will be the watchwords because the party I want to lead must be above reproach, 
and trust is earned, not requested."
Milliard outlined his five key priorities for a potential Quebec Liberal government: strengthening the economy, 
improving public services, supporting Quebec's regions outside major urban centres, promoting culture and 
addressing access to housing.
He highlighted flagship policies a Liberal government would pursue, including a telemedicine platform available 
seven days a week, a goal of 100,000 new housing starts per year and tax relief for small- and medium-sized 
businesses.
"I am nationalist, I am regionalist, I am federalist, and no, that is not contradictory," Milliard told the audience.
Former Quebec Liberal premiers Daniel Johnson and Philippe Couillard, along with past interim leaders, attended 
the event to welcome the new generation of party leadership. Rodriguez stepped down amid a crisis involving 
allegations of vote-buying and reimbursed donations during the leadership race he'd won in June. 
Originally from Lévis, Que., and former president of the Quebec Federation of Chambers of Commerce, Milliard 
faces the challenge of introducing himself to Quebec voters, having never held elected office at the provincial or 
federal level.
At Sunday's event, he promised to hold broad consultations on education if elected this fall, aiming to reform the 
system to better engage both students and teachers. "Our current system has reached its limit - the bell has rung," 
he said.
Page 2 of 3
Quebec Liberal Party welcomes new leader Charles Milliard takes over after predecessor's resignation last 
year
A pharmacist by training, Milliard said mental health would be a top priority, alongside expanding home-care 
services. He said a Liberal government would invest so seniors can stay as long as possible in their homes and 
regions, adding that uprooting seniors is "a scourge on society." 
Milliard further pledged to empower local governments, calling himself "the prime minister of decentralization in 
Quebec."
Later, in his first news conference as leader, Milliard said the coming week would be important for the party, 
including decisions at the first caucus meeting - notably on the future of MNA Marwah Rizqy. 
Rizqy had been parliamentary leader but was expelled from caucus last year after firing her chief of staff, 
Geneviève Hinse, without consulting then-leader Rodriguez, a move Rodriguez called a breach of trust that "did a 
lot of damage" to the party and sparked an internal crisis. 
Rizqy maintains she acted to preserve her integrity. Hinse has since filed a $500,000 lawsuit against Rizqy over her 
dismissal.
"This is one of the subjects we will address in the first caucus ... I need to discuss it with the team. I am not rushing 
things," said Milliard.
The Canadian Press

title: Quebec Liberals close ranks as UPAC opens criminal probe into vote-buying allegations
body:
QUEBEC - The province's anti-corruption unit (UPAC) has opened a formal criminal investigation into fundraising 
allegations involving the Quebec Liberal Party.
But Quebec's Liberal caucus says it stands behind party leader Pablo Rodriguez, despite calls from at least one 
party member that he step aside for the duration of the investigation or even permanently. Rodriguez said he's 
staying on and has nothing to hide.
"We confirm that our verifications are finished and that we are officially opening an investigation," UPAC 
spokesperson Mathieu Galarneau said in a statement.
"We will issue no further comment in order to protect as much as possible our actions and to respect the rights of 
the persons involved."
On Nov. 26, the police force said( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/upac-quebec-liberals-vote-
buying-allegations ) that it was looking into allegations of what it called certain "reprehensible acts" targeting the 
Liberal party.
UPAC did not provide details on what is motivating the investigation, but there have been allegations on the 
possible use of National Assembly funds for partisan reasons in the Pablo Rodriguez leadership race.
Rodriguez, who is now leader of the Liberals( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-
rodriguez-resignation-petition ), rapidly issued a statement on social media.
"It's important to get to the bottom of things," Rodriguez said. "The Liberal Party of Quebec and all of its members 
will fully co-operate (with UPAC). If someone has committed an illegal act, the truth will come out and, as leader, I 
will act without hesitation."
Later, meeting reporters at the legislature, Rodriguez emphasized that UPAC was not specific on what it is 
investigating.
"For us it's important to get the truth and all the truth," Rodriguez told the media. "If people did anything wrong, then 
they'll pay the price, they'll suffer the consequences."
Page 2 of 3
Quebec Liberals close ranks as UPAC opens criminal probe into vote-buying allegations
He said he saw no reason to step aside pending the results of the investigation.
"It's not about me," Rodriguez said. "I'm there, I'm duly voted on by the members. There's nothing that I have done 
wrong. I can assure them (at UPAC) and all Quebecers that we'll get to the bottom of this."
UPAC revealed it was having conversations with individuals the day La Presse reported news of a discussion that 
had taken place between then Liberal parliamentary leader Marwah Rizqy and federal MP Fayçal El-Khoury on 
Nov. 14 at the launch of the Deux-Montagnes REM extension.
El-Khoury had initially insisted he had no involvement in the Rodriguez campaign, but it was revealed later he had, 
in fact, raised money for it. The exchange caught the eye of Quebec's chief electoral office, various media have 
reported.
La Presse has since revealed that UPAC, the Unité permanente anticorruption, met with Rizqy after Rodriguez 
excluded her from the Liberal caucus in connection with her decision to fire her chief of staff, Geneviève Hinse, a 
close associate of Rodriguez.
Last week, Rodriguez permanently expelled Rizqy from the Liberal caucus( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/rodriguez-expells-rizqy-from-quebec-liberal-caucus-as-crisis-
grows ). He said she has refused to explain the firing beyond her initial statement to him about some kind of "fling 
flang" (fishy business) in the party's use of public money for partisan reasons.
The story took on a further air of mystery when the Journal de Montréal last month published text messages( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/rizqy-doubles-down-on-chief-of-staffs-firing-as-quebec-
liberals-set-to-meet-in-montreal ) between two unnamed people suggesting Liberal members had been paid $100 
(referred to as a "brownie" in the messages) for voting in favour of Rodriguez in the leadership race last spring.
The practice is not illegal under Quebec's electoral laws, but legislation tabled last week( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-brownie-bill-vote-buying-ban-leadership-races ) 
designed to plug that loophole is expected to be voted into law on Thursday, with support from all parties.
News of the UPAC investigation, however, sent another shock wave through the Liberal ranks. Most Liberal MNAs 
entered an emergency party caucus meeting at the legislature Wednesday without talking to reporters. One did.
"We had a leadership race, we will respect this leadership race," said Mille-Îles Liberal MNA Virginie Dufour. "Our 
leader is Pablo Rodriguez. I repeat, we want to get to the bottom of things. If people did illegal things, we want to 
know why."
Later, one person who is unhappy with Rodriguez emerged from the shadows to call for his head or for him to at 
least step aside for the duration of the UPAC investigation.
"I ask the party to immediately suspend Mr. Rodriguez for the duration of the investigation," Alexandre Tremblay-
Michaud, a lawyer and the former president of the Outremont Liberal riding association, told The Gazette.
"If Mr. Rodriguez has the interests of the party at heart, he should resign.
Until now, Tremblay-Michaud had been discreet, but he has been linked to a group of Liberals who wanted to 
organize a party general council in January where Rodriguez would face a confidence vote.
On their way out of the caucus, however, Liberals closed ranks around the leader, but some still appeared shaken 
by the news.
"We had a good caucus, good conversations," Liberal whip Marc Tanguay told reporters. "What is happening is 
serious. We are unanimous behind our leader Pablo Rodriguez. We will get through this. We have a job to do."
"We're behind our leader, we're behind our leader," said Mont-Royal-Outremont MNA Michelle Setlakwe.
Page 3 of 3
Quebec Liberals close ranks as UPAC opens criminal probe into vote-buying allegations
"I have full confidence in Mr. Rodriguez," said Pontiac MNA André Fortin. "I have full confidence in his integrity."
"Are we worried? Yes," said Nelligan MNA Monsef Derraji. "We are all very worried. But today, as legislators, we 
are not going to start putting anyone on trial. We must wait for the results (of the investigations) before drawing 
conclusions.
"Personally, I am fed up with what I am seeing. I am very worried."

title: Quebec Liberals lose two caucus members in a week as crisis continues
body:
QUÉBEC - The Quebec Liberals have lost two members of their caucus within a week and are facing multiple 
investigations as a crisis within the party shows no sign of abating.
The Liberals have been dogged by controversy for nearly three weeks, with one recent poll showing the party and 
its leader, former federal cabinet minister Pablo Rodriguez, have taken a substantial hit in public opinion. 
"Everything that's coming out now, it's preventing us from doing our best work," Monsef Derraji, a Liberal member of 
the legislature, told reporters in Quebec City on Friday. "I'm tired of hearing all these stories every day."
His comments came after Rodriguez announced Thursday evening that he had expelled a Montreal-area member 
of the legislature, Sona Lakhoyan Olivier, from his caucus because she is under investigation by Quebec's ethics 
commissioner. 
The office of the ethics commissioner announced it will investigate whether Lakhoyan Olivier used resources from 
her constituency office for partisan purposes during this year's Liberal leadership race, which Rodriguez won in 
June. 
"Under the circumstances, I have decided to exclude her from the Quebec Liberal Party caucus for the duration of 
this investigation," Rodriguez said on X. 
Lakhoyan Olivier wrote on social media Thursday that she has always followed the rules and will co-operate fully 
with the investigation.
At a press conference on Friday, Marc Tanguay, the party's chief whip, said it's customary for members of the 
legislature to be removed from their caucus while they're subject to ethics investigations. 
Another Liberal, Désirée McGraw, told reporters the Liberal caucus remains "100 per cent" behind Rodriguez. 
Still, that caucus now numbers just 18 people after Rodriguez expelled his former parliamentary leader, Marwah 
Rizqy, earlier this week, saying she lacked loyalty to him and to the party. 
Rizqy kicked off the crisis in the Liberal ranks when she fired her chief of staff last month. Rodriguez says she did 
not consult with him about the decision and has not explained her reasons. 

Page 2 of 3
Quebec Liberals lose two caucus members in a week as crisis continues
The Liberals are also facing allegations of possible vote-buying during the leadership race. Last month, Le Journal 
de Montréal published text messages suggesting some party members who voted for Rodriguez could have 
received cash rewards.
Montreal radio station 98.5 FM named Lakhoyan Olivier as one of the two people behind those text messages, but 
she has denied that claim and has sent a legal letter to station owner Cogeco.
The Canadian Press has not verified whether the text messages were authentic. It's also unclear whether the firing 
of Rizqy's chief of staff and the vote-buying allegations are connected. 
Rodriguez has asked a retired judge to investigate the allegations, and says anyone involved in such activity will be 
kicked out of the party. Quebec's anticorruption police have also said they are looking into the controversy. 
The crisis for the Liberals comes as the party tries to regain the support of Quebec voters, particularly 
francophones outside Montreal, ahead of next year's election. With the governing Coalition Avenir Québec polling 
badly, the Liberals are positioning themselves as the alternative to the Parti Québécois, which is promising a 
referendum on independence by 2030. 
But a recent Léger/Québecor poll showed the Liberals losing ground as the controversy drags on. The survey put 
the Liberals at 21 per cent, compared to 39 per cent for the PQ.
On Friday, the Quebec government tabled new legislation to ban vote-buying in leadership and nomination races. 
To the surprise of many lawmakers, Elections Quebec recently revealed that the province’s Elections Act does not 
prohibit people from making donations in exchange for votes in those campaigns. 
The bill, which has the support of the opposition parties, includes fines of up to $10,000 for a first offence and up to 
$30,000 for repeat offences within 10 years. 
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Dec. 5, 2025.

title: Quebec Liberals: Marc Tanguay resumes job of interim leader after Rodriguez resignation
body:
QUEBEC - The Quebec Liberals have called on a steady hand to steer the party through the difficult times ahead.
The party announced Friday that Marc Tanguay( https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/monsef-derrraji-
andre-fortin-consider-running-for-quebec-liberal-leadership ), the MNA for the riding of LaFontaine, will resume the 
job of interim leader in the wake of the resignation this week of leader Pablo Rodriguez( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/pablo-rodriguez-speaks-quebec-liberals-resignation ).
The decision was entrenched by the 18-member Liberal caucus at a virtual meeting Friday morning.
"Marc Tanguay possesses a deep knowledge of the party rank and file, coupled with 14 years of parliamentary 
experience," the Liberals said in a statement.
"I thank my colleagues in caucus and the executive committee of the party for their renewed confidence," Tanguay 
added in the same statement. "More than ever, our party, our great party, must regain its capacity for action and to 
incarnate progress."
Tanguay knows the job well. He was interim leader for two years and seven months following the resignation of 
former leader Dominique Anglade in November 2022( https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/dominque-
anglade-to-resign-as-quebec-liberal-leader-reports-say ).
In the last party leadership race, Tanguay had considered running for the permanent job but in the end chose to not 
run.
Rodriguez resigned from the party following a month-long crisis sparked by allegations of unethical fundraising in 
his leadership campaign( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-rodriguez-cash-
envelopes-campaign-allegations ).
The final straw came with the news that a Montreal businessman, identified in news reports as Emanuel Carbal( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/what-to-know-about-the-quebec-liberal-party-crisis ), a 
producer and importer of wine and port, had allegedly handed some of his employees cheques of $500 to refund 
their donations to the Rodriguez campaign.
Page 2 of 3
Quebec Liberals: Marc Tanguay resumes job of interim leader after Rodriguez resignation
Quebec's anti-corruption unit, UPAC, is looking into the practice, which is illegal under Quebec's electoral law.
The departure of Rodriguez forces the party to again find a permanent leader. The next general provincial election 
is in October 2026.
In the statement, the party says in the coming days its executive council will meet to decide the path forward. 
Although the Liberals have a way to fast-track a new leader( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-could-fast-track-a-new-leader-but-they-
probably-wont ) into office, it is believed it will hold a short leadership race to get a new leader in place by February.
So far Charles Milliard, who placed second to Rodriguez in last June's leadership vote, is in reflection about running 
again. The candidate who placed third, Karl Blackburn, has expressed interest as well.
Both are waiting to see the leadership campaign rules before deciding whether to run or not.
Saint-Laurent Liberal MNA Marwah Rizqy has ruled out running for the leadership as has the current Liberal 
parliamentary leader, André Fortin.

Title: Quebec Liberals: Marc Tanguay resumes job of interim leader after Rodriguez resignation

Body: QUEBEC - The Quebec Liberals have called on a steady hand to steer the party through the difficult times ahead.
The party announced Friday that Marc Tanguay( https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/monsef-derrraji-
andre-fortin-consider-running-for-quebec-liberal-leadership ), the MNA for the Montreal riding of LaFontaine, will 
resume the job of interim leader in the wake of the resignation this week of leader Pablo Rodriguez( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/pablo-rodriguez-speaks-quebec-liberals-resignation ).
The decision was entrenched by the 18-member Liberal caucus at a virtual meeting Friday morning.
"Marc Tanguay possesses a deep knowledge of the party rank and file, coupled with 14 years of parliamentary 
experience," the Liberals said in a statement.
"I thank my colleagues in caucus and the executive committee of the party for their renewed confidence," Tanguay 
added in the same statement. "More than ever, our party, our great party, must regain its capacity for action and to 
incarnate progress."

former leader Dominique Anglade in November 2022( https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/dominque-
anglade-to-resign-as-quebec-liberal-leader-reports-say ).

not run.

his leadership campaign( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-rodriguez-cash-
envelopes-campaign-allegations ).

title: Quebec Liberals: Rodriguez denies knowing campaign donors allegedly reimbursed with cash
body:
Campaign organizers for Quebec Liberal Party Leader Pablo Rodriguez say they are filing a complaint with the 
province's anti-corruption squad over a fundraising event where a businessman allegedly reimbursed guests for 
making campaign contributions.
The campaign said in a statement Tuesday that Rodriguez had no idea the businessman had done that, and 
confronted the latter after the Journal de Montréal( https://www.journaldemontreal.com/2025/12/16/campagne-de-
pablo-rodriguez--des-enveloppes-de-500-comptant-pour-rembourser-une-vingtaine-de-donateurs ) reported on the 
event which took place last April.
"When confronted, this person admitted they had, on their own initiative, reimbursed some of their own employees 
who did not have the means to participate in the event," campaign organizers said.
While Rodriguez did attend the event, the organizers said neither he nor his campaign had any idea that guests or 
donors had been reimbursed.
"This is unacceptable, unethical, contrary to the rules in place at the time, and was never part of the campaign's 
practices," the statement said. "It was carried out without authorization, without instructions and completely without 
the knowledge of Pablo Rodriguez and his team."
The move comes after the Journal reported that guests at the event had received envelopes with $500 cash in 
exchange for donating the same amount to Rodriguez's campaign. A spokesperson for Rodriguez told The Gazette 
he was "absolutely not" aware of any alleged transactions.
According to the Journal, the "businessman" who hosted the event decided that some guests would receive $500 - 
the maximum contribution amount allowed to a candidate during a leadership run - as repayment for having 
donated to the campaign. The Journal reported interviewing the businessman, promising not to disclose his name, 
as well as other sources who were "well aware" of the alleged payments.
While the Journal said that the businessman maintained that between two and four people received such payments, 
it reports having spoken to other sources who said that around 20 people received envelopes of cash.
The report is only the latest in a series of allegations that have plagued Rodriguez's leadership campaign for weeks.
Page 2 of 3
Quebec Liberals: Rodriguez denies knowing campaign donors allegedly reimbursed with cash
In November, the Journal reported allegations that certain Liberal Party members were given "brownies" - a slang 
term for $100 bills - in exchange for voting for Rodriguez to become Quebec Liberal leader. Quebec's anti-
corruption police are now investigating the provincial Liberals and the party itself has launched an independent 
inquiry into the allegations.
Meanwhile, two letters - one calling on Rodriguez to resign and the other supporting him as leader - have been 
circulating among Liberal ranks. The party's youth wing has confirmed it won't sign the letter in support of 
Rodriguez.
"This is not a position against or in favour of him," said Noah Faour-Charpentier, the youth wing's vice-president of 
communications. "Given the facts that are held up against Rodriguez... we see it fit to maintain a neutral position."
"We're trying to protect the institution" of the Quebec Liberal Party, Faour-Charpentier said.
Rodriguez is unlikely to survive the ongoing crisis facing his leadership, said Dónal Gill, assistant professor of 
political science at Concordia University. "We could be looking at a resignation (in) early January, probably," he 
said.
It isn't clear "what can be done to salvage what's left of any kind of momentum (the Liberals) had without Rodriguez 
going," he said.
Gill said the Liberals have long been associated with corruption and conflict-of-interest allegations "in the minds 
of many middle-ground and swing voters in Quebec," dating as far back as the premiership of Robert Bourassa.
Liberals need a clean break from the allegations now swirling around Rodriguez, Gill said, and "the only way to 
make that break is to say goodbye to the leader."
Leaders throughout history and of all stripes tend to cling on longer than benefits their party, he added. In such 
situations, "everybody knows it's over" but the leader themselves.
For the Liberals, "the laws of political gravity are dragging this party downward and it is Pablo Rodriguez that is the 
chief anchor," Gill said.
Rodriguez "won the leadership race largely on the basis of his status as a kind of a big fish in the federal game," he 
said.
During the campaign, and since, Rodriguez hadn't "exactly been putting forth new and dynamic and different kinds 
of thinking about what Quebec should be," Gill said, suggesting that replacing Rodriguez as leader could offer the 
Liberals an attempt at renewal.
To present a viable alternative to the Parti Québécois, which leads in recent polls, Gill said the Liberals now "need 
someone with a little bit more energy, a little bit more enthusiasm and vigour than Rodriguez was showing."

title: Quebec promises to punish guilty parties in SAAQclic fiasco
body:
QUEBEC - Saying she is just as angry as other Quebecers over the SAAQclic fiasco, the president of the treasury 
board Tuesday vowed to use every lever at the government's disposal to discipline and punish the guilty parties.
"Like all Quebecers, I am outraged over the revelations of the commission," France-Élaine Duranceau, who is 
responsible for the public sector, told reporters Tuesday. "Like all Quebecers, we want to punish those who are 
guilty.
"Real people, in the private sector, had they done something like this would have lost their jobs," she added. "We 
can't tolerate that in the public sector, someone who lies, someone who transmits false information or acts like the 
rules don't apply to them, gets out of it without any impact."
It was the government's first official reaction to the Gallant commission, which concluded the Société de l'assurance 
automobile du Québec lied( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/saaqclic-management-lied-to-
quebec-gallant-commission-report ) over a period of 10 years on the cost overruns and progress of its shift to the 
SAAQclic digital platform.
She was accompanied by the current Minster of Transport, Jonatan Julien, as well as Quebec's Minister for 
Cybersecurity and Digital Technology, Gilles Bélanger.
On Monday, Premier François Legault said his government was looking at all legal recourse against the 
management of the SAAQ( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/saaqclic-public-inquiry-report-
legault-caq ) allegedly involved in the scandal.
Duranceau on Tuesday added the possibility of imposing disciplinary measures on employees of the state-owned 
corporation and bureaucrats who played a role in the project.
She set out range of possible sanctions.
"We are going to be looking at what's feasible on the legal side and on the disciplinary side," Duranceau said.
"We can talk of suspension without pay, a demotion in their functions or have negative notes added to their 
(personnel) files, which would impede their advancement," Duranceau said.
Page 2 of 3
Quebec promises to punish guilty parties in SAAQclic fiasco
Julien, the minister responsible for the SAAQ, added that in his view the current CEO of the SAAQ, Serge 
Lamontagne, has "carte blanche," to act in any way he sees fit to act on the recommendations of Gallant as well.
Julien even identified some people who could be targeted by the government, including the former CEOs of the 
SAAQ, Nathalie Tremblay and Denis Marsolais (both since retired) as well as the architect of the digital platform, 
Karl Malenfant.
Malenfant in particular was criticized by commissioner Denis Gallant for his manner of controlling the project.
The SAAQ employs 5,000 people in Quebec.
On Tuesday, Duranceau announced the government is creating a follow-up committee to act on the 26 
recommendations for action included in the Gallant report.
Duranceau's announcement came a day after the SAAQ presented its "sincere apologies" for the failure of its digital 
platform launch in 2023 and has vowed to do better to regain the confidence of Quebecers.
In a statement issued late Monday following the publication of the report, the SAAQ said it will spare no effort to 
conform to the recommendations of the report.
"The SAAQ today wants to express its sincere apologies to all Quebecers for the failures that contributed to 
undermining the confidence of Quebecers in their institutions," the government agency said.
The SAAQ says it plans to fully co-operate with the government and notes it has enacted specific actions aimed at 
improving its governance.
"We have put in place new strategic controls, elaborated an action plan in contractual management, reinforced the 
framework for contract management and revised the profiles and competency requirements in the nomination of 
upper managers and the board of directors."
The apology and pledge to do better followed publication of a report Monday that revealed the SAAQ had been 
lying for years to the government about the real costs of the platform.
Instead of costing $458 million over 10 years, the final price tag will be $1.1 billion.

Title: Quebec promises to punish guilty parties in SAAQclic fiasco

Body: QUEBEC - Saying she is just as angry as other Quebecers over the SAAQclic fiasco, the president of the treasury 
board Tuesday vowed to use every lever at the government's disposal to discipline and punish the guilty parties.
"Like all Quebecers, I am outraged over the revelations of the commission," France-Élaine Duranceau, who is 
responsible for the public sector, told reporters Tuesday. "Like all Quebecers, we want to punish those who are 
guilty.
"Real people, in the private sector, had they done something like this would have lost their jobs," she added. "We 
can't tolerate that in the public sector, someone who lies, someone who transmits false information or acts like the 
rules don't apply to them, gets out of it without any impact."
It was the government's first official reaction to the Gallant commission, which concluded the Société de l'assurance 
automobile du Québec lied( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/saaqclic-management-lied-to-
quebec-gallant-commission-report ) over a period of 10 years on the cost overruns and progress of its shift to the 
SAAQclic digital platform.
She was accompanied by the current Minster of Transport, Jonatan Julien, as well as Quebec's Minister for 
Cybersecurity and Digital Technology, Gilles Bélanger.
On Monday, Premier François Legault said his government was looking at all legal recourse against the 
management of the SAAQ( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/saaqclic-public-inquiry-report-
legault-caq ) allegedly involved in the scandal.
Duranceau on Tuesday added the possibility of imposing disciplinary measures on employees of the state-owned 
corporation and bureaucrats who played a role in the project.
She set out range of possible sanctions.
"We are going to be looking at what's feasible on the legal side and on the disciplinary side," Duranceau said.
"We can talk of suspension without pay, a demotion in their functions or have negative notes added to their 
(personnel) files, which would impede their advancement," Duranceau said.

title: RECO board fired amid scandal Province steps in at real estate watchdog after outcry over iPro Realty case
body:
The Ford government has fired the entire board of directors at Ontario's real estate regulator to fix what the 
premier on Monday called "a total mess."
The Real Estate Council of Ontario (RECO) confirmed to the Star all eight members of its board "cease to hold 
office upon the appointment of the Administrator." 
Jean Lépine, who started this week as the administrator, was appointed by the province, which formally assumed 
control of the organization on Monday in the wake of the iPro scandal.
Stephen Crawford, minister of public and business service delivery and procurement, which oversees the 
regulator, gave Lépine "exclusive right to exercise all the powers and perform all the duties of the board, officers, 
and members of RECO," he wrote in a Nov. 28 letter to the regulator's board chair Katie Steinfeld and CEO Brenda 
Buchanan.
In a brief written statement on Monday, Lépine said he will spend the next several weeks "engaging across the 
sector to listen, learn, and gather insights" that will help him restore public confidence in RECO. 
A formal minister's order dated Sunday and made public Monday sets out the board's dismissal and the terms of 
Lépine's appointment, for which he will earn $2,000 per day.
The order does not explicitly say who else within RECO may soon be out of a job, but several industry insiders told 
the Star the administrator is expected to "clean house." 
Lépine's appointment followed widespread concerns about the regulator's ability to protect consumers from theft 
and fraud in the wake of the iPro Realty scandal, which saw the co-founders of one of Ontario's largest 
brokerages strike a deal with RECO to evade charges and fines after they "illegally disbursed" more than $10 
million from the company's trust accounts, which held consumer deposits.
RECO failed to immediately alert the public to what it called an unprecedented financial breach. Instead, it allowed 
iPro co-founders Rui Alves, a former RECO board member, and Fedele Colucci to continue operating their 
business for three months, transacting more than $700 million in residential real estate sales, a Star investigation 
reported. 
Page 2 of 3
RECO board fired amid scandal Province steps in at real estate watchdog after outcry over iPro Realty case
The minister's written order tasks Lépine, a communications expert with a background in government and industry 
relations, with implementing measures "to bring about systemic change within RECO and to restore public trust and 
confidence in RECO and the real estate services sector." 
By March 31, Lépine is expected to deliver to the ministry a plan for improving RECO's governance and 
organizational structures, culture, and operational policies. He must submit a progress report by June 30 and a final 
report by Dec. 31, which will be made public, according to the minister's order.
At an industry conference hosted by the Ontario Real Estate Association (OREA) on Monday, Premier Doug Ford 
spoke publicly for the first time about the regulator's failures. 
"I've been getting a lot of calls lately from real estate agents, and we're gonna fix that total mess over at RECO 
there," said Ford, speaking at the Hilton in downtown Toronto. "I've asked Minister Crawford, I've asked my chief of 
staff, I need a briefing every single day (on RECO)."
Ford said his "biggest concern" was ensuring real estate agents who lost their commission in the iPro case get paid 
the full amount owed to them. 
"My biggest concern is get that money into their pockets. If we have to cover 'em, these people work their backs off. 
They deserve the commission. We're gonna cover each and every single agent that's owed every single penny. 
And the lesson, make sure we keep an eye on this and never let it happen again."
RECO, a non-profit organization funded by its 100,000-plus members, will be paying for Lépine's services, 
Crawford's ministry order states.
"The Administrator shall be remunerated at the rate of $2,000 per diem, for up to 250 calendar days, beginning as 
of the date the Order is made, and up to a maximum remuneration rate of $500,000. The per diem rate is based on 
a 7.25 hour day and five (5) day work week."
The order notes "per diem" is the amount payable for work periods in excess of three hours daily.
 RECO is also expected to pay additional work-related costs incurred by Lépine up to a maximum of $35,000.
Lépine has spent the past two decades working in communications, government and investor relations. Most 
recently he served as "chief strategy officer" for Ontario One Call, a public safety administrative authority that 
people are legally required to call before digging for a project.

title: Reflected sunlight almost led to train collision near Victoria Bridge, safety board says
body:
Canada's Transportation Safety Board is calling on the federal government to expedite the implementation of 
automatic train control fail-safes after finding that a misinterpreted light led to a Via Rail train coming within half a 
kilometre of colliding with a freight train near the Victoria Bridge in 2024.
In its report on the incident( https://www.tsb.gc.ca/eng/rapports-reports/rail/2024/r24d0070/r24d0070.html ) released 
Tuesday, the TSB said sunlight reflecting off a signal light might have made it appear yellow instead of red, leading 
the Via train's engineers to believe they had authorization to proceed onto the track.
No one was injured in the incident and there were no passengers on the train.
"If train control systems rely only on administrative defences (rules, policies and procedures), potential signal 
recognition errors by crews will not be identified and corrected, increasing the risk of an accident," the TSB says in 
the report, noting it has been calling for some form of automated train control for years.
On Sept. 29, 2024, the Via Rail train, having just completed a trip from Toronto to Montreal, was making its way 
from Central Station to the Via maintenance facility in Point-St-Charles. The trip required backing up to the Victoria 
Bridge entrance, where it would switch onto the track heading for the facility.
At 5:32 p.m., with the late afternoon sun low in the sky in the west and the train slowly moving east, the engineer at 
the forward end of the train reported difficulty confirming the colour of a trackside light about 300 metres before the 
track switch. After asking the locomotive end to move the train closer to the signal, he believed the top light had 
changed from red to yellow, allowing the train to keep going. It continued to the switch, but he instructed the 
locomotive to stop when he realized the switch was not set for the train.
With part of one train car having passed the switch, the crew immediately made an emergency call on the radio to 
alert other traffic. A CN freight train was heading west across the bridge on the same track at about six kilometres 
per hour when, alerted by another freight train, it stopped about 500 metres from the switch.
Rail traffic control was automatically alerted to the track violation and also ensured the freight train came to a stop, 
the report said.
In its analysis, the TSB concluded that the trackside signal light showed red the entire time, and there was no 
mechanical failure that could explain a yellow indication. Instead, it said sunlight reflecting off the signal's outer lens 
Page 2 of 3
Reflected sunlight almost led to train collision near Victoria Bridge, safety board says
may have made it appear yellow. The top and bottom lights on the signal had different types of outer lenses (the 
TSB could not determine why), which may have contributed to the illusion.
"In certain conditions, a red light may appear yellowish to an observer when the incident light, reflected by the 
surface of the outer lens of the light, causes slight defocusing," the report said, citing a 2005 study published by 
Investigative Ophthalmology &; Visual Science( https://iovs.arvojournals.org/article.aspx?articleid=2181883 ).
The sun's position low in the sky (10 degrees above the horizon) and directly behind the observing engineer 
created ideal conditions for this effect, though the signal lights were equipped with extended hoods to mitigate the 
effect of sunlight reflection.
Four previous incidents since 2000 saw train crews mistakenly believe red lights were yellow because of reflected 
sunlight, the TSB said, including another one involving a Via Rail train misinterpreting the same signal light near the 
Victoria Bridge in 2006.
Much of the TSB's report focused on the hazards of relying solely on "administrative defences" - train crews 
following rules and procedures - to prevent trains from going past stop signals.
"Administrative defences, even when layered, still rely on strict crew adherence to rules and procedures and remain 
vulnerable to the inherent limitations of human cognition," it says. "These limitations underscore the need for 
additional layers of defence that do not rely solely on crew compliance to ensure the safe operation of trains."
Instead, since 2000, the TSB has called for some form of automatic train control that could bring a train to a stop 
automatically when it violates a stop signal. Such systems are used in Europe, Japan, Australia and the United 
States.
In April 2024, five months before this incident, the TSB sent a letter to Canada's transport minister strongly urging 
acceleration of physical fail-safe train controls on high-speed rail corridors and key routes.
"At the time of publication of this report, the TSB had not received a response."
Transport Canada published a notice of intent in 2022 about implementing enhanced train control technologies in 
Canada. A report published in October 2025( https://tc.canada.ca/en/corporate-services/consultations/what-we-
heard-implementing-enhanced-train-control-canada ) after a public consultation said the government will develop a 
regulatory framework to have enhanced train control implemented by 2030.
CN disagrees with findings
In an emailed statement Wednesday, CN spokesperson Ashley Michnowski said the railway company "respectfully 
disagrees with the TSB findings as many of them are not supported by a re-enactment or the facts."
"In contrast, the company provided to the TSB conclusive evidence that dispels those findings, including access to 
a video of a train operating at that location under very similar circumstances. This video corroborated that the signal 
was not affected by the sunlight," she said.
"Furthermore, while the investigation report cites a study where red signals can be affected by sunlight, it bears 
noting that the study suggests this occurs from distances of approximately 900 metres. In the matter under 
investigation, the train had been stopped at approximately 100 metres from the signal, making the study findings 
irrelevant to this investigation."
Michnowski also said CN has "rules and processes in place for when a railway employee cannot identify a signal's 
indication with certainty. While it is unclear why the investigation report did not reference these, it is important to 
note that railway employees should never act on a signal unless they are positive of its indication."

title: Registry gets update to include teachers under investigation
body:
Manitoba’s teacher registry is undergoing changes so the public is more in the know when educators are subject to 
an ongoing investigation.
The province announced the minor regulatory update Thursday, a little over a year after the initial version of the 
database came online.
“In the past, a teacher could’ve voluntarily surrendered their certificate and that voluntary surrender would not have 
been reflected on the registry,” Education Minister Tracy Schmidt said in an interview.
The changes apply to teachers and clinicians who have agreed to step away from the classroom as part of a legal 
undertaking, Schmidt said.
Despite being subject to investigations, these professionals were previously listed as being in good standing.
Temporary suspension notices will now be attached to individual profiles when an investigation is open. Once it’s 
resolved, the label will be deleted and the teacher may, depending on the result, end up on the disciplinary 
outcomes list.
The changes, which fall under the Education Administration Act, were made as of Dec. 12.
The minister noted that child protection experts identified them as a gap in the rollout of the original registry.
Schmidt’s office launched an informal advisory council on teacher professional conduct last year to collect 
feedback. Members are slated to reconvene in the spring.
Cameron Hauseman, an associate professor of educational administration at the University of Manitoba, called the 
update “a step in the right direction.”
“But… there’s a ways to go for the registry to be as robust and meaningful as it could be,” Hauseman said, noting 
there is little context provided to accompany the list of teachers and clinicians who’ve been disciplined at present.
Ex-high school teacher and football coach Kelsey McKay is simply listed as having had his licence “cancelled” on 
June 19, 2024.

Page 2 of 3
Registry gets update to include teachers under investigation
McKay is serving 20 years in prison after pleading guilty to nine counts of sexual assault and two counts of luring 
that involved nine teenage victims he coached.
A total of 85 teaching certificates were cancelled between 1990 and 2025, according to the registry.
The registry’s teacher profiles include current and former names, as well as their pay class and certificate standing. 
These profiles include limitations or conditions on an individual’s licence.
Hauseman, a former teacher, has been calling on the province to bolster these profiles so they outline a teacher’s 
training with regards to grade level and subject area.
Schmidt said she’s open to making further updates, although the province needs to balance “employment privacy.”
“We are trying to provide as much transparency, accountability and information as we can,” the minister said.

title: Regulator plans two-part inquiry into last year's cyberattack at N.S. utility
body:
HALIFAX - Nova Scotia’s energy regulator is planning a two-part inquiry into last year’s cyberattack at the 
province's private power utility. 
One set of hearings will examine the technical aspects of the March 2025 cyberattack at Nova Scotia Power where 
the personal information of 280,000 customers was accessed. Company officials have said the attack was likely by 
a Russia-based actor.
The Nova Scotia Energy Board has decided that a separate investigation will look at how the utility collected and 
stored customer data and how it estimated bills after losing communication with power meters.

barrage of complaints, legal threats and a separate investigation by the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of

title: Report underscores 'significant failures' in military police investigation into Fortin
body:
A new report has found that a military police investigation that led to a Canadian Forces major-general being 
charged with sexual assault was bungled from the beginning, with failures so bad that they undermine public 
confidence.
Dany Fortin, now retired, was charged in 2021 after allegations were raised that he sexually assaulted a fellow 
military student in 1988 at the Royal Military College in Saint-Jean, Que.
But the senior officer was acquitted Dec. 5, 2022, by Quebec judge Richard Meredith, who ruled that he was not 
convinced beyond a reasonable doubt that Fortin was the assailant.
Now, the new report by the Military Police Complaints Commission (MPCC) has outlined the serious flaws in the 
investigation of Fortin by the Canadian Forces National Investigation Service (CFNIS).
MPCC chairperson Tammy Tremblay said Tuesday that her investigation into the matter revealed that the CFNIS 
investigation was "compromised by tunnel vision, exhibited signs of investigative bias, inadequate supervisory 
oversight, and a failure to uphold core investigative standards."
"These shortcomings are not mere administrative oversights; they represent significant failures that erode public 
trust in military policing," Tremblay's report said.
Fortin had consistently denied the sexual assault allegation, but the charge against the officer, who had served in 
Afghanistan and Iraq, effectively ended his career.
In March 2023, he filed a lawsuit against then-prime minister Justin Trudeau, then-defence chief Gen. Wayne 
Eyre, former defence minister Harjit Sajjan, former health minister Patty Hajdu and former defence deputy 
minister Jody Thomas, among others. Fortin's statement of claim, filed in the Superior Court of Ontario, alleged 
that shoddy police work and political interference not only damaged his reputation, but also led to a sexual assault 
charge that had no basis in fact.
Fortin received an undisclosed settlement as a result of his lawsuit and left the military in July 2023 after 38 years of 
service.
Page 2 of 3
Report underscores 'significant failures' in military police investigation into Fortin
He also filed a complaint with the MPCC about the CFNIS, alleging the investigation was flawed and influenced by 
political pressure.
Tremblay's report outlined some of the significant problems with the military police investigation. Police did not 
record key interviews with witnesses and investigation files did not include detailed summaries or transcripts of 
witness statements.
"The available evidence indicates that the CFNIS investigation suffered from inadequate supervision, insufficient 
oversight, and deficient case management particularly in the assignment of tasks and the preservation of 
documentation," the report noted.
The MPCC determined that had hindered effective case management of the investigation.
Police also failed to interview three potential witnesses, according to the MPCC report. That raised concerns about 
whether police accepted the victim's statements and missed or neglected other investigative avenues. In addition, 
the high-profile investigation was not managed as a major case within the military police system.
The MPCC is a civilian, quasijudicial oversight agency that reviews and investigates complaints concerning military 
police conduct as well as allegations of interference in military police probes. It reports its findings and makes 
recommendations directly to the military police and defence leadership.
"This report is a stunning indictment of military police professional competence," Fortin said. "It is also, by 
extension, a black eye for senior military leadership that continues to allow these be- haviours and practices by the 
NIS to go unchecked."
Fortin said the many failures by CFNIS outlined in the report "reads like a tragicomedy of errors."
"It's clear the systemic weaknesses identified in my case continue to negatively impact many NIS investigations, 
including, but not limited to alleged misconduct of a sexual nature," he added. "The lack of CAF senior leader 
responsibility and institutional accountability, in the face of a seemingly never-ending exposé of NIS shortcomings 
hurts trust in the military by the public, those still serving, and those having retired."
The MPCC report also concluded that there was no outside influence on the case. The MPCC based that on 
statements from Eyre, Thomas and police officers.
Fortin had alleged the Liberal government had removed him from his role of leading the federal vaccine task force 
in 2021 without any due process. He also complained to the MPCC that the CFNIS investigation was motivated "in 
part by significant political and public pressure" to ensure that the Canadian Forces and the military were seen to 
be taking action on sexual misconduct cases.
Documents presented during Fortin's trial indicated that Eyre had written about a discussion with the deputy 
minister who talked about the "political pressure" surrounding the case and that "the government could fall."

title: Restoring confidence will be tough
body:
If you're still reeling from revelations of police corruption in Toronto, don't look to the province for reassurance 
anytime soon.
Seven Toronto cops were arrested last week amid allegations that confidential databases were accessed by police 
- on the job and allegedly on the take - to enable organized crime attacks. Three Peel Regional Police officers have 
also been suspended as York police continue investigating.
Public confidence has been rattled. So what's the provincial response so far?
Premier Doug Ford - cheerleader-in-chief for the province's police forces - has been uncharacteristically subdued. 
There are "bad apples" in every batch, he mused in the aftermath, but Ford still reflexively champions our cops as 
tops.
Solicitor General Michael Kerzner keeps piping up about police failures to rein in street protests. But he's been 
mum on police failures to curb corruption in their own backyard.
Sensing the silence, Ontario's inspector general of policing, Ryan Teschner, has now stepped up to announce he 
wants a fresh look at police procedures all across the province. Coming so soon after last week's bombshell - 
including criminal allegations of bribery, identity theft, conspiracy to commit murder and drug trafficking - his rapid 
response is commendable, but its impact is debatable.
The review will be outsourced to an outsider yet to be appointed, who will then report back at a time to be 
determined. The mission and the mandate appear to be all about policy and process, not crime and punishment.
That's good as far as it goes. But it doesn't go far enough to look at how corruption has allegedly crept into two of 
the biggest police forces in the province, with potential coverups that allowed criminality to continue unpunished 
until now.
The proposed provincial inspection sounds more like an audit - perhaps helpful for lessons learned in retrospect, 
rather than rooting out corruption in real time. While the findings will be made public, it's not a public inquiry with 
open hearings and a focused mandate, of the kind that other jurisdictions have convened in the past.
Page 2 of 3
Restoring confidence will be tough
Instead, it's a systematic review of policing - first requested by Toronto's chief - now extended across all 44 
municipal forces, plus the sprawling Ontario Provincial Police. It will look at officer supervision, screening and 
vetting, access to police databases, substance abuse and fitness for duty.
That's an ambitious mandate, perhaps over-ambitious in its geographic scope. That said, the inspector general 
noted Monday that, "although this issue originated with the Toronto Police Service, we have since learned that 
other organizations may be impacted."
Put another way, the rot isn't just regional but perhaps provincial, prone to spreading from one police force to 
another. Teschner reminded reporters that "Organized crime is insidious." So too, the response must be fastidious, 
for corruption is not easily eradicated.
A lawyer and former executive director of the Toronto Police Services Board, Teschner is no pushover. But he can 
only push so far.
A systematic but bureaucratic audit of systems and procedures by the inspector general's office is unlikely to 
restore public confidence when suspicions are so high. This review isn't designed to sniff out criminality, which 
remains the preserve of police investigators (presumably from outside forces) in tandem with Crown prosecutors. 
The Law Enforcement Complaints Agency will also pursue allegations, and the trials of the accused (27 in all) will 
likely take years to wend their way through our clogged court system.
What of the code of silence that envelopes police forces? To what extent did fellow officers in the Toronto and Peel 
police services collude or conceal?
In politics as in police work, the coverup is always worse than the crime - and harder to root out. The inspector 
general's review cannot just reinvent the wheel when it comes to securing databases and detecting intrusions - who 
did (or looked up) what information.
After all, cops already know that corruption and conspiracy and weaponizing police databases are all illegal. What 
about the gaps in police leadership, vision and vigilance that allowed corruption to fester unchallenged or 
unnoticed?
This review will be looking for answers over the long term - possibly a very long time. That will do little to address 
the public's more pressing concerns and fears. It may be a good first step. But it is by no means the last word in 
restoring the public's faith in the integrity of the system.

title: Rodriguez accuses opponents of playing a 'political game' amid corruption suggestions
body:
The day after the province's anticorruption unit confirmed it was meeting witnesses in connection with allegations 
against the Quebec Liberal Party, Leader Pablo Rodriguez accused his opponents of playing a "political game."
Earlier Thursday, Québec solidaire MNA Alejandra Zaga Mendez showed reporters a copy of PLQ Inc., a 2019 
book that investigated allegations of corruption in the Quebec Liberal Party under former premier Jean Charest.
"Every day, we wake up and we learn of a new scandal in the Liberal Party of Quebec," she said. "When we see 
UPAC (Unité permanente anticorruption) and the Liberal Party of Quebec in the same newspaper headline, it 
reminds us of just one thing."
Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon accused the Liberal party of a "culture of corruption," which he 
said stemmed from a loyalty to the "Canadian regime."
Rodriguez rejected St-Pierre Plamondon's assertion, defining his party as the oldest in Quebec, "the party of the 
economy" and "the party of a just society."
Québec solidaire's reference to alleged corruption under Charest "is just their political game," Rodriguez said, 
"because they don't have anything else to say."
UPAC confirmed Wednesday that it was looking into fundraising allegations involving the Quebec Liberal Party, but 
stressed it hadn't started a formal investigation.
Le Journal de Montréal reported Thursday that UPAC had met with Marwah Rizqy, who was removed from her post 
as parliamentary leader by Rodriguez last week after she fired her chief of staff, Geneviève Hinse.
"It's Marwah who decided to call in UPAC from what I understand," Rodriguez said, reacting to the report. "You 
know more than me," he added. He said he still didn't know why Rizqy removed Hinse from her role.
If UPAC proceeds with an investigation, "we're going to collaborate," he promised. "We have nothing to hide." In an 
email to The Gazette, UPAC said privacy rules prevent it from confirming whether officers had met with Rizqy.
Page 2 of 3
Rodriguez accuses opponents of playing a 'political game' amid corruption suggestions
The Liberal scandal has been centre stage for over a week, and now includes the conflict between Rizqy and 
Hinse, the involvement of anticorruption police, and allegations that some party members received $100 each to 
support Rodriguez in his successful run for leader.
Regardless of whether allegations against the Liberals prove true, "these things stick," said McGill University 
political scientist Daniel Béland.
Corruption allegations have "tainted" the Quebec Liberals' image "for a long time," he said, in part because of the 
Charbonneau Commission, which investigated corruption in the construction industry.
The Parti Québécois "has been saying for a long time that the Liberals are corrupt," Béland said, so "it makes 
sense for the PQ to return to this" now.
"For them, it's a great opportunity," he said. "Whether it's true or false, it's almost irrelevant at this stage."
On Wednesday, Justice Minister Simon Jolin-Barrette also weighed in, calling Rodriguez's party "the same old 
Liberal party" rife with "the same illegal practices, the same ethically questionable practices."
A Pallas Data poll published by L'actualité on Wednesday showed only 13 per cent of Quebecers have a favourable 
impression of Rodriguez - placing him behind St-Pierre Plamondon, Québec solidaire's Ruba Ghazal and Quebec 
Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime, and tying him with Premier François Legault.
"The polling numbers are really bad," Béland said. While Legault's score might be expected given his seven years 
in power, 13 per cent favourability for the new leader of the biggest opposition party is abysmal, he said.
"The question for the (Liberals) is whether there's still time to change leaders before the next provincial election," 
Béland said. "Or you stick with Pablo Rodriguez knowing that he's not well perceived by the population."
Rodriguez is the only Quebec leader less popular than his party, the Pallas Data poll showed. According to the poll, 
25 per cent of Quebecers intend to vote for the Liberals.

title: Rodriguez says it's a 'political game' to accuse Quebec Liberals of a 'culture of corruption'
body:
QUEBEC - The day after the province's anticorruption unit confirmed it was meeting witnesses( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/upac-quebec-liberals-vote-buying-allegations ) in connection 
with allegations against the Quebec Liberal Party, leader Pablo Rodriguez accused his opponents of playing a 
"political game."
Earlier Thursday, Québec solidaire MNA Alejandra Zaga Mendez had been playing show and tell, holding up to 
reporters a copy of PLQ Inc., a 2019 book that investigated allegations of corruption in the Quebec Liberal Party 
under former premier Jean Charest.
"Every day, we wake up and we learn of a new scandal in the Liberal Party of Quebec," she said. "When we see 
UPAC and the Liberal Party of Quebec in the same newspaper headline, it reminds us of just one thing."
Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon accused the Liberal party of a "culture of corruption," which he 
said stemmed from a loyalty to the "Canadian regime."
Rodriguez rejected St-Pierre Plamondon's assertion, defining his party as the oldest in Quebec, "the party of the 
economy" and "the party of a just society."
Québec solidaire's reference to alleged corruption under Charest "is just their political game," Rodriguez said, 
"because they don't have anything else to say."
First reported in the Journal de Montréal, the Unité permanente anticorruption (UPAC) confirmed Wednesday that it 
was looking into fundraising allegations involving the Quebec Liberal Party, but stressed that it hadn't started a 
formal investigation.
The Journal reported Thursday that UPAC had met with Marwah Rizqy, who Pablo Rodriguez removed from her 
post as parliamentary leader after she fired Geneviève Hinse, her chief of staff.
"It's Marwah who decided to call in UPAC from what I understand," Rodriguez said, reacting to the report. "You 
know more than me," he added. He said he still didn't know why Rizqy had removed Hinse from her role.
If UPAC proceeds with an investigation, "we're going to collaborate," he promised. "We have nothing to hide."
Page 2 of 3
Rodriguez says it's a 'political game' to accuse Quebec Liberals of a 'culture of corruption'
In an email to The Gazette, UPAC said that privacy rules prevented it from confirming whether officers had met with 
Rizqy.
The Liberals' scandal has now been centre stage for over a week, and now includes the conflict between Rizqy 
and Hinse, the involvement of anticorruption police and allegations that some party members received $100 each to 
support Rodriguez in his successful run for leader.
Regardless of whether allegations against the Liberals prove true, "these things stick," said McGill University 
political scientist Daniel Béland.
Corruption allegations have "tainted" the Quebec Liberals' image "for a long time," he said, in part because of the 
Charbonneau commission, which investigated corruption in the construction industry.
The Parti Québécois "has been saying for a long time that the Liberals are corrupt," he said, so "it makes sense for 
the PQ to return to this" now.
"For them it's a great opportunity," he said. "Whether it's true or false, it's almost irrelevant at this stage."
On Wednesday, Justice Minister Simon Jolin-Barrette had also weighed in, calling Rodriguez's party "the same old 
Liberal party," rife with "the same illegal practices, the same ethically questionable practices."
A Pallas Data poll published by L'actualité on Wednesday showed only 13 per cent of Quebecers have a favourable 
impression of Rodriguez - placing him behind Plamondon, Québec solidaire's Ruba Ghazal and Quebec 
Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime - and tying him with Premier François Legault.
"The polling numbers are really bad," Béland said. While Legault's score might be expected given his eight years in 
power, 13 per cent favourability for the new leader of the biggest opposition party is abysmal, he said.
"The question for the (Liberals) is whether there's still time to change leaders before the next provincial election," 
Béland said. "Or you stick with Pablo Rodriguez knowing that he's not well perceived by the population."
Rodriguez is the only leader less popular than his party, the Pallas Data poll said, reporting that 25 per cent of 
Quebecers intend to vote for the Liberals.

title: Rodriguez's departure should boost outlook for Quebec Liberals
body:
Two weeks ago, a National Post headline read: Liberal scandals a gift to the PQ. That was the day after Pablo 
Rodriguez announced he was stepping down as Liberal leader, following weeks of allegations about supposed 
irregularities with the leadership campaign he won six months ago.
I suspect, however, that this turn of events could end up instead as "a Christmas gift to the Liberals" - and 
federalists - 10 months before the Quebec election.
Toward the end of its second term, the governing Coalition Avenir Québec seems a spent force. Polls show a 
majority of Quebecers, desperate for an alternative, have been favouring the Parti Québécois led by Paul St-Pierre 
Plamondon, despite opposing the party's raison d'être of separation from Canada and their promise to hold another 
referendum.
Under Rodriguez, the Liberals weren't becoming that default option and struggled to appeal to francophone voters 
in the regions. Although the PQ's lead over the Liberals had narrowed, overall percentages are misleading, largely 
because of the Liberals' disproportionate non-francophone vote concentrated in the Montreal region, which 
comprises only 33 of 125 ridings.
The Rodriguez departure opens the door to the likely coronation of the leadership contender who finished a close 
second, Charles Milliard.
After watching the debates and listening to interviews with candidates, it seemed obvious to me that Milliard stood 
above the rest in possessing all the attributes for a potential saviour of the party. The choice of Rodriguez left me 
scratching my head. Despite his inspiring personal story as a political refugee coming to this country, rising to the 
highest echelons of political power in Ottawa, I believe that Rodriguez wasn't the right fit here and would not have 
won the provincial election.
Milliard was born in Lévis and has ties in the Mauricie and Bas-St-Laurent regions. He lived in Montreal, studied in 
Quebec City, and now resides in the Eastern Townships. The two issues top of mind for Quebecers are health care 
and the economy; Milliard's professional career straddles both sectors. He is a pharmacist by profession, has an 
MBA and headed up the Fédération des chambres de commerce du Québec with deep roots in regional economic 
development.
Coming from the outside, with strong business credentials, like Prime Minister Mark Carney, he isn't laden with 
political baggage that weighed down Rodriguez.
Page 2 of 3
Rodriguez's departure should boost outlook for Quebec Liberals
Karl Blackburn, who finished third, announced he won't be running, which at least avoids the possibility of divisions 
developing in the party between those two camps.
Although Milliard looks it, he had better be squeaky clean. If he has any skeletons in his closet, you can be sure that 
a Journal de Montréal archeologist will eventually dig them up.
Some suggest Milliard is relatively unknown and didn't spark greater public awareness during the leadership race. 
But it was like that for the PQ leader as well. Milliard is younger than St-Pierre Plamondon and exudes energy and 
charisma. His arrival on the daily political scene and the bright lights of an eventual election campaign will amplify 
his stature. He has that potential "it factor." Whether he has the toughness to endure the Quebec media maelstrom 
remains to be seen.
As for anglophones who have propped up the Liberals for decades, how will he walk that line between capturing the 
francophone soft-nationalist vote without throwing the community under the bus in this Quebec zero-sum game of 
language politics?
To date, he has been adept at saying that he wants to unify all Quebecers around the issues that matter most - the 
economy, health care and educationstressing that protecting French does not require the diminution of the 
anglophone community. Hopefully he'll remain true to those values.
In Quebec politics, the cult of leadership is very important. Virtually every premier in our history has been a native 
Quebecer. With Milliard as the Liberal leader, I believe this preordained PQ victory next October would be much 
less likely than it was a few weeks ago. Robert Libman is an architect and planning consultant who has served as 
Equality Party leader and MNA, mayor of Côte-St-Luc and a member of the Montreal executive committee.

title: Russian dissidents call on Ottawa to resettle their peers facing deportation in U.S.
body:
OTTAWA - Prominent Russian democracy activists are urging Ottawa to resettle dozens of their peers who tried to 
claim asylum in the U.S. and now face deportation and imprisonment in Russia.
The activists told The Canadian Press 30 Russian nationals being held by U.S. Immigration and Customs 
Enforcement would face extremely grave consequences if they're sent back. They said as many as one thousand 
pro-democracy Russians in the U.S. are facing the prospect of deportation.
"We wanted to build alliances here in Canada, because solidarity is our biggest weapon against dictators," said 
Natalia Arno, founder of the Free Russia Foundation. "Canada, with its voice, is a very, very relevant country for 
us."
Arno visited Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal this past week to meet with Canadian officials alongside Ilya Yashin, an 
opposition politician.
Arno and Yashin said they've advised federal officials on how Canada's embassy in Moscow could be used to 
support the democracy movement. They said the most effective way to support democracy in Russia is to stand up 
for Ukraine.
Arno, who lives in Washington, was forced to leave Russia in 2012. Waves of Russian citizens have fled the 
country as Moscow has cracked down on civil society, particularly since Russia's 2014 invasion of Crimea, the 2015 
assassination of Boris Nemtsov — a prominent critic of Russian President Vladimir Putin — and the 2022 full-scale 
invasion of Ukraine.
Dozens of Russians who have made asylum claims through the legal process in the U.S. have been either detained 
or are trying to live with no clear status, said Yashin, a former opposition party leader and Moscow city councillor.
"We are trying to find a way to defend them, and how to save their lives," he said.
Arno and Yashin noted that the U.S. sent at least two planeloads of deportees to Russia this year; Arno estimates 
those flights carried about 100 people.

Page 2 of 4
Russian dissidents call on Ottawa to resettle their peers facing deportation in U.S.
They cited the case of Leonid Melekhin, an opposition supporter who was denied asylum in the U.S. and was 
arrested upon his return to Russia this year. There are contradicting reports about whether Melekhin was deported 
or returned voluntarily.
Melekhin now faces terrorism charges related to a poster that alluded to hanging Putin.
They also cited the case of Artyom Vovchenko, who was conscripted into the army and escaped Russia for the 
U.S., only to be deported by Washington in August. Yashin said Vovchenko has dropped out of sight and may have 
been deployed to fight in Ukraine.
Yashin argued the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump is bent on getting as many foreigners out of the 
United States as possible, and doesn't much care where they end up.
He said Canada could ask the U.S. to send its Russian nationals here.
Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada did not answer directly when asked whether the government would 
be open to creating a program to resettle Russian dissidents from the U.S.
"Canada maintains a rigorous process to assess asylum claims that balances our humanitarian objectives, legal 
obligations, and safety and security measures," wrote department spokesperson Rémi Larivière.
Global Affairs Canada confirmed its officials met with Arno and Yashin on Wednesday.
"Discussions included a broad overview of the domestic situation in Russia and their support for Ukraine in the face 
of Russia’s war of aggression," wrote department spokesperson Clémence Grevey.
Arno said those in Russia's pro-democracy movement were "the first victims of the Kremlin regime" and also "the 
first to warn the world about the criminal, dangerous, corrupt and murderous nature of Putin's regime.
"We are the ones who would like to take responsibility and change our country for the better, and we do need 
allies."
Arno said Canada should consider resettling more Ukrainians if the U.S. ends the temporary status that allows 
thousands of them to live there.
She said Russia's invasion is being fought by ethnic minorities pulled from Russia's remote regions.
"It is a genocide in Ukraine, but it's simultaneously genocide inside Russia," she said.
On Wednesday, Arno and Yashin took part in the recurring protest outside the Russian embassy in Ottawa staged 
by supporters of Ukraine.
Their visit came amid a public rift between Russian dissidents and Ukrainian activists. Many Ukrainians have 
questioned why Russian civilians haven't staged mass protests and note that some pro-democracy Russians have 
played down the idea that Ukraine is a distinct nation.
Arno and Yashin said Ukraine's struggle for peace and sovereignty is the key to the future of the entire continent, 
Russia included.
"Putin's ambition is to change the world order, and he is going to ruin the European security system, he's going to 
ruin all the world order," Yashin said.
"If Putin wins in Ukraine, his regime will become stronger, there will be more repression against people like me, and 
Russia just loses its future."
Yashin said nationalist bloggers reporting on Russia's war on Ukraine often criticize their fellow Russians for trying 
to avoid conscription, adding "Russian people do not support this war."
Page 3 of 4
Russian dissidents call on Ottawa to resettle their peers facing deportation in U.S.
He and Arno said Western leaders — rattled by the risk of political chaos in a country with a massive nuclear 
arsenal — are far too timid about calling for an end to Putin's regime.
In March 2023, when Mélanie Joly was foreign affairs minister, she caused a stir when she publicly mulled the 
prospect of "regime change in Russia" due to Moscow's growing isolation. The Liberals haven't repeated that 
message since.
"The Kremlin is in a very bad kind of position at the moment," Arno said. "We need to continue putting pressure on 
all the vulnerabilities."
Yashin also suggested Canada shift its language on sanctions to refer to them as targeting the Putin regime, 
instead of Russia as a country. He said Russian media outlets have spoken of "sanctions against Russia" to push a 
propaganda narrative claiming Western countries are motivated by hate against the Russian people themselves.
"It's much more clever not to create this collective guilt situation, but try to find allies in Russian society," he said.
Arno said Canada can highlight the work of Russian dissidents, including political prisoners, by speaking about their 
bravery in ways that resonate with Russians.
Yashin and Arno said Russian dissidents could help Canada tailor its sanctions and share information on how 
they've managed to evade increasing censorship online.
Arno said Russian dissidents look to Canada as an example of what their country could someday become — a 
pluralist, ethnically diverse country that defends democracy and human rights.
"We always say in discussions that Canada is the most relevant example," she said.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Dec. 6, 2025.
